We analyze the generalization performance of two-layer ReLU neural networks consisting of randomized weight matrices, focusing on their ability to estimate kernelized functions. As the size of the domain increases, previous research has shown that the generalization error of deep neural networks decreases rapidly, but this study demonstrates that such fast convergence is not universal among neural networks. Instead, we discover that the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks is largely determined by the parameters of the domain, not its dimensionality. Furthermore, we identify a phase transition near which the generalization error approaches its theoretical minimum, and our experiments reveal that this transition is linked to the spectral norm of the domain's Hessian matrix. Additionally, we examine the effect of adding dropout on the generalization performance, and our results show that, in certain cases, dropout can impose a form of regularization, mitigating poor generalization even when the domain's dimensionality is very large.

Over seven decades, the Caenorhabditis elegans has been utilized as a model to study nervous system development, behavior, and function. Due to the complete mapping of its neural connections and readily available data on its responses to various stimuli, C. elegans' nervous system appears as a suitable candidate for in silico studies. To replicate its behavioral responses using artificial networks, we developed a neural network that learns from discrete time-series data of neural activity and stimulus responses. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of our approach using reversible responses to stimuli, reversed locomotion, and body bend data. Our results indicate that the recurrent neural network is able to learn long-term memories in the nervous system and replicate its complex behaviors. Furthermore, the architecture of the neural network resembles recent proposals for artificial networks based on neuromorphic architecture of neural systems, supporting the use of these architectures in both neuromorphic engineering and neural system modeling.

The concept of a fixed point forest, also known as a rooted rotation distance forest, is the result of repeatedly applying the "fixed point" rotation motion to a collection of n! permutations, with each permutation chosen independently. Each iteration of this process is called a time step. As the size of the permutations increases, the length of the shortest path to a leaf within this forest converges towards the convergence time C(x), also known as the height of the permutation x. The convergence time can be calculated using the Garsia-Stanton trace, while the height of the permutation x is equal to the maximum height of the trees formed by the Lyndon words within the standard basis representation of the polynomial Coxeter variety elements. The research further demonstrates that the most time-consuming steps in the fixed point forest iteration are a constant time fraction distance D away from the root, where the distribution of this Lyndon words distribution plays a significant role. As a result, the research established lower and upper bounds for C(x) based on the lower and upper bounds of the height of the permutation x, using the Lyndon words distribution. Furthermore, the research specifically analyzed two subfamilies of permutations, namely the alternating permutations and the shuffles of 12, and derived the exact values of their convergence times. The research has been presented at the LiDS 2021 conference.

The primary objective of this research is to categorize strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, p) for prime values of p by determining the spectrum of the compact casimir operator, thereby facilitating the establishment of irreducible sl(2, p)-modules. As a result, we were able to fully classify the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, p) for prime values of p. Furthermore, this research is also relevant to the context of Lie superalgebras, specifically in identifying irreducible integrable SL(2, p)'-modules, which were then applied in developing integrable modules for the Virasoro algebra under cyclic boundary conditions. A detailed outline of the outcome in this context, along with the determination of cohomology modules of the Virasoro acocommutator, was also given.

To find the molecular pentaquark states $\Xi_c^{(\prime)}(3080)$ and $\Xi_2c$, we analyze the Diquark-Diquark-Quark model's interactions involved in $\Xi_c \chi_c0 \Xi_c^{(\prime)}$, $\Xi_c \chi1^{--} \Xi_c^{(\prime)}$, $\Xi_c \chi_c \pi \Xi_D^{(*)}$, $\Xi_c \eta_c \Xi_D^{(*)}$, and $\chi_c \pi \Xi_D^{(*)}$. The interactions $\Xi_c \chi_c0 \Xi_c^{(\prime)}$ and $\Xi_c \chi1^{--} \Xi_c^{(\prime)}$ explain the strong decays of $\Xi_{c}(3123)$ and $\Xi_2c$, while the remaining interactions predict new states $\Xi_c^{(\prime)}(3080)$ and $\Xi_2c$. The predicted states $\Xi_c^{(\prime)}(3080)$ are charmonium-like pentaquark molecular states with quark substructure $udccs\bar d^*(\bar c)s$ and $udcss\bar c$ with some extra quarks from diquark-diquark-Quark model, bearing I=1 and color antitriplets. This paper investigates Zinbiel algebras with a finite dimension using a specific law and a particular bracket system that involves a cyclic element. The study reveals that these algebras are always nilpotent or solvable when the dimension is limited, and it also involves a more in-depth examination of the properties of nilpotent and solvable Zinbiel algebras under specific conditions, such as when the bracket and cyclicity conditions are reversed or when the dimension meets specific requirements. The research further focuses on linearly commutative Zinbiel algebras under various dimension conditions and derives a complete description of their properties in this context. Additionally, the study identifies a new class of algebras that are both nilpotent and solvable under certain dimension conditions and are characterized by a specific constitution involving the alternating sum of a sequence of vectors.

We consider scattering for inhomogeneous cubic Schrödinger equations in three dimensions with focusing and defocusing parameters. Our work yields specific requirements for initial data to ensure scattering occurs, and this research further demonstrates the nonuniqueness of potential solutions under certain conditions. Specifically, for the focusing model, we show that having zero initial data in one sphere while being nonzero elsewhere results in nonuniqueness, provided the initial value is small. This result aligns with previous findings by Foschi and Foschi-Sigal. Furthermore, for the defocusing model, we establish nonuniqueness for large initial conditions with specific properties.

The models developed for the Spatial SIS Dynamics with migration - DOCS and AIR - both account for migration. They both use an asymptotic analysis but differ in their treatment of small changes to parameters, leading to distinct equations. While the AIR model neglects migration in low migration scenarios, the DOCS model assumes the inverse, neglecting migration in high migration scenarios, which is counterintuitive. By contrasting the two models, I clarify differences in assumptions, derive both models from the same functional expansion, and provide unified approximations that account for both. These unified models, one for moderate and one for low migration, eliminate inconsistencies and expand upon earlier single-migration models. Numerical simulations confirm that the unified models perform better than their predecessor in moderately high migration scenarios. These unified models coalesce to yield a simpler equation under high migration conditions, which suggests an optimal threshold for migration below which the SIS dynamics can be largely disregarded. This implies that in areas with intense enough migration, spreading dynamics can often be sufficed by considering the inverse-AIR model.

The investigation into orbital resonances within compact planetary systems presents both significant challenges and opportunities to understand planetary properties and the overall structure of their environments.  Given that the planets in these systems are closely intertwined and the timescales for their orbital interactions are relatively short, simulations are best conducted using high-speed and accurate long-term integration approaches.  We evaluated the performance of several long-time integration methods, including Jacobi, PENTool, and Compact5, for systems with different levels of orbital complexity and found that a modified version of PENTool, originally developed for quasi-periodic motion analysis, excels at integrating various planetary configurations.  We discovered that this version of PENTool can effectively simulate scenarios for millions of years with an error margin of less than one thousandth of a day, and can accurately predict orbital resonances, long-term precession rates, and statistical measures such as the semi-major axes and eccentricity distributions.  Notably, our research found that PENTool outperformed other methods by accurately modeling the subtle effects of orbital interaction on eccentricity, whereas other methods sometimes displayed inconsistencies or inaccuracies.  By demonstrating the capabilities of PENTool in accurately modeling orbital dynamics, our research validates its effectiveness for a wide range of compact planetary systems and its potential as a reliable tool for analyzing orbital configurations and statistical properties.

We derive a formula for the Euler-Poincaré polynomial of the cohomology of the orbit space resulting from compactifying the action of a linear automorphism on $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ by its group of units, and establish that this orbit space corresponds to the $k$-fold branched cover of the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold $K(1,n)$ when $k$ is relatively prime to $n$, for all positive integers $k$.

The jet energy flow reconstruction technique developed for the SiD Detector at the future ILC is highly flexible. Due to its jet energy reconstruction based on particle flows, the detector can effectively deal with jets originating from a variety of sources, whether it's detecting a single top quark or an ensemble of quarks and gluons from multi-parton collisions at higher energy levels. Additionally, this method helps to maintain accurate resolutions across a broad range of photon and hadron energies within the detector's calorimeter. We employed a combination of both analytical and simulated methods to evaluate the performance of the detector's calorimeter. We investigated the jet energy resolution in the electron-positron collision at a center-of-mass energy of 250 GeV and also examined how the reconstruction handles jets originating from a top quark decaying within a W boson.

Using data obtained from extensive molecular-dynamics simulations, it's demonstrated that two distinct pathways exist for the transition from the low-density amorphous ice (LDA) to the high-density amorphous ice (HDA) phase. These pathways involve the transformation through a hexagonal ice (I$h$) and another pathway occurring gradually without passing through the hexagonal structure. The study focuses on the different pathways' impact on the hydrogen-bond network and how the density of the two phases changes. The results show that the transformation through the hexagonal structure results in minimal changes to the hydrogen-bond network, whereas the direct pathway involves substantial variations. The study highlights that the structure of the hydrogen bonds in LDA plays a crucial role in the transition to the high-density phase. The findings of this study contribute to the ongoing debate about the existence of the hexagonal structure as an intermediate step in the LDA to HDA transition.

Results showing EPR data are highly sensitive to contact processes and spin 
interactions, and new methods to analyze such data are greatly needed. Among 
gold, graphite, and silicon, gold displays the highest local density of states 
local to a single site. By experimenting with different electron spin resonance 
techniques with various microcontacts, we observed diverse contact-induced 
processes and measured their rates. Our research employed a range of materials 
for the sample, and we found the convergence of theory and practice could be 
achieved by analyzing experimental data through the lens of Gaussian-like 
diffusion. Ultimately, our findings could lead to the development of innovative 
methods for electron spin resonance and other spin-related techniques.

We've introduced a dependency graph for maintaining formal proof archives, where the node in-degree reflects the occurrence of each lemma within those proofs. Our experiments revealed that these in-degrees adhere to scale-free distributions, which prompted an exploration into their characteristics using a memory-less, preferential attachment model. This led to a detailed examination of a mathematical framework put forth by the authors, as well as a co-author graph constructed from a reduced version of Isabelle's mathematical theorem library. This thesis includes an investigation into hypotheses for the observed power-law distributions, an assessment of the mechanism governing the preferential attachment model, and a demonstration of the utility of this framework for identifying and ranking lemmas based on their utility within the system. Additionally, we've suggested methods for using this graph to inform strategies for evaluating and optimizing both automated reasoning tools and existing mathematical knowledge bases.

To gain insight into the magnetospheric ULF wave phenomenon, which spans decades, our research demonstrates the application of time-scale modification techniques to create manageable, interactive visualizations of these waves as recorded by the MAG at IMF's GEM/CEDAR Campaign 2002 site. By transforming the dataset to concentrate on singular events or reduce its dimensionality, our approach enhances the scientists' understanding of the phenomenon, making it more appealing for exploration. A comprehensive evaluation justifies the trade-offs between visualization quality and interactivity and suggests that the adopted solutions successfully meet the requirements of the domain experts. In addition, our solution provides flexibility as it can be adapted to other observation tools and is compatible with a wide range of other complex visualizations.

The counterterm method developed in AdS_3 spacetime is applied to a system comprising a charged rotating black brane in d=5 dimensions. A consistent action principle is established, yielding a Lagrangian free from charged and spinning effects. This is exemplified by deriving rotational Ward identities, as well as a relation between angular momentum, mass, and counterterms. Specifically, the study demonstrates that the counterterm method can be utilized in scenarios involving both angular momentum and a non-trivial mass, thus extending its applicability. Furthermore, the work provides the necessary framework for systematically evaluating the effects of rotation and mass on counterterms, which could be influential in areas such as holographic RG flows and black hole collisions.

Our knowledge base relies on external resources like Wordnet and Princeton's Pomalynka Database to provide a comprehensive understanding of individual words. Our framework builds upon a Lagovicki and Plahar developed text processing system, which enables us to handle words encountered for the first time during processing. We've incorporated a network of concepts that allows related words to share nodes, thereby alleviating the problem of word proliferation. Additionally, our system disambiguates word meanings by considering the context in which they are used, utilizing a similarity measure to determine the family relations of words. We've also incorporated a sequence model that incorporates a sequence of words, which serves as the primary driver of our system's performance. We've successfully tested our approach on various tasks such as information extraction and question-answering, achieving impressive results particularly on the question-asking domain where our system excels at providing accurate and relevant answers.

The quantized Weyl algebras arise naturally from the universal enveloping $C^*$-algebras of $q$-deformed canonical commutative relations (CCR). For the $C^*$-algebras thus generated, isomorphism with their classical counterparts occurs under specific parameters where the commutator values equal $\pm i$. Utilizing a central extension of an algebra of commutative functions on the circle, this article reestablishes the isomorphism between universal enveloping $C^*$-algebras for $q$-CCR and classical CCR under the commutator values $\pm i$. A detailed assessment of this reestablishment involves its implications for quantum theories based on Weyl algebras, especially in understanding how these theories compare to classical theories based on classical CCR. Additionally, this article provides concrete Choiquet-Ramsay equivalences establishing isomorphisms between these algebras, including a demonstration that classical extensions of commutative functions on the circle are fundamental models for studying generally nonabelian infinite $C^*$-algebras. Furthermore, it is shown that the quantized Weyl algebras are essential for studying generally nonabelian, extensively-studied $C^*$-algebras. Finally, it is suggested that the quantized Weyl algebras are generally superfluous in such studies.

The original semantics of GP 2, a graph language, have been modified to address certain issues related to the distribution algorithm for reducing graphs. These modifications led to the discovery of a new, complementary characterization of GP 2 reducibility, showcasing a fundamental discrepancy between GP 2's original and revised semantic interpretations. Specifically, GP 2's original rules do not entirely eliminate dead ends, whereas the revised rules do. As a result, GP 2's original and revised semantic profiles are distinguishable in terms of blocking behavior, time complexity, and the presence of new, derived dead ends.

We developed a computational model to predict radiation patterns from a disk surrounding a Be/X-ray binary star, taking into consideration the impact of X-ray emission and radio radiation from the star itself. Our analysis focused on the VFTS 723 system, a Be/X-ray binary in the Large Magellanic Cloud, for theoretical purposes. To fine-tune our predictions, we compared our model's outcomes with actual observations of radio and X-ray spectra from this system. Our results indicated a good correlation between theoretical and actual observations at longer wavelengths, but discrepancies at X-ray wavelengths due to additional emission sources not accounted for in the model. Our study has implications for a comprehensive study of the VFTS 723 system's emission morphology, suggesting the existence of a circumstellar torus rather than a disk structure. Our predictions also shed light on the emergence of radio and X-ray peaks at specific orbital phases. Our theoretical model offers a useful tool for the analytical dissection of Be/X-ray binary systems' emission across radio and X-ray spectral ranges.

The article provides evidence that there are no factorizations using the minimal polynomials of certain cosine values for the fifth and sixth Chebyshev polynomials and their variants. It also offers a new explanation for why the sixth Chebyshev polynomial does not factor into three polynomials of degree two, building on previous findings by Kopczynski.

High-performance protection systems are vital components of modern power systems, responsible for activating circuit breakers to prevent damage and threats to system stability and safety. For this reason, they are designed to detect a wide variety of electrical faults within milliseconds. By employing sophisticated machine learning techniques, researchers have made significant improvements in fault detection capabilities. In particular, several advanced deep learning methods have been applied for fault classification, achieving remarkable success in complex situations. In contrast, a proposed approach utilizes a tandem of feature extraction and classification approaches - the Balanced Evaluation of Artificial Neural Networks, or BEAN. BEAN involves using a combination of wavelet transforms and PCA to extract key features from data, which are then fed into multiple deep learning classifiers. We tested BEAN's efficacy in detecting various types of internal and external electrical faults using the widely-used New Jersey Model 1A1 system. Our findings indicate that BEAN outperforms several deep learning methods, achieving balanced accuracy rates of 99.2% for internal faults and 99.7% for external faults. Furthermore, our approach provides a valuable insight into the effectiveness of different feature extraction techniques.

In mmWave multicasting with multiplexing, several users share the same spectrum while sharing resources. Our investigation focuses on a scenario where a base station, positioned at the center, broadcasts to $K$ equally spaced user antennas on the circular perimeter of a massive multiple-input-multiple-output system. Our analysis begins with a detailed, explicit characterization of the channel rank as the number of users increases, followed by an examination of its distributional properties. Based on these findings, we calculated the signal-to-interference ratio and developed a sequence of lower and upper bounds for this value. These bounds, expressed in terms of the integral of the Arcosine function, can be simplified using asymptotic approximations that show considerable improvement, particularly when the number of users is substantial and mmWave frequency ranges are high. Our research indicates that equipping the base station with multiple antennas can yield system enhancements of up to three orders of magnitude. Our approximation strategy is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of system configurations, thus offering valuable insights into the design and optimization of mmWave multicasting systems.

We present examples where the residual finiteness growth of a group exceeds exponential growth in two specific instances: solvable groups with isometry properties and iterated wreath products of finite groups. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of the residual finiteness growth series for the iterated wreath products, whereas the calculation approach for the isometric solvable groups' growth series relies on a more indirect method.

We investigate the boundary control of a flexible metric graph, focusing on a specific star-shaped graph with metric edges and bounded geometry. We demonstrate the exponential stability of the associated semigroup when flexibility is present on the edges' metrics. Contrasting this, we show that without elasticity on the slopes of the edges, the resulting system is not stable. Additionally, we discuss how these findings can be applied to provide optimal, low-input-control results for a class of third-order differential equations.

Researchers employed the Bayesian neural networks approach, an application of Bayesian inference to convolutional neural networks, in predicting nuclear shell energies. Traditionally, shell energies have been determined through complex and computationally expensive calculations based on the density functional theory, but with the rise of machine learning, researchers have explored whether these techniques can predict future shell energies with sufficient accuracy. Using training data for 85 isotopes, researchers established that Bayesian neural networks yield reliable shell energies, both within and outside the presently known range. In the unknown region beyond calcium (Z=20), researchers discovered new shell energies and projections for N = 112, 114, and 116. Moreover, researchers found energy gaps at N = 100, 104, and 108 in Og, which weren't present in the nearest known isotopes. Researchers speculate that because of these predicted energy minima, Og may exhibit a mixture of spherical and deformed configurations. In terms of N = 112, 114, and 116, researchers predict that Mo isotopes will exhibit superdeformability, culminating in new rotational band projections in the neutron-rich region at L = 38, 40, and 42. These predictions are based on the understanding that nuclear shell energies are the primary driving force behind rotational band projections in the superdeformed rotation regime. Researchers predict Mo isotopes will exhibit a significant number of new rotational band projections across a wide range of rotational angular momentum. We've developed two types of HEMT-based mixer frequencies at 110 GHz and 140 GHz using previously established architectural designs. We investigated the mixing efficiency and operational ranges of these mixers both theoretically and experimentally. We found that in both cases, the theoretical and experimental results align closely. To determine the optimal architectural design, we examined and evaluated various mixers under different operational conditions. We compared the performance of HEMT-based mixers to that of conventional Schottky-based mixers, showing significant improvements in frequency range and mixing efficiency. Furthermore, we evaluated the performance of HEMT-based mixers at cryogenic temperatures, highlighting their potential as a lower-temperature alternative for future superconducting quantum compute systems.

The anomalous optical drag effect is distinguished from the standard optical drag effect by having a displacement in a perpendicular direction to the light propagation path. We investigated this phenomenon in a two-dimensional electron gas by examining threshold currents for producing zero-resistance states. We discovered that the threshold current experiences a drag force in a direction transverse to the light's path, which we attributed to the electron flow being redirected by a potential barrier created by the drag effect's stress. A model considering the electron gas as a capacitor was able to accurately explain the observed results.

In recent years, there has been a heightened sense of urgency surrounding risk-averse decision-making strategies, prompting researchers to develop robust optimization techniques that take into account various forms of uncertain data. Specifically, this paper focuses on adapting a general and highly scalable Lagrangian dual method developed by Di Lorenzo and Frangioni for solving certain types of linear or quadratic optimization problems to scenarios involving binary or categorical data. To achieve this, we introduce a novel type of reformulation and applies it to the De Morgan law, yielding a dual problem with an expanded set of variables. By doing so, we create opportunities for cutting plane methods and other optimization techniques to provide more accurate approximations and, consequently, improve computational efficiency in dual-based approaches. Our approach enables robust optimization with a high degree of precision while maintaining a level of flexibility that allows for the promotion of valid feasible solutions. Moreover, we illustrate the effectiveness of our method in solving robust mixed-integer optimization problems in both 2D and 3D spatial environments.

City officials and urban planners are now able to gauge social sentiments in a more cost-effective and continuous manner, thanks to the integration of social media, data mining, and machine learning techniques. This approach begins by harvesting a considerable amount of data from various online sources, after which relevant information is isolated and further processed using specialized algorithms to process and analyze the data. A key benefit of this method is that it facilitates real-time monitoring and disclosure of observed patterns and correlations. To illustrate the analytical capabilities of this approach, two case studies will be examined, focusing on tracking public perceptions of local institutions such as the metro and analyzing citizen reactions to events like the COVID-19 pandemic.

A long-established tradition in data analysis is the study of patterns within data, focusing on discovering new patterns to advance scientific knowledge and driving data analysis. Pattern discovery through data annotation yields valuable data exploration tools and enriches pattern spaces, yet requiring manual labeling poses significant data analysis and annotation challenges. To alleviate some of these challenges, we propose the integration of unsupervised learning into the pattern discovery pipeline. By leveraging unsupervised learning, we can develop effective methods for automatic pattern identification, facilitating further pattern exploration and, ultimately, more accurate data classification. In our study, we developed a novel unsupervised feature learning technique centered around data visualization and incorporated it into the standard pattern discovery pipeline. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing unsupervised learning techniques based on supervised performance, which we aim to achieve without the challenges associated with human supervision.

Unlike human intelligence, most machine learning models cannot learn new skills without re-learning the underlying rules. However, in certain cases, it's possible for these models to acquire new knowledge without losing existing abilities. This study examines the ability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to transfer knowledge across similar graph tasks, aiming to understand the factors contributing to learn-to-forgget mechanisms in GNNs, as well as how to control them. To achieve this, we use perturbation-based tests to explore the robustness of GNNs in various scenarios, and our findings suggest that both the structure of the graph tasks and the type of GNN model impact its ability to transfer knowledge. Notably, our experiments show that similar community structure between source and target tasks enhances the transferability of GNNs, and meta-learning can be employed to tackle this issue. Based on these results, we propose a GNN architecture that can adapt to new tasks without compromising its performance, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this model using real-world benchmarks.

We propose a novel hierarchical approach for recommender systems for multi-user scenarios. At the top level, user and item groups are determined by an Indian Buffet Process (IBP), after which each entity within these groups is associated with a set of features. Then, an exponential Bayesian clustering technique generates clusters of items based on their shared features. Ultimately, an interactive learning method recommends items by incrementally acquiring labels for users and utilizing these labels in item clustering. The combination of IBP and exponential Bayesian clustering allows our method to efficiently handle both sparse and rich data sets. Furthermore, our approach accommodates cold start issues for users or items not observed during the training process by assigning them novel features. Evaluation of our algorithm via a synthetic data set and Amazon book reviews demonstrates its cold start and generalization capabilities as well as significant improvements in both click-through rate and personalization compared to other competing techniques.

The set disjointness problem, typically dealing with elements from two groups, determines if a particular element is common to both groups or exists exclusively in one.  This problem has a single-element variant known as mostly set disjointness where the determination is made unless one group contains a single element.  A study by Chakrabarty demonstrated a lower bound of Ω(n) for worst-case complexity using a single-element variant, thus counteracting a potential circuit lower bound.  A further extension, known as mostly vector disjointness, has been explored where the objective is to identify two subsets where one might contain a single element with the determination made for all other elements.  A set of lower bounds have been established for mostly vector disjointness resulting in mostly set disjointness being P-complete, thus proving P has a two-player non-zero sum games completeness.  A related theory has also been studied where the objective of mostly vector disjointness is modified to determine if a particular element is part of one of two other subsets, thus known as pointed vector disjointness.  A set of lower bounds have been established for pointed vector disjointness resulting in significantly improved P-complete proof for mostly set disjointness as well as circuit lower bounds.  A final modification, known as harmonic augmentation, has also been studied where the objective of mostly vector disjointness is modified to determine if a particular element, represented by 1, is part of two other subsets, thus known to determine a P-complete modification of mostly set disjointness.

We present a comprehensive account of the magnetic phase transitions in the classical Eu magnet, as derived from Eu\$_2$Sb\$_2$, in which two adjacent magnetic phases, $O4$ and $P4/mmd$, coexist for temperatures between approximately 30.5 and 27.55 Kelvin. Detailed studies of the symmetry properties and group theories of the magnetic symmetry systems involved have been conducted. The analysis demonstrates that the two magnetic phases are separated by a second-order phase transition characterized by specific critical exponents $\delta$, $\gamma$, and $\delta$. Additionally, a field-induced phase transition occurs at 17.5 Kelvin, beyond which an easy-plane antiferromagnetic state emerges. Ultimately, a comprehensive phase diagram illustrating the magnetic phases and transition lines has been established.

We suggest utilizing an atomically thick MoTe2 membrane as a component in quantum devices. Our study demonstrates that extremely thin MoTe2 membranes can be effectively combined with a system of nanowires made from Nb3Al/Al, which is then used in a honeycomb lattice structure. Our results reveal the 2D electronic properties of MoTe2, showing energy bands consisting of two separated electron pockets. The separation of these pockets can be controlled by adjusting a magnetic field, thus providing a means to study and analyze irregular band structure properties through Fermi's energy surface. Our research set up a foundation for applying these membranes as a sensing tool to measure quantum phenomena or to develop innovative materials for electronic devices. Additionally, we established a new platform to study 2D ferromagnetic materials using the Luttingen theorem.

A theoretical framework has been established to investigate how a magnetic field affects the movement of electrons in a material in both a directional and scalar manner. Within this framework, researchers discovered that an abnormal velocity caused by multiple electrons can produce a variety of anomalous properties associated with a material being an insulator. This relationship was uncovered through a broader examination of various systems, including rotating metals, Weyl semimetals in superconductors, superconductors, Kerr rotators, and others. In these systems, the property causing a material to be an insulator can arise from a combination of the material being non-uniform and non-uniformly charged, as well as from a type of symmetry known as time reversal. Furthermore, researchers discovered that an abnormal velocity caused by multiple electrons can also produce a variety of anomalous properties associated with a material being a magnet. This relationship was uncovered through a broader examination of various systems, including Kerr rotators, pyroelectric materials, and others. In these systems, the property causing a material to be a magnet can arise from a type of symmetry known as time reversal.

When ventilating multiple patients from a single ventilator is necessary, maintaining each patient's preferred tidal volume is crucial. To address this issue, we developed an algorithm enabling two patients to be ventilated simultaneously from a single ventilator. The system monitors the ventilator's phase in real-time, accurately predicts cycle duration, and ensures correct tidal volume delivery for each patient based on their respective respiratory rates, desired tidal volumes, and individual end-expiratory volumes. The algorithm's effectiveness was verified through both theoretical and clinical trials. Its potential extension to ventilating an unlimited number of patients is also discussed.

For complex iterates of certain rational maps with finite points of intersection, a corresponding group exists that describes deck transformations. This group's structure is explored further, revealing its influence on the number of such deck transformations. Certain properties of this group are also classified based on its order and whether it is cyclic or a higher order mathematical structure. This investigation also reveals relationships between these deck transformations and areas in the complex plane where the corresponding rational map exhibits 'butterfly' characteristics.

By drawing from previous research on monolayer semiconductor properties, we establish a relationship between transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) thickness and optical band gaps, before using density functional theory to study the structural properties of these materials. Through a computational analysis of various structural configurations, we find that increasing the transition metal layer in TMD structures, such as MoS2 and WSe2, results in a proportional increase in the work function, ionization energy, and electron affinity. Notably, we observe that transition metal layers in the center of the helical stack have a lesser impact on these energy measures than transition metal layers at the interface or near the surface. Additionally, we find that monolayer-like ribbons with internal transition metal layers exhibit large band-edge shifts due to phonon effects, allowing for tunable optoelectronic properties. These findings are critical in understanding the band-edge physics of these TMD materials in the thick, multi-layered state.

A particular model of learning delta lenses, known as full asymptotic learning deltas, can be seen as special types of morphisms within a category called FullAsymptoticLearningDeltas. By incorporating a new notion, called weak full asymptotic learning deltas, a corresponding subcategory is formed, showing how these lenses can be connected through sequences of minor adjustments. A new theory is thus established, unifying two earlier frameworks, and giving rise to a new concept, called weak full asymptotic learning sequences. A key property of this theory was proven, revealing that these sequences can be characterized by two distinct forms of quasi-mappings, known as asymptotic endomorphisms and weak full asymptotic endomorphisms.

This research focuses on estimating oscillatory integrals of the form $\int_{\Omega} e^{tS(x)}p(x)\,dx$ in the range $t\geq 0$, given observations of the function $S(x)$ on a set $\Omega$. The function $S(x)$ represents the product of a phase function $s(x)$ and amplitude function $t p(x)$. The study establishes an efficient algorithm for approximating the oscillatory integral in the fast Monte Carlo framework. The approach works as long as the phase and amplitude functions meet certain regularity requirements and are infinitely differentiable. The method involves first approximating the oscillatory integral using a Monte Carlo integration, which is then refined using Taylor expansions of the phase and amplitude functions. The study also includes a concrete numerical example that demonstrates the efficiency and accuracy of the proposed algorithm under specific conditions.

A novel iteration method, the general synthetic iteration scheme, has been developed for use in Boltzmann collisions. This approach has been shown to improve solution convergence in rarefied gas flows, achieving results comparable to highly accurate particle-based simulations. The scheme's efficacy has been tested in two steady-state scenarios: elastic collisions and chemical reactions. The first scenario involved collisional equilibrium with the Maxwell distribution of velocities, while the second scenario included multiple reaction rates and non-equilibrium species velocity distributions. The analytical properties of the GSIS suggest its potential as a high-accuracy solver for complex fluid dynamics and chemistry problems, both in space and time.

If sterile axions exist, the axion quark nugget model provides an explanation 
for the similarity between dark matter and visible matter in the Universe due to 
their potentially comparable densities. This hypothesis is being investigated 
with a possible connection to the QCD axion. The first-order phase transition of 
axion quark nuggets in the early Universe may have generated the baryon asymmetry, 
a finding supported by two studies. One investigation found that axion quark 
nugget radiation in the early Universe could account for the background radiation 
of the cosmic microwave background, while another study analyzed transitions between 
different forms of axion quark nugget matter and their impact on the baryon 
asymmetry, the dark matter component, and the need for a lepton asymmetry for 
matter-antimatter cancellation via sphaleron processes.

Researchers at the CMS have discovered a previously observed signal from a Higgs-like boson, statistically significant at a 3.3σ level, with a specific range of masses between 125.0 and 127.5 GeV. This finding is based on 7 TeV and 8 TeV data from 5.1 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions, and is presented in terms of glycinosine production, a process that does not involve Higgs boson decays into bosons. An additional signal was also found at a 2.5σ level, with a similar range of masses, based on a different data set of 19.7 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. These observations support the idea that there may be mass-dependent obstacles to producing the Higgs boson via glycinosine, which could provide insight into new physics that affects high-energy interactions between particles.

Let $q$ be the standard quadratic generator of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}]$, and let $p$
be an odd, reducible prime not equal to 3. The given paper's central argument involves
utilizing the properties of Siegel modular forms to demonstrate $p$-divisibility in the
Ramanujan $\tau$-function as expressed in (1), and further investigating the forms' $p$-stability
under the action of $\text{Sp}(2, \mathbb{Z})_+\$. Furthermore, related conjectures regarding the
$p$-divisibility of other $\tau$-function values are proposed. Notably, (16) validates the
speculation previously presented in [2017, conjetura].

In this study, we build upon the framework established by Ieysorno and Pavlov in \cite{IP21}, expanding on the concept of rigid fibrations in a quasitopological setting. We demonstrate that in the context of rigid fibrations, the following relationships hold: (i) the group of homotopies, $[\Sigma^n S^m, F]$, is isomorphic to the $n$-th quasitopological homotopy group, $\pi^Q_n F$, and (ii) the group of homotopies, $[\Sigma^n B \pi^Q_m, F]$, is isomorphic to the $(n,m)$-th quasitopological homotopy group, $\pi^Q_{n,m} F$. We then prove that in the context of group-like spaces, the group of homotopies, $[\Sigma^n S^m, F]$, is isomorphic to the group of homotopies, $[\pi^Q_m, F]$. We further establish that in the context of group-like spaces, the group of homotopies, $[\Sigma^n B \pi^m, F]$ is isomorphic to the group of homotopies, $[\pi^Q_{n,m} B \pi^m, F]$.

In experiments involving ultra-cold quantum systems, patterns formed by fermions are observed through their spin polarization. By numerically solving many-body Schrödinger equations, researchers have discovered a variety of crystal structures, which are classified based on localized spin arrangements. These patterns are rooted in a 3D version of the Hénon-Grossmann model, which describes interactions between dark solitons and vortex rings. Notably, the simplest Pauli crystal resembles a hyper-cubic lattice where each point represents a pair of fermions with opposite spins. To investigate these patterns, researchers studied their stability, utilizing techniques such as the linear stability analysis and the calculation of relative entropy. They also explored how these patterns transform in response to external distortions and examined their connections to well-known quantum system behaviors, including fermionic condensates, dark solitons, and vortex rings. These studies contribute to our understanding of quantum phase transitions triggered by external fluctuations and facilitate research into novel states of matter.

The ZNN algorithm is efficiently utilized to solve nonlinear differential equations in a discrete form, contrasting efficiently with continuous ordinary differential equation solvers like Runge-Kutta methods. By directly utilizing discrete data without the need for derivative calculations, the ZNN method exhibits proactive characteristics, distinct from the inherently reactive nature of ODE solvers. Although initially developed for nonlinear equation systems, the ZNN algorithm can efficiently solve linear equation systems as well. However, the speed advantages offered by ZNN are largely attributed to its incorporation of machine learning techniques. Nonetheless, the standard mathematical models employed in physical sciences often feature well-defined analytical methods for solving linear equations. Consequently, the primary benefits of the ZNN algorithm stem from its ability to directly utilize discrete data without the need for derivative calculations. Moreover, in scenarios involving large datasets and approximations of equations (e.g. in climate models), the ZNN method can still provide significant speed advantages. Lastly, despite its name suggesting otherwise, the ZNN algorithm is capable of efficiently solving linear equation systems as well as nonlinear equations.

Rod cells play a pivotal role in human and animal vision, especially under low-light conditions, which makes their functional characteristics crucial to their role in visual processing. By examining the responses of rod cells to different light intensities, researchers have gained a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying rod cells' function. It has been established that rod cells have two main visual pathways - one focused on central light sources and the other on peripheral objects - which are linked to the three types of photopigments found in the cells, each responding to different light wavelengths at varying intensity levels. Additionally, the inner structures of rod cells play a crucial part in the cells' light-sensing abilities and play a key role in understanding the cells' responses to rapid changes in light exposure, as well as their sensitivity to specific wavelengths of light. Studying the interactions between these pathways can provide valuable insights into the complex mechanisms underlying rod cells' function and how they contribute to the overall visual processing system, a knowledge which can ultimately lead to a more comprehensive understanding of human and animal vision.

The widely-used Wolter I X-ray telescope design is prone to higher-order error terms during fabrication and installation, which can severely impair its performance. To rectify this issue, our investigation delves into the impact of these factors. Initially, we derived higher-order polynomial terms affecting the geometric performance of Wolter I optics. Subsequently, the limits on these terms were determined for existing mirrors, which showed that even minor deviations can result in discernible irregularities in the background and emission from hot plasma. Ultimately, our research highlights the necessity of minimizing these aberrations in the next generation of hard X-ray telescopes.

A novel method, based on a general approach by Wallin \textit{et al.} (Proc. R. Soc. A \textbf{477}, 20210145 (2021)), is utilized to investigate reentrant effects in moiré materials under the influence of long-range Coulomb interaction. Through comparative analysis, it is demonstrated that Wallin \textit{et al.'s} results for bilayer graphene can be easily extended to include Coulomb effects, as well as that they are consistent with previous findings by Liu \textit{et al.} (Phys. Rev. B \textbf{103}, 125305 (2021)). Furthermore, it is revealed that Wallin \textit{et al}'s results can be generalised to describe reentrant effects in other moiré systems, such as those formed by WS$_2$-MoS$_2$ and WSe$_2$, as well as bilayer moiré systems, thereby offering valuable insights for experimental design in both moiré and multi-dome systems.

In a typical steganographic system, a secret message is hidden within a cover object by adjusting its transparent aspect, for example, luminance in images. A proposed alternative in this research involves embedding a secret message by altering the encryption method used to encrypt a stream of random bits. A theoretical analysis of this steganographic system revealed that its security has superior capabilities compared to steganography using standard encryption, offering increased security parameters. Furthermore, experimental results showed significant improvements in security parameters when compared to steganography using standard encryption. Despite not detailing specific algorithms for this steganographic system in this research, it is anticipated that this approach could lead to substantial advancements in secure communication systems.

In the unit commitment problem, the process of screening constraints is crucial but computationally costly due to its ZDP nature. We propose replacing complex constraints with simpler, linear models trained by machine learning, thus eliminating unnecessary computations and decreasing solve times. By incorporating these models into a two-stage solution method, we achieve a significant speed-up in the solution time for large power grids. Experimental results on the MEG2 test system demonstrate a 40% reduction in solve time when incorporating these models, resulting in a solution time of under 10 seconds with a 12-second preprocessing time. Consequently, the total time taken to solve the unit commitment problem is under 20 seconds.

Magmatic crystalline compounds often exhibit unique properties that can be modified by applying high pressure.  $\beta$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, obtained through high-pressure and high-temperature crystallization, is a notable example. Its unusual metal-insulator phase transition at relatively low pressures has piqued the interest of researchers. To gain insight into this transition, researchers at Oxford utilized high-pressure and high-energy X-ray scattering techniques to collect precise structural data. Their analysis revealed a sudden and irreversible change at pressures higher than 1.2 GPa, consistent with experimental findings on metal-insulator phase transitions in this compound. To further understand these transitions, researchers at Oxford modeled the behavior using high-pressure and high-temperature phase diagrams. Notably, at pressures over 1.2 GPa and temperatures above 180 K, a new insulating crystal structure occurs, whereas at higher temperatures and pressures below 1.2 GPa, the original metallic crystal structure persists even though it is no longer stable under the higher pressure conditions. Upon sufficient heating, the metallic crystal structure transforms into a different metallic insulating crystal configuration that was previously present at even higher temperatures. These findings highlight how increasing pressure affects the material's electrical properties, as well as how pressure interacts with temperature to determine a material's insulating or metallic properties.

In the Synthetic Control method, weighted averages are used to estimate counterfactual outcomes for a specific treatment unit by selecting relevant comparable pre-treatment units. Traditional implementations often result in unutilized observational data, as units treated via different mechanisms or with unclear treatment information are discarded. We present an alternative approach that repuroses control units that were previously discarded due to unknown treatment information or suspicious co-variates. We demonstrate how to expand the set of eligible units from those with clear treatment information to those that can be estimated using machine learning. We achieve this estimation using data on treatment information and co-variates from multiple post-treatment periods. Post-treatment, new controls can also be leveraged to update estimates. We showcase the updated methodology in two notable applications – Puerto Rico's 2017 power outage and the UK's 2018 telephone shutdown, which previously relied on approximately 90% of available data.

Over the past few years, local differential privacy (LDP) has gained popularity as a robust method for safeguarding sensitive user data within decentralized settings, such as mobile devices. The growing interest in LDP is largely driven by its capacity to protect user data locally, thereby preventing centralized service providers from abusing their trust. Recent studies have successfully incorporated LDP into various machine learning tasks, including supervised and unsupervised learning. However, graph learning poses a unique challenge due to the complex nature of graphs that are inherently data-dependent. In response, researchers have proposed a family of differential graph operators, aimed at developing private graph learning solutions that account for both statistical and structural dependencies within graphs. Notably, the methods proposed so far rely on either gradient-based optimization or approximate maximum likelihood estimators, which may not provide a comprehensive general solution. Our work addresses this limitation by introducing a general framework for private graph learning through differential embedding, expanding the scope of private graph learning solutions beyond gradient-based models. Our method involves minimizing a regularized empirical risk estimator while ensuring the satisfaction of local differential privacy and spectral constraints. Our theoretical and practical contributions demonstrate that the minimum empirical risk and global embedding objectives have consistent limits as the sample size increases, thereby validating the effectiveness of our method in achieving accurate and generalizable embeddings even with a single labeled sample. Furthermore, our practical implementations showcase the versatility of our method in producing high-quality embeddings that surpass state-of-the-art results across various real-world node classification benchmarks.

The occurrence of electron injection over a relatively short spatial extent, resulting in a collimated beam of electrons, is predominantly explained by the oscillating electric field generated at the edge of a plasma bubble created by the interaction of two colors of lasers. However, when the two-color laser pulses exhibit a significant phase difference, the electron injection process is expected to differ due to an altered dynamics and altered forces acting within the bubble. This study experimentally investigates the effect of the phase difference on the electron injection process. The results show that a significant phase difference can hinder electron injection at the edge of a plasma bubble by altering the electric field and electron density there due to a change in the effective location of the critical plasma density. This implies that, when the two-color laser pulses have distinct phase differences, the electron injection is restricted to a smaller volume and the electrons must travel longer distances before reaching the screen, thereby reducing their kinetic energies. This study confirms that the laser envelope phase not only influences the electron dynamics but also determines the electron injection process and subsequent electron density at the rear of the target, ultimately affecting the overall explosive emission process.

This study offers a comprehensive theoretical evaluation of the detection sensitivity for the 2p and resonant 0p modes of double electron capture in a nuclear physics context. The analysis involves varying the nuclear and atomic parameters systematically to investigate the dependence of detection sensitivity on electron shell involvement. We've incorporated a realistic nuclear potential model and employed the Dirac-Hartree-Fock method to calculate the Dirac wave functions of an electron in the closed K-shell and a hole in the continuum. The findings indicate that the detection sensitivity of both 2p and resonant 0p modes is largely independent of the mass number and primarily depends on the fine structure splitting of the 1s state and the binding energy of an electron in the K-shell. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that the detection sensitivity of the 2p mode can be increased by utilizing a slower beam and lower background radiation energy compared to the resonant 0p mode.

Our analysis suggests that $\Delta F \widetillde{F} = \Delta F$, a relation that, if true, would yield a crucial insight into the scale dependence of the vector and axial-vector currents in QCD. This, in turn, would allow us to derive a precise expression for the twist-2 gluon condensate and rigorously establish its value, thereby resolving the long-standing discrepancy among QCD moments associated with the $\tau$-function. Furthermore, our approach would enable the systematic expansion of the QCD spectral function and the hadronic mass in the infinite-momentum limit, facilitating a deeper understanding of the behavior of the hadronic mass at large $b$-parameters.

Our new approach enhances colored object reconstruction by expanding on the concept of Visual Object Counting, allowing the use of a single RGB image to identify objects of interest and generate the corresponding colors and poses. This method demonstrates improved adaptability and high reconstruction accuracy compared to existing techniques. To further optimize performance, we present a range of advanced colorization and reconstruction strategies. Our results show that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art colorfusion in both flexibility and effectiveness and surpasses visual object counting in accuracy. The code and additional resources can be found on our GitHub repository.

The five-dimensional generalized Hamiltonian Ermakov system's classification is the focus, 
a system that includes a combination of linear, quadratic, and cubic terms. 
A new algebraic framework is introduced to classify the five-dimensional system, 
resulting in multiple distinct classes. 
These classes are distinguished by the system's dimensionality, 
its interaction with a specific vector space, and the dynamics that govern its behavior. 
In contrast to previous studies, the structure of the two-dimensional generalized Hamiltonian Ermakov system 
was classified within a straightforward framework, 
while the present study reveals the complexities involved in classifying its higher-dimensional counterparts.

For effective use of transportation systems, reliable real-time information is necessary. This document highlights how innovative approaches like data mining and machine learning enhance the availability of information in public transportation and improve the maintenance of urban infrastructure. Additionally, we share our expertise and experiences gained from collecting and analyzing large datasets of transportation in Lisbon, Portugal. Specifically, we focus on two specific applications: a public transportation fare integration system and an alerting system for urban infrastructure failures. For the first system, we applied data mining and machine learning methods to integrate fares across different transportation providers. Regarding the latter, we developed a machine learning-based alerting system to notify residents of urban residents about upcoming urban infrastructure failures. This document provides an overview of the projects, discussing the used datasets, applied algorithms, and technical solutions. Moreover, we share our experiences with collaborating agencies, establishing data partnerships, and implementing the systems in the cities. Finally, we participate in a public discussion on the utilized data and related topics.

The objective of few-shot learning is to excel in classification with limited resources, typically within the range of 1-5 samples per class. This task has various applications, such as discovering new chemical compounds using simulation tools to predict biological activity. Predicting the activity requires predicting a target molecule's affinity to specific, highly variable protein binding sites. Employing support vector machines as the base classifier, we report state-of-the-art performance in this domain, achieving projected accuracy of 70% and 58% for existing and missing data sets respectively. This success can be attributed to our framework's effectiveness in managing data outliers and efficiently utilizing limited available data. Specifically, we demonstrate that our method performs well across diverse benchmark data sets.

We investigated a pair of edge states in a topological superconductor, specifically F/S ring systems with n pairs of Fermi liquid and p-wave superconductor segments, in the presence of O(2) symmetry. The localized current operator generated by the operator that creates a non-invertible charge defect, results in the emergence of a low-energy excitations characterized by an SO(3) global symmetry and a non-zero Chern number. Consequently, a magnetization texture develops in the edge states, while an low-energy spin-1 bosonic mode is linked to a deformed 0-form symmetry. Notably, our findings demonstrate that a simple fermionic current operator can induce a substantial set of operators that flank the non-invertible charge defect, thereby preserving the low-energy physics. In contrast to the standard chern insulator, our edge states exhibit a distinctive set of surface states, characterized by a four-fold degeneracy, an overall degeneracy of 4n, and a specific set of symmetries. The latter includes a generalized fermionic U(1) symmetry, along with a set of O(3) spin-1/2 symmetries encompassing SO(3) and U(1)/Z_2.

Two orientability criteria for split graphs are proposed, one for general cases and another for those with a smaller independent set. The first allows for semi-transitive orientability recognition through splitting trees, whereas the second correlates orientability with tree characteristics. Additionally, two constructions that yield even-minute graphs are presented, demonstrating that no universal orientability criterion exists for all split graphs with a small independent set.

To analyze tau lepton performance, researchers use a comprehensive approach that
combines actual experimental conditions with a global network of advanced computers.
This technique identifies how effectively the distinction between genuine tau leptons and
misinterpreted particles can be made, employing various classification techniques and
training the system on large datasets featuring different types of misleading particles.
Recent studies have created more precise methods, incorporating a range of inputs and
employing cutting-edge neural network techniques, which incorporate multiple features and
use advanced statistical models to analyze particle behavior.
These breakthroughs have led to significant improvements in differentiating genuine tau
leptons from misleading particles, with increased efficiency to misidentify particles
now at 1/5000 compared to 1/2000 previously. Additionally, incorporating a sophisticated
statistical model to analyze various factors such as location and angle in the detector,
the new approach further improves differentiation efficiency to misidentify particles now at
1/6000 compared to 1/2500 previously. While these advances are significant, further work is
still needed to develop more precise methods, with efficiency to misidentify particles
now at 1/30000 compared to 1/6000 previously.

A key advantage of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) is the ability to assess prediction uncertainty. This capability has the potential to enhance data analysis protocols in astronomy by identifying regions with insecure diagnoses, thereby allowing for more effective use of follow-up observations. We explored the validity of BNN uncertainty estimation by comparing it with traditional statistical methods on a dataset involving galaxy morphologies. The results show that BNN uncertainty can be utilized as an alternative uncertainty measure, potentially offering additional advantages due to its inherent capability to learn the distribution of data and handle non-linear relationships.

A key limitation of conventional Brillouin light scattering techniques lies in their inability to manipulate mechanical modes on demand, hindering interactions between disparate symmetries. We incorporate an actuated mechanical system into an optomechanical cavity built within a multilayer glass structure for investigating intermodal Brillouin interactions. Our results reveal the potential of mechanical influence in enhancing or suppressing interactions between modes of various symmetries, offering opportunities in Brillouin light scattering applications.

The exchange laws for the generalized standard odd graded symmetries of the finite Coxeter group Bn are determined, and they are found to be dependent on the Coxeter length and elements of the descent set within a generalized standard sequence.

In recent years, various minimax zero-sum two-player problems have been proposed, with applications in reinforcement learning, game theory, and operations research. These problems can be formulated as specific convex optimization issues and solved using techniques from zonotope calculus to derive an analytical solution. Despite the speed of this method, it becomes computationally impractical for real-time decision-making when the number of strategies is substantial. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel local search algorithm, E2LS, designed to expedite the solution to a broad range of minimax zero-sum two-player problems. We compared the performance of the proposed E2LS algorithm with the existing E2S method on several problem formulations, including the well-known Sutton's model and Braess' model. Our findings indicate that E2LS achieves a substantial speed-up in finding the optimal solution. Furthermore, we utilized the E2LS algorithm to solve a network planning problem and evaluated its properties through an experimental study. Our results show that the solution obtained from E2LS is close to the analytical result with a negligible difference, and the derived solution exhibits a strict convexity. Additionally, we found that the strategic solution from E2LS generates equivalent outcomes as the simultaneous equilibrium strategies.

In recent years, the task of forecasting customer churn has gained significant importance from both business and data science perspectives. Business-wise, early churn prediction enables operators to implement measures to prevent losses, whereas data scientists see this task as an intriguing challenge that necessitates handling complex time-series data. This paper examines the efficiency of various time-series models in analyzing churn prevention, examining how different training approaches are reflected in test outcomes, and what time-series properties impact these findings. Our investigation utilizes real-world churn datasets from telecommunications and internet providers, enabling us to compare the performance of models like AR, SAR, LSTM, and multi-task CNNs, trained with or without past churn history. We also developed a multi-task CNN that predicts both the next step in the time-series and the future churn status, facilitating a more precise assessment of uncertainty in our predictions. Our results reveal that engaging a sequence-based time-series model improves its capacity to utilize time-series data, albeit not substantially. In contrast, forfeiting churn history altogether results in a considerable loss of predictive accuracy. Interestingly, our models failed to harness information on seasonal fluctuations, despite this being inherent in the datasets. Furthermore, our multi-task approach yields robustness and better uncertainty assessment capabilities for the models. Notably, our highest-performing models attain test AUC scores of 0.8771 and 0.9145 for the Dataset 1 and Dataset 2, respectively.

The ongoing discussion on the conserved current cascades in four-dimensional ${\rm Z}_2$ spinors has prompted a fresh investigation into the conserved currents within a specific anisotropic Ising Field Theory, specifically when the irrelevance of the $L_{-4}$ $\bar L_{-4}$ $\Phi$ irrelevant operator is taken into account. By establishing the hierarchy of the relevant and irrelevant operators within the anisotropic Ising Field Theory, we demonstrate the lack of integrability when the aforementioned irrelevance is considered, thereby revealing that the sequence of the ${\rm Z}_2$ spinors falls short of a conserved current. Notably, a similar breakdown in integrability is found when the ${\rm Z}_2$ spinors' action is reduced to a sum of the cosine functions, as commonly seen in the Ising quantum criticality. Consequently, we infer that the conserved current cascades within a specific anisotropic Ising Field Theory, namely ${\rm Z}_2$ spinors, are unlikely to emerge. By extending our understanding, we also show that the ${\rm Z}_2$ spinors' lack of integrability originates from the conservation of the supercurrents created by the $psu(2|1)^{(3)}$ symmetry at the two-dimensional critical point level. The lattice calculation's results on gluon TMDPDFs, including its factorization properties, were thoroughly examined.
A comparison of the lattice calculations by IBM and Muenster groups on the left-right correlation of gluon field strengths supported the factorization formula derived from the soft-collinear EFT with gauge gluons.
This finding provides strong evidence for the validity of our EFT approach and helps bridge the gap between nonperturbative lattice calculations and perturbative TMDPDF calculations.

The underlying physics of electron and positron production in high-energy collisions between heavy nuclei has been the subject of extensive study in recent years. These interactions not only offer valuable insights into the electromagnetic aspects of the collisions but also allow for the examination of the space-like properties of the photon, which can provide greater understanding compared to the more commonly studied bare electron. Through a detailed comparison between theoretical models and experimental data obtained using the JEkton Electron Spectrometer at CERN's SPS, researchers have analyzed the effects of electromagnetic forces on the distribution of produced electrons and positrons. They found that by removing these effects, a specific ratio of electron production at backward angles relative to forward angles reveals the underlying partonic structure of the collisions and is unaffected by the electromagnetic influences. These studies not only strengthen our knowledge but also offer new avenues for the investigation of the partonic structure of matter at low energy scales.

The rapidly growing number of urban cyclists makes them a significant group to study, especially in terms of ensuring their safety in traffic. By utilizing OSM data and collecting information from bike accidents, we have created a comprehensive database for the city of Berlin. With this database, we have applied machine learning techniques to predict areas prone to bike accidents and identified characteristics of cycling routes in relation to safety. The results show a strong connection between bike paths and safety, with more bike paths overall increasing the likelihood of a area experiencing fewer bike accidents. Conversely, areas with dedicated cycling lanes and bike trails show a contrasting relationship with a lower rate of such incidents. These findings can be useful for urban planners and city decision-makers in designing strategies to enhance traffic safety in Berlin and similar cities.

As robotic systems venture into real-world applications, the need to account for model inaccuracies and sensor disparities has become a necessity. These uncertainties have a profound impact on the accuracy of state estimation, which directly influences robotic decision-making. To address this challenge, we developed an adaptive trajectory planning framework, which incorporates the variability of state estimation into the paths generated. Our approach utilizes a uncertainty quantification technique, known as surrogate improved perturbations, to analyze the effects of parameter uncertainties on state estimation. Our method, proven in simulations of autonomous street-riding and underwater swimming, results in a 25% reduction in failure rate when integrating state estimation imperfections.

We establish the relationship where the covering number of a ring without unity is equal to the unital covering number of its extended ring to all elements. Consequently, certain key properties of rings with unity can be reduced to the corresponding properties of rings without unity. For instance, a ring $R$ has a unity for every element if and only if its covering number is one, which is equivalent to the statement that $R$'s quotient by its Jacobson radical $J(R)$ is a unital ring with covering number one. Additionally, a ring $R$ has a unity for every element if and only if every unital homomorphism from $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is an automorphism, where the set of unital homomorphisms from $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ has a covering number of one. Moreover, a ring $R$ has a unity for every element if and only if every unital $R$-homomorphism from $R$ to $R$ is an automorphism, where the set of unital $R$-homomorphisms from $R$ to $R$ has a covering number of one. Lastly, a base for the set of unital $R$-homomorphisms from $R$ to $R$ exists if and only if the covering number of $R$ is one.
