Several vertically executed federated learning protocols have been shown to be susceptible to privacy breaches.  A recent study presented an attack on this protocol by training a generator network to create artificial data similar to the hidden features of actual data, allowing the attacker to approximate individual gradients with accuracy and potentially compromise user privacy. We extend an existing model to analyze user loss privacy in federated models and provide a mathematical framework for analyzing privacy loss. We find that the attacker can pinpoint user-specific variables with very high accuracy using a limited amount of gradient information, thereby enabling them to circumvent gradient protection mechanisms.  Based on our findings, we suggest several methods to enhance the security of vertical federated learning against privacy breaches, with an emphasis on developing prototyping frameworks to enhance the protection of vertical FL protocols.

Utilizing the light-cone QCD sum rule, researchers have studied the decay $B^+ \to p \bar{\Lambda} \eta'$ in the dark sector. This investigation relies on the existence of dark baryons, specifically $B^{+}_{\textrm{dark}}$ and $\Lambda^{+}_{\textrm{dark}}$, which are predicted by sum rule analysis. The dark baryons have masses $M_{B_{\texm{dark}}}=5.52\pm0.14^{+0.46}_{-0.77}\,{\rm GeV}$ and $M_{\Lambda_{\texm{dark}}}=5.46\pm0.20^{+0.46}_{-0.67}\,{\rm GeV}$, and their weak decay to $p \bar{\Lambda} \eta'$ is influenced by various charm and strange quark contributions. This, in turn, determines the mass of a hypothetical particle $\chi$ that is produced in the $B^+ \to p \bar{\Lambda} \eta'$ decay and has properties resembling those of an axion. The study found that the transition $B^+ \to \chi \Lambda \eta'$ has upper bounds on the decay width of about $10^{-10}\,{\rm GeV}$, contingent on the $\chi$ particle's mass, dark baryon parameters, and various bary

Current approaches for managing crisis situations are focused on either maintaining overall system performance or protecting individual agencies from attack, but it is unclear how to optimize these performance measures in the face of terrorist threats. Our research allows these performance measures to vary based on the capabilities of opposing agencies and introduces a game-theoretic framework for evaluating the most effective defensive strategies. By analyzing this model, we demonstrate that a collective approach to resource allocation results in better outcomes than individual agencies making independent decisions, although some level of cooperation is required. Additionally, we provide bounds on the potential loss in performance that can result from uncooperative behavior. Finally, our analysis examines the characteristics of terrorist attacks that make defensive strategies less effective.

A comprehensive study on phase transitions of spherically symmetric cavity black holes in Einstein-Higgs theory is conducted, and novel findings are discovered.  The theoretical foundation of this research is based on a 5D Einstein-Higgs model representing a cavity containing a black hole.  The solution to the modified Klein-Gordon equation for the Higgs field enables us to derive thermodynamic equations and analyze the black hole's phase transitions.  Our analysis shows that the intrinsic electric potential significantly impacts the phase transition behavior, yielding a high-pressure hyperboloid in the phase diagram.  Furthermore, in the absence of the electric potential, our results reveal a first-order phase transition similar to those found in other models.  Lastly, a brief examination is taken to a 5D Einstein-Yang-Mills theory representing a cavity containing a black hole, and our investigation shows that the nature of the phase transition remains unchanged compared to the Einstein-Higgs theory.

This study presents an innovative sampling strategy for bag of words computing, which proves to be highly effective when handling lengthy documents and large caches. By bag sampling, the RAM usage is efficiently minimized and search speed is accelerated. Our research reveals that bag sampling consistently surpasses other methods of computing document ranking, namely Salton's original approach and First Choice. Moreover, the proposed strategy also enhances the search speed and average performance of the well-established index data structure, XOR trie. Our experiments show that using two million terms is enough to achieve optimal results, an improvement from the previously required 32 million terms. Consequently, the proposed strategy allows for faster document retrieval times, specifically an average 22% boost in average rank and a maximum 59% in worst-case rank compared to existing techniques. Our analysis also demonstrates that using more processors can still achieve significant speed-up in our model, an advantage over other approaches. Furthermore, we found that using the first term of a document for caching and salton's method can further enhance the search speed, resulting in a combination of these methods. Our suggested strategy has been formally proven and validated, showing its superiority in theoretical models as well as real-world applications.

Semi-supervised node classification on graphs, particularly with Graph Neural Networks, often relies on pseudo-labeling to utilize the limited labeled data efficiently. However, current pseudo-labeling methods may overexpand the class of a node based on incomplete information from its neighbors. To address this issue, we've developed a comprehensive framework for pseudo-labeling graph nodes. Our approach, CANE, considers both a node's local class density and the confidence of its predicted label when assigning labels to unsupervised nodes. Furthermore, CANE utilizes the collective knowledge shared among nodes to refine its class distribution and achieve better label efficiency. Our experimental results show that CANE outperforms existing pseudo-labeling methods and scales efficiently, requiring significantly fewer supervised nodes to produce comparable results. CANE can also be used as a general technique to enhance the training process of GNNs, particularly in semi-supervised node classification tasks.

The performance of plasma wakefield acceleration stage, named BWFA, is examined through its capabilities in producing betatron radiation. BWFA features an alternating phase relationship between the electron beam and the wakefield, achieved by using a grasing angle greater than the critical angle, resulting in a combination of strong electron bunching and a naturally mismatched beam radius, which reduces chromatic effects. However, radial size discrepancies between the electron beam and the plasma disruption cause a beam distribution imbalance over short distances, affecting the betatron radiation yield. Notably, this imbalance has a negligible impact on the global energy transfer to the drive beam but significantly impedes the acceleration of the driven beam. Consequently, a technique is proposed to rectify the beam distribution through a regulated injection into the plasma. By controlling the beam injection, the required asymmetry can be attained, ultimately facilitating both high-energy transfer to the drive beam and the effective application of Betatron radiation as an insightful diagnostic and acceleration tool in plasma-based accelerators.

This paper presents an application of the perturbed tree algorithm to private learning of unpruned decision trees, achieving varying levels of precision by allowing the learner to compromise between accuracy and data privacy. Experiments were conducted using datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository to compare the empirical utility of the developed method to an unaltered, publicly released version of C4.5 algorithm. Although the results indicate a noticeable decline in accuracy with larger dataset sizes, the new approach is still more precise than the fully private option. Moreover, approximately 80% confidence in the findings was maintained, with higher confidence observed in scenarios featuring smaller datasets. As a mid-point evaluation, this work examined an earlier version of this research featuring an incomplete implementation and discovered that privacy was maintained at a $80\pm5%$ rate. This outcome demonstrated that even partially implementing this technique, with roughly half the efficacy, still yielded reliable results without noticeable degradation in decision rates.

We introduce a revised moment-matching algorithm that minimizes regularized R'enyi divergence, ensuring the minimizer exists and can be precisely calculated. The new algorithm builds upon our previous work with maximum variants and shares properties with it, while also having its own distinct characteristics. Unlike standard moment-matching methods, our algorithm accommodates a wide range of values for the R'enyi order and maintains stability in the presence of additive noise. Furthermore, it can be used as a building block for regularized free entropy estimation and has practical applications in studying random graphs and complex systems, as well as optimizing inference procedures in graphical models. Our study also reveals that the proposed algorithm is closely related to the George algorithm used in Bayesian inference.

In the analysis of complex transaction data with multiple links, sparse chain event graph models have shown to be efficient alternatives to full linkage models. However, existing versions often struggle to produce distinct model configurations or require lengthy computation times. To address these shortcomings, new product Dirichlet priors for model parameters have been developed, which facilitates robust model selection and significantly reduces computation time. A novel Monte Carlo integration technique is presented to efficiently sample parameters for each model given its configuration. Through comprehensive simulation datasets of varying sizes, the proposed method is compared against alternative approaches, showing substantial performance improvements in terms of posterior recall and computation time. Applications to real-world datasets also demonstrate the superior efficiency of the proposed method in identifying sparse chain event graph models.

In a scenario involving the heavy ball method on a convex objective function with extra strictness, our goal is to minimize it using an iterative first-order process, with a step size that meets a specific threshold. Assuming a sufficiently large number of iterations, our work provides a minimize-maximize representation of the minimizer's suboptimality gap in terms of step size and damping coefficient, even in statistically worst-case scenarios. By means of variance control techniques, our minimax expression enables the derivation of convergence rates for both average and worst-case scenarios. In particular, our results reveal that doubling the damping coefficient results in a convergence rate that is comparable to that of the gradient descent method, albeit with an increased constant factor. Moreover, our proof relies solely on second-moment techniques and is non-parametric, meaning it does not rely on specific properties of the objective function.

This work introduces a novel method for adjusting the field of view of a distance sensor in mobile robots that follow a wall. Our approach takes into account the sensor's field of view when calculating the turning angle necessary to maintain wall proximity, utilizing the raycasting algorithm to determine the point on the wall towards which the robot should turn. Our method enables these robots to successfully track a wall even in situations where the angle between the sensor and the wall is narrow, provided that the wall is sufficiently close. Moreover, our approach allows mobile robots that follow a wall to navigate around corners, thanks to the flexible nature of our method which enables it to generalize to various types of scenarios, including scenarios where the angle between the sensor and the wall is far narrower than 90 degrees.

In a theoretical study, the superconducting gap parameter and microwave conductivity were examined across various levels of doping within the two-dimensional t-t'-t'' Hubbard model, using the self-consistent renormalization approach. A moderate amount of electron doping was simulated by adjusting the ratios of the hole-doping levels. The results indicated that the microwave conductivity exhibits two distinct states: one resembling BCS conductivity at low doping levels and another resembling a gapped state at higher doping levels. This transition from the superconducting state to a non-superconducting state can be accurately predicted by calculating the squared wave function of the gap parameter.

We investigate the solution space of the inverse curvature flow equation. Specifically, we consider a general anisotropic inverse curvature flow on closed convex curves in two-dimensional space. Our approach builds upon previous work by Demange and Ghosh, which focused on isotropic inverse curvature flow, and we establish new results by relaxing one of their conditions, demonstrating that a solution exists and is unique under different and mutually exclusive sets of conditions.

Our study centers around its failure, using the example of achieving precise control over individual cells within a plant's undulating leaf, as the plant grows over several days. To optimize movement, we used reinforcement learning to design policy functions for a simulated robotic arm tasked with mimicking a plant's temporal responses to light. The simulated robot, modeled after the tip of a plant cell, had to navigate a two-dimensional environment to perfect the replication of natural phototropism and circumnutation movements. However, when tested in a three-day trial, our best models struggled to adapt to changes in environmental conditions, such as increased light intensity, and their actions became less feasible as the plant aged, rendering them of limited practical use. The study demonstrates the potential of AI in analysis but also addresses the practical limitations and new challenges that arise from combining plant biology with machine learning techniques.

Researchers found that the scaling limit of the two-dimensional Ising model, established by David Wilson, consists of a conformally invariant field theory. Later, this was further developed by Donald Speegle who found that the self-avoiding polygon in a two-dimensional lattice, formed by randomly selecting adjacent edges, consists of simple random walks. Here, it is demonstrated that the combination of the two results implies the existence of a unique, conformally invariant self-avoiding polygon in a two-dimensional plane. Moreover, it was shown that the expected number of sides in this polygon grows as the area of the region increases. Additionally, it was found that the expected number of sides exhibits a variance that decreases like $O(1)$, signifying a first-order phase transition. To achieve this, a variant of the prior work by Pierre Le Gall was utilized, and it was established that the expected number of sides can be expressed through a conformally invariant integral. Moreover, it was derived that the expected number of sides, when normalized by $\sqrt{A}$, converges to a unique constant as the area $A$ increases.

High-throughput quantitative image analysis is vital for radiomics, enabling the extraction of quantifiable image-based biomarkers for patient stratification, prognostics, and surrogates of treatment response. Growing interest in machine learning has now made it a core component of radiomics. However, its full potential is restricted by image analysis artifacts stemming from image acquisition processes, degradation, and manipulation which are also amplified by the high-throughput approach, requiring each image to be processed multiple times. Conventional radiomics pipelines fail to rectify these errors, hindering the reliability and reproducibility of resulting features. This study investigates the extent of errors made by image analysis steps, including segmentation, segmentation evaluation, region-of-interest delineation, and feature calculation. It highlights the necessity of developing more robust techniques that can operate efficiently on large datasets, producing reliable and reproducible results, especially in the context of single-time-point analysis that is standard in radiomics.

Our theoretical calculations using the isospin-extended, resonation-based kaon photoproduction model have been performed to analyze the photoproduction cross sections and longitudinal polarization observables of the $K^+\Lambda$ system. We specifically focused on the second and third peaks in the cross section at approximately 1.7 and 1.8 GeV, respectively, and found that they are mainly attributed to the $\Sigma(1680)$ and $\Sigma(1750)$ resonances. Notably, these resonances have not been extensively studied in the context of kaon photoproduction reactions. Our study also enabled us to derive a set of coupled Betty-Salpeter equations for the $K^+\Lambda$ system, which can be utilized to generate high-quality experimental information by comparing calculations with data from upcoming and existing experiments.

To facilitate research in NLP and other fields, it is essential to create
a common framework for pre-processing pipelines that can be used, modified, and
evaluated collaboratively. Our proposal outlines a shared interface for
pre-processing pipelines that can be executed locally, remotely, and in the
cloud. By presenting a practical implementation based on Python and
DistributedSys, this document aims to inspire a broader discussion on the
design of a general utility for pre-processing pipelines that is suitable for
both research and production environments.

In 1929, Epicurus' ancient theory of a static, infinite universe was revived in a modified form. We present a model based on this idea, which aims to integrate dark energy and static scenarios for dark matter. This model involves a universe with no expansion but still compatible with the cosmological principle. Instead of expansion, gravitational forces act similarly to dark energy. A relationship similar to the Verlinde's modified gravity theory connects matter and dark energy. This static model offers a unified explanation for the universe's observed dynamics in its current state.

We introduce a Gaussian latent variable model to analyze student enrollment data, generating class schedules from underlying, hidden factors. The model is based on a probabilistic approach to course selection and caters to varying student preferences across different groups. It can capture a range of structures, from independent choices to correlated patterns, and is applicable to both large and small student populations. The model is tested on course enrollment data from two universities and demonstrates superior fit and accurate predictions when compared to a baseline approach. Additionally, we use the model to provide university admissions offices with valuable insights into student preferences and behavior.

A mathematical relationship called a differential game models interactions among multiple vehicle teams in a "swarm" or "schooling" state.  Researchers applied a principle known as Pontryagin's principle to translate the characteristics of these interactions into equations that can be simplified and analyzed.  This method reveals that optimal team behaviors can be described using a specific type of function, called a superposition of basic functions, and can also provide information about the speed of certain types of vehicle arrangements.  Although some of the results generated are theoretical "endless" limits, this approach is shown to have value in understanding and predicting behaviors within more realistic vehicle arrangements.  This method may also be used to develop guidelines for designing safe vehicle systems.

Logistic regression, a fundamental model in machine learning, often falls prey to data poisoning attacks. In our research, we examine a specific form of poisoning where the attacker directly manipulates the dataset by substituting genuine data with fabricated information. Our study expands existing knowledge on poisoning attacks within logistic regression, specifically in the dimension where $n\gg p$. Building upon a robust Bayesian approach, we develop a stylized logistic regression model and provide solid quantifiable metrics for data poisoning impacts, including convergence rates and accuracy measures. Our protective strategies against poisoning involve utilizing robust statistical priors and a Bayesian-Adjusted Stochastic Gradient Descent (sgd) method, dubbed CA-sgd. Our comprehensive analysis, encompassing convergence behavior, accuracy, and poisoning assessment, demonstrates the efficacy of these measures in safeguarding the model against poisoning when the number of data samples greatly exceeds the number of features.

Our task is to assess the sophistication of headlines written by humans and AI models, which we've trained samples of to mimic human writing styles. We used the BERT-NLI framework to train models for evaluating the authenticity of headlines, based on a large dataset transformed from the COSMA dataset. The transformed dataset, dubbed COSMA-HEX, comprises 57,393 transformed sentences, which surpass the typical size of datasets used in natural language processing, making our task more complex. Among the transformer models we tested, HEIC-BERT-G giant outperformed other models, achieving an impressive 93.56% accuracy in identifying human-written headlines, surpassing other models by 3-9%. Moreover, our results indicate that the largest transformer models we tested, including HEIC-BERT-G, exhibit higher accuracy in distinguishing human and computer-generated text. Finally, our work lays out future directions for creating more realistic AI-generated text, which could eventually contribute to a future society where human evaluation of AI is feasible is not feasible.

A novel method is developed to compute the density of states for chiral spin liquids in terms of their lattice topology. By employing this technique, we investigate the impact of a specific perturbation on a well-known chiral spin liquid in a square lattice, finding that it exhibits two distinct phases at low temperatures. One phase displays even density of plaquettes while the other has an odd density, leading to a gap in the system. Surprisingly, our results show that the location of the gap is determined by the density of odd plaquettes rather than the density of defects as previously suggested. Additionally, our research uncovers a relationship between the density of odd plaquettes and a global parameter of the system. Moreover, a broader application of this method reveals that the method is adaptable to various lattices, including those with multiple loops. Furthermore, our predictions for the density of states for chiral spin liquids on the square and triangular lattices align closely with simulation results from quantum Monte Carlo studies.

In light of the findings from Tau-LEE18, recent studies have examined the variance of antenna gains in large antenna arrays and suggested real-time calibration to mitigate this issue. To incorporate this insight into the parameters of the TILT experiment, a key aspect to consider is how the calibration process affects the antenna gain variance. Working under the assumption of "no correlation" within a sub-array, mathematical expressions for the antenna gain variance are derived in terms of the calibration parameters. Utilizing these expressions, the impact of real-time calibration on the antenna gain variance is evaluated and shown to significantly differ from its initial assessment. Specifically, real-time calibration does not successfully minimize the antenna gain variance to its initial level in the "very wideband" regime. Notably, calibration may even exacerbate the error, whereas it was previously thought to be essential for minimizing the phase error and maximizing signal efficacy in the "very wideband" regime for arrays with a large number of antennas.

The traditional Markowitz portfolio allocation technique is renowned for its capacity to measure risk. Nonetheless, the optimization problem inherent to this method can become impractical when dealing with large asset sets. This research demonstrates how to leverage machine learning, specifically autoencoding CGAN, in conjunction with a Markowitz-based portfolio framework, to enhance portfolio allocation efficiency and scalability. Our results show that, when applied to the S\&P 500 index, this hybrid approach consistently yields better portfolio performances compared to the standard Markowitz method, often in both real-world and simulated scenarios. To facilitate ease of use, the hybrid model's source code has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform.

To maintain theoretical consistency in transition functions between different Wilson coefficient evolutions, we apply the same VFN scheme parameters across distinct transitions, thereby simplifying the F2 structure function mapping process at the level of parton distributions. This approach ensures consistency between the QCD evolution of parton distributions and the VFN scheme. By solving a differential equation, we derive a precise calculation for the Adjoint transition function. Furthermore, we use the VINCIA parton shower to numerically determine A(gq)(N), and we show that incorporating higher-order terms in small-N asymptotics significantly improves the approximation. This improvement enables more accurate parton reconstruction and radiative corrections for high-energy proton collisions.

For several decades now, deep learning has been dominant in addressing visual perception challenges, particularly those involving large and carefully balanced data sets. However, their performance often significantly falters in scenarios involving limited or disproportionately weighted data in classification tasks. Due to this, Bayesian neural networks, which provide approximate uncertainty estimates, have gained popularity as a way to develop more robust models. Although they have shown potential, there is still lattice GRU (LeLUG) in the field that needs to be filled by further research. Our paper focuses on this topic. We have implemented a Bayesian approach on top of ResNet, incorporated an uncertainty-based loss function, and integrated a novel data augmentation method. The results indicate that by combining these components, it is possible to achieve an accuracy of 93.8% on the previously privately sponsored Publicly Shared Medical Images (PSMI) data set, surpassing the existing highest recorded performance. LeLUG's architecture's ability to capture the structure of the data is notably enhanced, resulting in more refined uncertainty estimates and significantly improved classification results. Furthermore, our approach's inclusion of uncertainty quantification enables direct assessment of reliability and prediction blockage rates. LeLUG's versatility is further demonstrated by our observation that it achieves nearly equivalent performance using different combinations of core components, illustrating its flexibility and substance. LeLUG's code is available online for public access at the address: https://github.com/MYELIN-HUB/LeLUG

The significant rise of social media over the past two decades has led to an unprecedented increase in the generation of content, making it a crucial platform for gathering news and information. Despite various efforts to bridge the gap between user-generated content and the general public, many platforms still pose substantial accessibility hurdles. Our comprehensive investigation involved replicating posts from eight top social media platforms to explore the difficulties users encounter in accessing this content. Our study employed both automated and manual methods to analyze nearly 19,000 posts, revealing that about a quarter of them contain complex visual content, making it inaccessible to users with disabilities. Our research fills a substantial gap in the field by exploring web accessibility from a unique perspective, providing valuable insights that can guide researchers, policymakers, and content creators in reducing barriers to content accessibility.

A crucial yet underdeveloped area of study in weighted graphs is the tensor join of two networks. This join, a novel mathematical construction, holds significant potential to expand our understanding of graph properties. Researchers have successfully used the tensor join to derive new insights into the characteristics of weighted graphs, particularly in relation to spectrum-based metrics. This work surpasses previous achievements by enabling the computation of a range of spectral properties in weighted hypergraphs, thanks to the introduction of the tensor join. To validate and verify our theoretical findings, we utilized established algorithms for approximating hypergraph spectra. The results of our experiments not only demonstrate the effectiveness of our theoretical predictions but also highlight the potential applications and advantages of joining graphs in both theoretical and practical contexts.

The quality of the images taken by the Hubble Space Telescope are the highest so far, but due to limitations in the space to which it can reach, observers are unable to study more distant objects in the far reaches of the universe that we know exist. Our team worked on testing a new technique called wavefront sensing and control using an infrared telescope located high on a mountain, and despite having several flaws, the telescope allowed us to take extremely clear images of stars using only two sessions. Our findings confirm that the telescope is functioning properly and we were able to remove many of its natural distortions. Our final image of the cluster M22, containing over 200,000 stars, is one of the biggest and most detailed ever seen, and it will help us to learn more about its evolution. Our results show that INSIST is just as good as the Hubble Space Telescope, and perhaps a bit better due to its larger diameter. Its high resolution allowed us to study the movements of over 60,000 stars, and it may be possible to see similar quality images of galaxies located several billion light-years away. Our research may also lead to developing new technologies to repair and improve the Hubble Space Telescope before it is retired.

In clinical trials, continuous outcomes often exhibit patterns that deviate from a completely random distribution. Research has shown that constrained longitudinal data analysis is a superior approach compared to ignoring such correlations or removing them through transformation. Furthermore, it has been observed that this method is not consistently the optimal strategy, prompting the exploration of alternative techniques. In this study, a new method that combines constrained analysis with a specific type of smoothing technique is proposed. The proposed method demonstrates several desirable characteristics, including the potential for significant statistical significance in trials, manually adjustable parameters to balance precision and efficiency, and ease of interpretation with respect to treatment effects. A simulation study was conducted to assess the proposed method's performance and compare it to the standard constrained analysis. The results showed that the new method achieves higher power in scenarios with a specific type of data pattern, while retaining power comparable to the standard constrained analysis in other scenarios. Additionally, the method's performance was comparable to an existing optimized approach in simulations involving varying degrees of data clustering.

A novel technique inspired by supervised learning, known as conformational space annealing, is introduced to enhance molecular simulation sampling. The method's central idea revolves around the concept of a dynamic, evolving bias potential energy function crafted to optimize sampling in the molecular system's reaction path. Furthermore, it leverages machine-learned potential energy function derivatives to refine the biasing, thereby streamlining the configuration space exploration process. Our approach demonstrates that machine-learned potential energy function derivatives prove more efficient than traditional, grid-based approximation. Case studies focusing on a peptide folding system and a zeolite formation process clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel method. It was observed that the CSA method efficiently replicates essential steps in the system's reaction path, particularly the formation of the MTL bond in a zeolite system, which was previously impossible to achieve with the conventional umbrella sampling technique. Overall, our results highlight the tremendous potential of CSA in successfully mapping out a system's reaction path, particularly in cases where first-principles modeling is feasible but simulation sampling is hindered due to energy minima separation.

The study initially outlines the conceptual underpinnings of a parabolic Hessian equation that complements a well-known elliptic equation with singular coefficients, suggesting a parallel between the two. Leveraging this relationship, estimates of $L^{n/(n-1)}$ terms are tied to the solution of the parabolic equation, whereas previous research in this area concerned $L^N$ estimates, where N is the conjugate exponent of the given singular coefficients. The solution to the parabolic equation is demonstrated using a perturbation approach combined with an energy method, the latter of which is adapted from prior applications to the elliptic equation.

This study aims to investigate various methods for translating the simply typed lambda-calculus into Church encodings, providing a broader understanding of this translation despite its limitations in capturing untyped functions. We examine several encoding strategies, assessing their expressiveness in terms of a new measure, which quantifies a translation's ability to reflect the overall structure of a term. This measure, called 'fidelity', distinguishes encodings that faithfully capture the overall structure of a term from those that only accurately reflect partial aspects of a term's constitution. We demonstrate that some injections into lambda-terms fail to convey the overall structure of untyped lambda-terms, whereas other injections, such as those employing (optionally) Curry-style embeddings, successfully capture this structure. Specifically, we show that a certain injection, incorporating a weak form of sum-yielding combinations, effectively conveys the overall structure of untyped lambda-terms, constituting a new bounds-on-operators scheme. We demonstrate this scheme's soundness with a typed internal language, established within the weak lambda-typed lambda-calculus, and leverage it to prove a fundamental theorem stating that this internal language's normal forms precisely correspond to the evaluations of all lambda-terms, both typed and untyped.

This study investigates the application of Lions-type measure derivatives in the context of nonlinear stochastic differential equations. By extending the measure impact technique to a Lions-type derivative, we establish a new method for solving variable exponent differential equations and present a key inequality. This approach is applied to a nonlinear stochastic differential equation to derive a condition for its existence and uniqueness, as well as to obtain a lower bound for the positive solutions. The result is a key inequality, known as Carmona and Zhong's inequality, and the long-term behavior of the solutions is proven to converge absolutely continuously to an invariant probability measure.

To generalize various topological results to groups, we introduce a family of group representations, each defined on a group's powerset. This allows us to discuss separation axioms and compactness in relation to these representations, with specific cases resembling well-known topologies such as normality and the hull-kernel theorem. A deeper analysis of a particular representation yields new results on topological groups, including the extension of a theorem by Arhangel'skii-Boros and a revised version of Puzynin's theorem.

The increasing utilization of database functions in public-cloud infrastructure has raised concerns about database data breaches. To resolve this issue, our approach disembeds database operations from its host and secures the data in the user's private environment. This technique accomplishes this goal by translating SQL queries into a sequence of the best possible approximations of query results using only partial database data. With an improved execution speed and reduced error margin when compared to partial execution, our method facilitates faster completion of operations with minimal inaccuracies, even in the absence of entire database contents. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses partial evaluation methods like stream slicing and chunking, and showcases its efficacy with real-world data sets and queries.

This research expands on existing collision avoidance strategies in robotics by incorporating a more accurate prediction model that utilizes error data. A new framework was developed to estimate the collision risk by combining probability distributions of robots' and obstacles' states. An optimized control strategy was designed to minimize risk by calculating the derivative of combined collision risk probability and applying a threshold. Simulation results indicate significant improvement in response time when using this refined model, although the overall speed is influenced by the complexity of the environment and the method used to calculate the combined distribution. Incorporating uncertainty and accounting for other robots' safety in the proposed framework is also explored.

Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Andromeda XXV, lies beyond the Milky Way's disk and possesses an extremely low brightness relative to mass ratio. Our study analyzes the galaxy's stellar population using data from the MaNGA survey, focusing on photometric periods and additional ancillary periods. We discovered that Andromeda XXV exhibits two distinct stellar populations, each with differing ages and metal contents, based on the spectral energy distribution fitting. The older population is very faint and contributes the majority of the galaxy's mass, while the younger population is brighter but holds only a small mass share. Both populations agree with previously established characteristics. Our results also indicate a relatively high metal content among the galaxy's older stars and a small iron abundance, which is consistent with other dwarf galaxies of similar characteristics.

In massive Machine-type Radio (mMRA), uplink grant-free access is being explored as a potential solution for low-power devices. To facilitate this, a novel form of sequence design has been proposed, which utilizes non-orthogonal sequences to boost multi-user multiplexing capacity and reduce and output variance in the aerometer. Theoretical findings indicate that non-orthogonal sequences can achieve a generalised version of the Loeliger bound in a low-Interferrence environment. Moreover, Paterson's bound has shown that optimal sequence length is directly proportional to the number of possible sequence phases. The linear nature of this relationship was found to offer improved sequence storage efficiency in comparison to orthogonal sequences. The theoretical optimality of this sequence length was then validated through simulations of an unlicensed band in a high-Interferrence environment, where the performance of these sequences was observed to surpass that of orthogonal sequences in both uplink and downlink modes.

To simulate long-term adiabatic dynamics in moist air, we develop models based on the consistent approximation of κ, leading to the creation of the κtilde and κtildebar approximations. These approximations mimic the properties of the limiting logarithmic equation, which is the exact diabatic solution for pure water vapor, but with significant reductions in computational complexity. Furthermore, these models allow for larger time steps and enhanced computational efficiency, and are therefore more suitable for long-term simulations. In particular, the κtildebar model is proposed as an alternative to the standard κ approximation, providing a method for determining when the κ approximation is applicable and reliable. We also establish a theoretical framework, which facilitates a quantitative understanding of the errors associated with the κ approximation, thus providing a basis for improving simulations. To illustrate its impact, we demonstrate that implementing the κtildebar model in cloud-resolving models can accurately reproduce the results obtained with the exact limiting equation, using time steps that are approximately two orders of magnitude longer. It is expected that the κtildebar model will be particularly beneficial in resolving clouds where simulations often necessitate the long-term integration of complex systems.

We introduce an exterior algebra alternative, tailored to $\mathbb F_1^{\pm}$-algebras as generalizations of $\mathbb F_1$-algebras, which also encompass Boolean algebras and rig algebras. This new concept is shown to be a natural extension of the classical exterior algebra, with its free modules equivalent to the collections of minimal independent sets in weighted linearly independent collections, thus serving as the basis for an abstract matroid framework. Furthermore, we establish a duality theorem, demonstrating a close relationship between dual matroids, interior and exterior algebra operators, and the dual of the Grothendieck ring of independent sets. Lastly, we examine the common underlying theory of $\mathbb F_1^{\pm}$-algebras and matroids as they pertain to algebraic and combinatorial structures.

Recent studies have demonstrated that attention-based neural networks can effectively tackle complex dialogue state tracking tasks, but have yet to be integrated into conventional decoding frameworks for state tracking. In contrast, traditional CNN-based models with attention have been successfully applied to similar tasks, and we now propose a new approach that combines the two by replacing the conventional CNN encoder with a an attentional confusion network encoder. This hybrid model shows significant improvements over its single-component counterparts, and we have also verified its reliability through cross-validation using the DSTEC challenge dataset. Notably, our model has successfully matched the performance of leading models on the dataset while boasting a more versatile architecture.

A method for calculating weighted sums of invariants on a moduli space of vector bundles, weighted by points on a projective space, is established. This method involves using a regularised sum, effectively counting general positions, to overcome issues with finite scheme points. As an example, the regularised sum invariants for symplectic and quiver varieties are determined and shown to coincide with known regularised sum invariants from a prior study. Building on this, the regularised sum invariants for different types of Hilbert schemes are calculated and it is demonstrated that they match expectations derived from a prior investigation.

A particular type of access structure, known as universal structures, have drawn attention due to their relatively low complexity. It's been proven that a specific type of universal structure, featuring n minimal qualified sets, has an asymptotic complexity of n log n. This result has led to the hypothesis that similar structures, featuring various minimal qualified sets, also exhibit a complexity linearly proportional to n. In an effort to test this hypothesis, we first introduce a concept called disjunctive structures, which encompass a specific category of universal structures, and we formulate a specific substructure, termed the minimal core. In this formulation, the minimal core represents the collection of all minimal qualified subsets, and we demonstrate that it constitutes a crucial component of the original structure. In an additional effort to examine this concept's utility, we introduce a specific type of structures, known as shared universal structures, and we demonstrate that the shared minimal core represents a crucial component of this concept as well. In this concept, the shared minimal core constitutes the collection of all minimal qualified subsets that are common across all participants. In an additional effort to examine this concept's utility, we introduce a specific type of structures, known as shared universal structures, and we demonstrate that the shared minimal core constitutes a crucial component of this concept as well. In this concept, the shared minimal core constitutes the collection of all minimal qualified subsets that are common across all participants. In an additional effort to examine this concept's utility, we introduce a specific type of structures,

Quantum systems experience decoherence due to loss of coherence, which can be caused by various noise types, the source of which remains unknown. Determining the best noise model to use is crucial for making informed measurements. While previous research suggested using optimal estimators for gooney, the current noise model of the day, other models, including gauge, george, and gregory, may be more accurate. By comparing the performance of optimal estimators for each model, this study evaluates their effectiveness in distinguishing between different noise types. Focusing on two-qubit systems and measurements of the von Neumann entropy, our findings show that optimal estimators for these models achieve significantly better assessment of decoherence than previous optimal gooney models. Moreover, the optimal gooney estimator from previous research is not optimal for other noise types, which implies that previous optimality results can be costly in terms of estimation performance. Since optimal estimators for different noise types may vary, learning which model is most suitable can lead to a substantial improvement in measuring and quantifying decoherence.

Investigations into edge localized modes (ELMs) have historically focused on their gyrokinetic representations, requiring expensive supercomputing power to study. A cost-effective alternative, first introduced in 2018, utilized a combined computational approach to investigate how ELMs cause ion loss through simulations. For the first time, this approach's methodology is being used to investigate the creation of palm tree modes (PTMs) that appear on the Poloidal Pitch Angle (PA) space grid. By simulating ELMs through the finite-orbit-width approximation and combining the results with the PTM density structure from full-f kinetic simulations, this research reveals how PTM densities evolve and offer new insights into the geometric properties of ELMs. Crucially, this work Confirms that PTMs are generated from the same magnetic island source as ELMs and proposes that PA modes could act as'seeds' for ELMs.

While various techniques have been developed to facilitate continual learning in the face of ever-expanding datasets, few of these methods have been rigorously evaluated using pre-trained models developed for other specific tasks. This research investigates the effectiveness of a simple nearest mean classifier in this context and finds that it often surpasses more complex, continually learning methods when using pre-trained models. Our findings are based on various benchmark datasets, each modified to increase in difficulty and size, and highlight the importance of evaluating learning methods across a range of scenarios.

Language technology has advanced to the point where it is now a necessary tool for identifying hate speech, despite the Socio-cultural and semantic complexities involved. However, it is the socio-cultural context in which hate speech is understood that truly hinders its detection. Researchers have attempted to integrate socio-cultural context into machine detection of hate speech by utilizing various approaches, including the development of hate speech definitions and training data specifically for NLP tasks. Our research aims to explore the socio-cultural context within German hate speech through a linguistic and semantic analysis, also examining contemporary detection systems and highlighting the need for further research in this area.

We examine collective oscillations in connected networks of smooth muscle cells, focusing specifically on the differences caused by the distribution widths of individual cell properties. Our findings suggest that altering the widths significantly impacts the frequency and stability of oscillating pairs, while maintaining the same mean values does not necessarily lead to identical results. Broadly distributed parameters facilitate the emergence of stable oscillations in pairs, but fail to do so at more uniform parameter settings. We have also computed stability ratios for pairs of connected cells, providing a theoretical starting point for further investigations into higher-order network interactions.

A new approach for automated bug fixing using deep learning has been developed.
The method, known as DeepBug, was tested on 2462 bugs from three open-source
systems and compared to prior research which used smaller datasets.  The
evaluation found that DeepBug successfully identified 31% of bugs and exactly
mirrored human fixes for 8% of cases. Furthermore, it determined fixes for
44% of bugs and matched the effectiveness of human fixes for 22% of cases.
Compared to prior research, DeepBug outperformed DeepSE on similar datasets
and outperformed three other systems on new datasets with increased bug
complexity. The tests showed that DeepBug consistently surpassed the other
systems.

This research offers a novel inner perspective on achieving optimal communication performance in various settings, including coding for abstract channel descriptions and coded interference systems where multiple channels overlap.  Interference systems are modeled where different channels share resources at the level of encoded messages, rather than just the receiver end, allowing for a sharper understanding of overall channel performance.  Inner bounds based on this approach lead to improved estimates of overall channel performance in key communication scenarios, including broadcast channels and two-channel overlap systems.  Furthermore, the proposed theory addresses a long-standing question about achieving optimal performance in channels with overlapping channels, where previous estimates based on different methods yielded different outcomes.  The researchers also provide coded interference systems examples where the new inner bounds yield better estimates of overall channel performance than previous methods.  Finally, the researchers offer potential avenues for enhancing the inner bounds of coded interference systems, including expanding the theory to encoded message systems with more than two channels.

This research expands upon the multifidelity discriminant analysis (MDA) method, initially developed for analyzing particle distributions in ratio, in order to study angular properties of particles in the transverse momentum plane. New coefficients for measuring asymmetry patterns have been introduced and their formulas derived, along with the development of multifidelity observables that can be used with the discriminant analysis to obtain precise estimates. The method is applied to data from CMS experiments to create full-simulated f-models which help assess bias in generating pseudo-experiments based on smooth hadron correlations. The results suggest pseudo-experiments may exhibit biased assessments of certain asymmetries, while remaining accurate in measuring ratios of observables.

The application of machine learning in healthcare is significant, but it's crucial that health data is not compromised when training models. Certain risk-prone machine learning models, like those engineered with gradient descent, can expose sensitive information if the training process is not secure. While efforts have been made to quantify and mitigate the risks of model output, the dangers associated with auxiliary information disclosed during the prediction process have been largely neglected. We've developed an improved machine learning model that prioritizes protection and minimizes the likelihood of information leakage, making it the first to rigorously quantify the risks associated with auxiliary information revealed at the moment of prediction. Our model's added layer of security employs reversible transformations and jigsaw puzzle-style fragmentation, making it the first to rigorously quantify the risks associated with information leakage. Our analysis confirms that traditional gradient-based training can exacerbate information leakage risks. Conversely, our novel model not only eliminates the possibility of gradient-based information leakage but also reduces the risk of predictive information leakage by a substantial factor. Our work offers an efficient solution for designing machine learning models that prioritize the security of auxiliary information and real-world applications, providing empirical evidence that selective information disclosure can provide an added layer of security.

Recent advancements in wireless communication systems have driven research on decentralized graph neural networks (DGNNs) to predict wireless channel behaviors effectively. However, DGNNs lack robustness when confronted with unexpected variations in wireless channels, contrary to their performance in typical test datasets. To enhance the reliability of DGNNs, this work suggests training them with synthetic data generated by operating the models on a distribution different from the original one. By doing so, DGNNs can better predict wireless channels under unpredictable conditions, extending their capabilities to real-world scenarios. Building upon this concept, a new meta-learning framework, called SMGNN, is introduced to create synthetic data by modeling the distribution of real wireless channels. SMGNN employs two components: a GNN-based synthesizer that produces high-quality synthetic data to aid GNN training, especially in GNNs with distributional biases. The effectiveness of SMGNN is demonstrated through various wireless channel estimations and comparisons with multiple baseline methods. The research findings confirm that SMGNN can significantly boost the reliability of DGNNs while maintaining their learning efficiency. Ultimately, SMGNN presents a novel, efficient approach to address wireless communication challenges using DGNNs.

We analyze the connection between a city's size and the severity of violent crime in the United States. Drawing on a comprehensive database of American cities spanning nearly nine decades, we employ cutting-edge quantile regression techniques to examine how the risk of crime varies among smaller cities relative to New York City, controlling for factors like police presence and regional socioeconomic conditions. The results reveal that, historically, cities near the metropolis experience more severe crime, and since 2010, tighter city competition may contribute to higher homicide rates in these areas. Conversely, cities surrounded by numerous other cities and universities tend to exhibit lower crime rates, possibly due to increased competition for resources or the presence of higher education, which may deter crime.

Generalizing Nesterov's acceleration technique to stochastic gradient descent has been attempted previous, however previous attempts failed to match the convergence rate of the accelerated method when using adaptive step sizes generated by backtracking. We provide theoretical evidence that accelerating SGD with adaptive step sizes is feasible, achieving a convergence rate comparable to the accelerated method when using fixed step sizes. We validate this theory through successful empirical applications in training overparameterized models and developing a robust loss function for training to minimize overfitting.

The role of axions and axion-like particles in the history of the cosmos continues to be investigated by both traditional astrophysical and cosmological methods. Although the primary function of this research is to understand dark matter's influence on large-scale structure formation and the universe's thermal background, we evaluate recent signs of annihilation-driven ALP radiation and axion dark matter-induced modifications to the cosmological Hubble expansion. By interpreting these elements within a unified framework, called the axion landscape, we find that certain characteristics of the ALP system, such as local scale symmetry and dark matter's gravitational interactions, are supported by observations of the cosmic microwave background and the large-scale structure. Notably, our findings indicate that the mass of the primary axion, $f_1$, is significantly heavier than the previously suggested range of approximately keV, while the mass of the second axion, $f_2$, is constrained to be much lighter. Although this does not necessarily imply that the primary axion is not a suitable dark matter candidate, it does mean that the influence of $f_1$ on the early universe's kinematic state is less significant than previously estimated. Furthermore, our study shows that the predicted dark matter density, $\Omega_{\rm DM}$, is largely unaffected by the specific mass scales of the axion fields. Additionally, our analysis highlights the substantial potential of upcoming experiments to reveal the characteristics of the axion landscape through measurements of the Hubble expansion, dark matter

The theory of nonlinear self-oscillating systems is closely related to a bosonic oscillator that interacts with its surroundings. Researchers have extensively studied the latter as a fundamental model in theoretical physics. In our work, we apply a version of this bosonic oscillator model that incorporates nonlinear damping to understand the behavior of nonlinear self-oscillating systems. To validate our approach, we use it to examine a widely utilized model of a nonlinear oscillator subjected to random forces. Our analysis reveals that random damping has a dual effect: not only does it thermalize the oscillator but also it gives rise to random limit cycles. The probability of finding the oscillator in a specific energy state follows a temperature-dependent dynamical spiral pattern. With an increase in the damping's nonlinear aspect, this spiral tightens and its characteristics merge with the dynamical behavior of a linear oscillator in a high-damping environment. Our findings also show that while precise oscillations are scarce, the presence of quasi-limit cycles is quite universal. They appear at various non-linear damping levels and are also present in a hypothetical "dissipative dielectric" with dielectric constants much larger than those seen in normal materials.

Our proposed approach, DexGraspNet, represents a significant innovation in grasping inferences for robotic hands, enabling the creation of more stable and diverse hand positions with an robotic hand. Through the utilization of a differentiable model that combines a grasp network with a physical simulator, DexGraspNet synthesizes more robust hand positions compared to previous methods and offers improved accuracy. Our experimental results demonstrate that DexGraspNet surpasses existing techniques, yielding better performance in terms of grasp stability and diversity for a range of robotic hands, including hands adapted from MRI data and a 6 DoF robotic hand modeled from a fish claw. To facilitate research in grasp synthesis, we are releasing DexGraspNet along with several other contributions, including a novel Grasp Synthesis Benchmark and a Grasp Synthesis Dataset that expands upon the traditional Grasp Dataset. These tools provide valuable tools for the evaluation of newly proposed methods and offer insights into current limitations in the field.

To enhance the efficiency of synthetic aperture sonar systems by alleviating their high sampling rates, we present a novel, flexible, and adaptive sampling technique based on compress sensing. In the proposed rCASPR method, the sampling schedule is optimized along exponential B-spline trajectories, facilitated by a CS algorithm with guaranteed success under specific conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that rCASPR yields a diminished point-source blurring (increasing image contrast by approximately 50%) and produces reconstructions of greater image size with shorter acquisition times, when compared to traditional linear sampling. Moreover, rCASPR's ability to adjust its reconstruction parameters does not incur additional data collection, thereby offering a flexible trade-off between reconstruction quality and data collection rate.

Teacher-student learning methodologies have garnered significant interest recently, with initial focus on diffuse knowledge transmission from teacher to student models. This paper argues that teacher-student learning constitutes a two-phase process: initial channel-based knowledge transfer via channel pruning, followed by parameter optimisation. Channel pruning has long been applied as a model compression technique to eliminate redundant channels and retain key ones. This work reveals that these pruned channels directly embody the essence of teacher-student learning objectives and serve as optimal channel parameters for student models. Consequently, we propose a two-phased TS framework. Firstly, conventional channel pruning is leveraged to extract crucial parameters from teacher models. These pruned channels, incorporated into student models, are then optimised using a novel, two-part learning objective. Such a framework upholds theoretical efficacy and during evaluation on various benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms prevailing teacher-student learning approaches in model compression experiments. Additionally, our research demonstrates that these pruned channels serve as effective initialisations for student models, enhancing training convergence speed. Code accompanying this paper can be found here: https://github.com/whylee/TS-model-compression-paper.

We investigate the variant of the van der Berg-Wunderlich conjecture and focus on a specific topology related to it. Our approach involves dividing the problem into more manageable parts by selecting particular subsets of linear-like submersion functions. We will introduce two new topological invariants within a specific group action and demonstrate their relevance to the problem at hand. By constructing these invariants, we aim to provide a clearer understanding of the problem's structure, ultimately enabling us to prove the more restricted 'additive' form of the conjecture. Additionally, we can also validate the'multiplicative' version of the conjecture for the specified subset, thereby providing a comprehensive explanation of the given conjecture in a broader context.

Ecosystems that rely on grazing, such as those found in the Australian outback and the steppes of Asia, often face decline due to climate change causing drought and over-grazing. Drawing on the principles of percolation theory, researchers study how changes in aridity and spatial interactions among plants, herbivores, and vegetation influences the long-term survival of these ecosystems. Typically, ecological systems respond to increased disturbance by shifting locally to a more critical or random state. However, incorporating the influence of spatial connections beyond immediate surroundings using non-local interactions proves to greatly enhance the ability of these ecosystems to resist the effects of increasing aridity. Furthermore, incorporating the influence of temporal connections also reveals that non-local interactions play a pivotal role in the ecosystem's resilience during transitions to random states. Lastly, the influence of spatial connections beyond immediate surroundings supplements existing explanations of ecosystem dynamics, such as the tipping points in grassland ecosystems, contributing to greater ecosystem resilience during increases in aridity.

In various applications like speech processing and text analysis, adaptive input influences the operation of traditional estimators in these methods. Current techniques of dimensionality reduction often rely on non-robust estimators and provide no protection against the effects of adaptive input. To address this, we've developed an estimator that combines dimensionality reduction with robust protection against adaptive input. We've also explored the capabilities of this estimator in both theory and practice and demonstrated its benefits in real-world datasets.

Three distinct structural configurations of the $[{\rm Cu_2O_2}]^{2+}$ model, influenced by different angular distances, have been investigated using graphitic nanotube and peptide nanotube surfaces. Calculations of isomerization energies between these configurations have revealed considerable variations. Notably, the rotation-based isomerization process exhibits a dependence on the bond angles of the model, resulting in significantly differing energies - 0.70, 1.30, and 1.80 eV - for configurations characterized by distinct angular distances.

High-frequency trading (HFT) involves transferring data at extremely high speeds, ideally in sub-100 picosecond timeframes, which current internet and cloud infrastructure cannot accommodate. Quasi-quantum communication technologies, such as optical fiber systems utilizing quantum-distributed keys and classical simulatable protocols, may offer a viable solution for HFT. This study demonstrates the feasibility of using HFT over long distances using only classical protocols in optical fiber networks, which can also meet the requirements of quantum computing counterparts. Our experiment successfully distributed 32GB of data over 534S kilometers in the EMU laboratory of the National Optical Fiber Laboratory, Nankai University, utilizing a line of 10 optical fibers. Our results, achieved with a simplified setup using two optical switches and two photodetectors, demonstrate data transfer over 534 kilometers with an 83.72% success rate, and we found that the connection remained stable even during testing at extremely high speeds, such as in the vicinity of 400MHz. Our protocol operates in a distributed fashion, and we were able to demonstrate its effectiveness on multiple nodes without requiring central coordination, utilizing an incentive system based on blockchain technology to ensure security and trustfulness. Our protocol also exhibits high resistance to interference and attacks, with an 82.02% success rate when subject to various forms of noise and eavesdropping.
