A straightforward mathematical framework is developed to accurately compare the temperature fluctuations of cosmic microwave background (CMB) Te,V values to the corresponding inflationary perturbations. It's acknowledged that CMB temperature anisotropies are the visual representation of inflationary perturbations. Although there is widespread understanding of both concepts, there seems to be a lack of a basic mathematical framework that connects them directly. This work aims to address this gap in knowledge. A fundamental framework in this paper expresses CMB temperature anisotropies as the sum of inflationary perturbations and secondary physical processes, and further assumes that these perturbations can be described through a complete set of linear equations. As a result, a particular method for distinguishing the primordial CMB signal from observational data is offered. Furthermore, it is emphasized that observing the CMB anisotropes does not provide the value of the Hubble parameter during inflation, and that determining the Hubble parameter during inflation is equivalent to calculating the spatial derivative of the Hubble parameter. Additionally, an interpretation of inflationary perturbations as a cosmic wave function in the classical de Sitter space is offered.

A recent global analysis of the two Higgs doublet model revealed that the type-X version successfully addresses both the discrepancies in the muon's magnetic moment and the mass of the W boson. This study investigates whether a global optical phenomenology approach can pinpoint the parameter space responsible for matching experimental observations in the Standard Model. By utilizing a global fit to various measurements, we demonstrate that type-X two Higgs doublet model can once again rectify the discrepancies in the muon's magnetic moment and the W boson mass. Nonetheless, a slightly larger total annihilation width for the Higgs boson results from incorporating the latest measurements from LHC. Moreover, a significant relationship exists between the coupling of the Higgs boson to gauge bosons and the curvature of the preferred curvature of the Higgs boson field, which arises from incorporating CKM matrix constraints. This investigation also identifies a potential explanation for the anomalies in lepton universality from a specific type-X two Higgs doublet model scenario. However, a more significant total annihilation width for the Higgs boson is needed to match the measurements from Bell II laboratory. Furthermore, using a global phenomenological approach, we identify a potential role for the type-X two Higgs doublet model in resolving the discrepancies between the predictions of the Standard Model and the observations from SN1987a concerning the cosmic neutrino background. A more stringent constraint is placed on the neutrinoless double beta decay of the Higgs boson at future references

Crowdsourcing has numerous applications in software engineering due to its potential to tap into infinite resources of information. In the context of evolving software, concept location is a critical process that facilitates the identification of changes between versions of source code. Most existing concept location approaches rely on manual or automated input, but they often struggle with the limitations of having only one source of information. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel approach that leverages crowdsourcing to accelerate concept location. Specifically, this technique involves leveraging external knowledge to refine initial concepts, ultimately improving the accuracy of this location in existing software. To evaluate this method, two leading concept location tools were modified to incorporate crowdsourcing, and the results demonstrated a substantial reduction in the number of required searches by an average of 62%.

Conversational AI models are increasingly used for applications like customer service and language assessment, but they have a limitation: they can't tell real conversations from artificially generated ones. This fake language, although creative, doesn't follow the rules of natural conversation. A recent method for detecting artificially generated text, called Neural Entrainment Distance (NED), can determine the authenticity of conversations through its analysis of imitation networks' ability to synchronize with target networks. In extensive testing with various services' models, it was found that NED could identify real conversations in over 90% of cases. This effectiveness makes NED a valuable tool for validating the performance of these models in applications. However, it was observed that further refinement of imitiation networks using NED could enhance the distance metric, opening new areas of research. Conversely, further enhancement of genuine conversations using NED could diminish its effectiveness, which warrants more research. Therefore, it is recommended that services' effectiveness be evaluated alongside conventional metrics and that the benefits and drawbacks of using NED be carefully considered.

Our research involves generating artificial spectra for galaxies using simulated data
for several key optical spectral lines, which we then analyze by applying various tools,
including a BPT diagram based on the [OIII]II, [NII]I, H$\alpha$, H$\beta$, and
H$\gamma$ lines. We aim to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by making
predictions for 13 characteristics of galaxy spectra, including strong spectral line
intensities, Hubble space telescope color indices, and various ionization and gas
density indicators. We compare the performance of multiple machine learning models in
reconstructing the target variables, employing a consistent framework where a
training dataset is separated from a separate evaluation dataset, and assessing the
quality of predictions using a subset of the original data. We also make publicly
available the corresponding python code, as well as comprehensive lists of the
machine learning models, pre-trained neural networks, and other functions used in our
research, ensuring full transparency in our results. Our research makes significant
contributions to generating high-quality artificial galaxy spectra, which can be
utilized in various astronomy research applications, and is particularly suited for
simulating large collections of galaxy data with numerous spectral measurements.

Most current action segmentation approaches rely on individual video frames with overall accuracy levels reaching 83%. However, existing methods only consider the temporal relationships between actions, neglecting how actions interrelate within a scene. This deficiency is addressed by our proposed algorithm, Co-occurrence Action Parsing, which ensembles past action segments with concurrent ones in the scene to enhance accuracy. Evaluating our method on the NTU-RGB+D and Kinetics-HD datasets, we achieve notable gains of 8.2% and 7.1% mAP improvements, respectively, outperforming previous state-of-the-art action segmentation methods.

Building on measurements of the Λb → Λνℓ decays with high-energy proton-proton collisions, researchers have analyzed the Λb → Λνℓ decays, featuring neutrino-antineutrino latticework final states, ℓ = e, μ, and neutrino-antineutrino latticework states, ℓ=τ. These analyses were achieved thanks to advanced identification methods enabling the detection of hadron decays in the Λb → Λνℓ chain even in the presence of substantial background from top quark decays. Calculations of the relative production rates of Λb → Λνℓ decays involving W and Higgs bosons have been performed and their implications have been examined. Moreover, a model incorporating the hadron decays of the W and Higgs bosons has been used to provide the first direct observation of these processes in the Λb → Λνℓ chain, and the subsequent cross-sections for the Λb → Λνℓ decays have been determined.

Automated grading systems enable instructors to offer various types of feedback to students automatically, typically using code coverage as a metric. We evaluated the effectiveness of four simulated feedback methods in a Java testing environment, comparing coverage and performance outcomes. The methods comprised straightforward error messages, reference solutions, positive feedback, and a combination of the previous two approaches. Surprisingly, despite consistently providing four different feedback types, a significant portion of code segments remained untested across conditions. When examining the most effective feedback methods, we found that providing both error messages and example solutions within feedback did not yield significantly better coverage results compared to simply providing example solutions. Furthermore, students whose feedback was limited to code coverage metrics performed equally well as those receiving more detailed feedback. The findings suggest that current automated grading systems may not be providing the expected insights to enhance students' performance. One potential solution could lie in employing search-based techniques to recommend relevant test cases that students have yet to write.

Unsupervised domain adaptation without source data presents significant difficulties for classical domain adaptation techniques, as it's impossible to calculate source distribution parameters. To resolve this problem, we've developed an unsupervised domain adaptation method that removes the need for source data. This approach involves creating artificial source distribution parameters by analyzing target data distribution and establishing a correlation between source and target data. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior performance on unsolved domain adaptation problems, as it performs better or comparable to existing methods on solved problems, as evidenced by our experiments using the widely-used Geodesic Deviation metric and classification tasks.

Inside a gas core reactor, a pressurized gas orbited an actuator wheel, forming reaction wheels that generated thrust. The thruster's performance relied heavily on its gas properties, which the authors explored through simulations and experiments within a closed testing facility. To obtain precise measurements, they conducted experiments under low-pressure environments replicated from the actual gas core reactor. The researchers found that reducing the pressure decreased the thruster's pressure drop and improved its combustion stability. Conversely, a pressure increase prompted larger gas flow rate deviations and diminished combustion stability, ultimately restricting the thruster's efficiency. Specifically, the pressure variation affected the mass flow rate by up to 25%, though the pressure drop remained a consistent 10% throughout the simulations.

We propose a novel neural network architecture that incorporates a structured layout with a symmetrical, rotating layout near the origin, and a static interpretation of detector variables. This approach benefits from existing detector simulation data, which is typically invested in by experimental collaborations, allowing us to initialize weights based on these variables. Using a factorized Gaussian prior and alternating estimation and prediction steps, we can efficiently train the network to optimize various objectives. Due to the network's inherent stability, gradient descent can be used for initialization, leading to consistent results. Additionally, we can easily implement new objectives without recalimating the network's weights. Utilizing this architecture, we achieved state-of-the-art performance in top-t t-bar channel classification and developed a method for identifying the spin of sub-jet particles in jet fragmentation processes, making it suitable for analysis in final-state jet physics.

In order to model the accurate spectral characteristics of Ultra-Hot Jupiters and M-dwarfs, it's crucial to utilize atmospheric models that generate a consistent line-list of TiO/TiO2 features. However recent developments in line-lists for TiO and TiO2 have yielded different results, especially in the UV and blue regions of the spectrum. By analyzing the TiO and TiO2 data sets, including those from the curated line-lists from Banzmer et al. (2018) and Kaminski et al. (2017), we discovered significant differences in UV and blue line characteristics, which lead us to recommend the Banzmer et al. data set for modeling these types of planets and low-mass stars. Furthermore, we found that using the Banzmer et al. data set results in models that align with the observed spectral and eclipse features of the hot Jupiter WASP-12b. Nonetheless, our attempt to model its highly irradiated exosphere using either TiO or TiO2 led to the conclusion that achieving a full thermal pressure reproduction proves challenging with the current TiO/ TiO2 data sets. Ultimately, directly observing the molar TiO/ TiO2 absorption in the exosphere of WASP-12b reveals the necessity of refining the TiO/ TiO2 data for an accurate description of the thermal pressure of these types of exoplanets.

This document explains the implementation of the ASPParser, a parser that uses Answer Set Programming, specifically designed for logic programs with annotated tags. The algorithm is particularly suited for grammars with recursive structures, including aggregate rules, in the EL-KR language. The implementation of the ASPParser is unique as it is the first known instance of integrating a programming language interpreter with a logic programming language, in this case, using aggregates. Our approach involves translating tagged logic programs into the standard Prolog language, using the MonoReify tool, which provides a comprehensive implementation of logic programs with annotations. The resulting Prolog language, along with the provided logic program, is then compiled using the Reify tool and treated as a conventional Prolog program, callable through a web interface. The associated paper, "Efficient Analysis of Aggregate-Labeled Logic Programs with Answer Set Programming," details the methodology used in this project.

A new framework for expressing the second law of thermodynamics has been developed, 
building upon a previous theory that described the dynamics of multiple resource systems.
The first law was reformulated by introducing a quasi-Serbinowski operator which keeps 
a system's overall resource state unchanged. By incorporating the Ginzburg-Landau operator, 
a new inequality was established, capturing the essential characteristics of irreversible 
processes and verifying the second law. The versatility of this approach was demonstrated 
by applying it to the management of both thermal and coherent photon resources.

To develop estimators for various information metrics such as mutual information, several recent studies utilized moments of random variables. Their findings were later adapted to design scalable algorithms for discovering latent variables in large datasets. This work capitalizes on the connection between information metrics and moments to introduce novel estimation techniques, which enhance existing methods in two key ways: allowing a predefined level of estimation error and addressing datasets with arbitrary distribution assumptions. Additionally, we provide technical considerations regarding the optimization of general Inequality-based estimators, similar to those derived from the Second Moment Method in computer science, statistical, and mathematical fields.

When dealing with time series that exhibit heavy-tailed distributions, a unit root test for multiplicative heteroskedasticity is developed to improve on previous estimators that were optimized for normal distributions. A consistent estimator for a component that causes heavy tails is introduced along with a test statistic, resulting in a more robust test in the presence of finite variance and multiplicative heteroskedasticity. A simulation study shows that the proposed test is effective with smaller sample sizes and resists the influence of outlier-induced power distortion. Furthermore, the test's performance remains reliable under various scenarios, including changing sample sizes, when sample sizes are large or small, and in datasets with or without common stochastic trends. When applied to real currency data, the test indicates the presence of common trends shared by several currencies over long periods of time. Additionally, the test identifies individual currencies that exhibit unique trends.

From a quantum coding perspective, we systematically examine the properties of the two-dimensional, rank-three hyperbolic group homomorphisms. These group homomorphisms are characterised by a specific form, allowing their Cayley complexes to be defined as a five-dimensional space with a Coxeter group structure. By harnessing the integrity of the code's structure and its associated quantum metrics, we design a variety of quantum codes with superior performance parameters. Key achievements of this study include developing quantum codes with high distillability ratios and constructing codes of varying lengths by controlling the shape of the underlying hexagonal grid.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem involves identifying a subset of vertices in a graph such that every vertex at a distance of $r$ or less is included in this subset. Our research explores the distributed version of this problem, focusing on the conditional model where $n$ is the graph's size and $\Delta$ is the maximum degree. Our results show that the distance-$r$ dominating set problem can be efficiently solved in a distributed setting for fixed $r$ and $\Delta$ but efficient solution proves challenging for larger values of $r$ with the current methods. We have therefore established a new, non-trivial lower bound for fixed $\Delta$ but small $r$, which indicates that the problem of solving fixed $r$ might be more complex than initially suspected.

In higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs), we investigate how noise affects the bulk to edge transport of protected modes even in the absence of edge defects. By quantifying edge and bulk mobility gaps, we establish a criterion to assess the completeness of edge modes. The study shows that while disorder typically closes the bulk mobility gap in 2D and 3D topological insulators, it remains open in 2D and 4D HOTIs, differing from the behavior seen in conventional topological insulators. Furthermore, we clarify the relationship between the mobility gap and edge band gap in hotspots, revealing that in hotspots the edge and bulk gaps can coexist, but at thermal equilibrium, the edge and bulk gaps remain separated. Our findings provide an experimental benchmark for verifying the presence of HOTIs in systems with surface states.

The 13 TeV proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS Collaboration at the CERN LHC in 2016 are analyzed for a search on compressed, long-lived charginos in supersymmetry. This research focused on a specific set of final states comprising hadronic and electromagnetic signals from jet-like structures, and it presented a new technique to identify jet-like shapes. To enhance sensitivity, a multijet reconstruction method was applied to share sensor information equally among jets with similar characteristics. Ultimately, a multivariate approach combining these three methods yielded an observed upper limit on the signal cross section at 95% confidence level. This limit, of 5 to 62 percent, is the most restrictive to date and is applicable to a variety of chargino masses and branching fractions.

Our approach enhances the reliability of light field rendering by leveraging additional geometric constraints when working with sparse views. Typically, learning-based methods rely on two or more views to establish stereo or epipolar geometry, but we introduce novel techniques to establish more connections: utilizing object boundaries and depth disparities to establish geometric relationships between views, we increase the number of constraining pairs by 1.5 to 2.5 times. We implement these concepts in a trainable network, which we call GeoLF, and evaluate its performance using both synthetic and real-world data under various conditions, including limited viewing angles, heavy occlusion, and noisy input. GeoLF consistently outperforms existing methods in terms of scene reconstruction and reconstructed geometry reliability.

Our research involved conducting speckle interferometric observations at the ANU 1.3m telescope, totaling 435 images and covering 399 datasets across 363 nights from 2015-2020. Additionally, we collected 225 images and 188 datasets across 141 nights from 2015-2020 using APO 0.78m telescope. By combining and analyzing data from both telescuses, we identified 88 new binary or stellar systems, as well as several previously known systems. Consequently, we updated and revised the nearby stellar catalog and subsystem list. Our findings bring the total number of known subsystems within 10-50 parsecs to 202, marking a significant escalation in knowledge. By using Gaia Data Release 2's parallax measurements, we determined the physical scales of angular separations from 10 to a few thousand seconds. By utilizing Gaia Data Release 2's data, we established the distribution of the discovered subsystems' angular separations and found a substantial number of the discovered subsystems to be within 50-100 AU. Our findings highlight the importance of speckle spectroscopy in speckle interferometry and how it allows for the study of cool stars across a wide range of stellar masses. By utilizing the Tully-Fisher relation, we established a reference scale for stellar discovery and found a pattern where the discovery rate decreased as stellar mass increased. Our findings pointed out a disparity in stellar discovery rates among different types of stars.

We present the operator-product expansion for the $\lambda_{2}^{6}$ vertex, establishing its chiral structure based on the tree-level scattering matrix. This expansion is unique, defined solely by 16 independent Lorentz-bostom factors, which fit into a specific symmetry framework. We demonstrate that these factors, when viewed as a set of functions within the lightcone gauge, satisfy an associativity condition, a fundamental requirement for correlators in self-dual QCD. Furthermore, by applying Wigner's little group action, we can transform the 16 factors into a set of impact parameters associated with null vectors, effectively reducing the problem to the center-of-mass frame. We then match the asymptotic behavior of the operator-product expansion within the center-of-mass frame to the $\lambda_{2}^{6}$ scattering matrix, providing an alternative derivation of Glusckov's impact factor conjecture.

Radio bursts powered by shock waves are common on the sun's surface. A particular type of burst, called a type II radio burst, occurs when a solar jet creates a shock wave that steers other shock waves into its path. The interaction of these shock waves accelerates particles, producing radio waves at great distances from the sun. Although the process is complex and relatively poorly understood, scientists have begun to study it in great detail using modern observatories. A recent study used data from a wide range of telescopes to track the development of a shock wave associated with a type II radio burst that occurred on the sun's surface. The researchers found that the shock wave was created by a solar jet moving at just 76 km/s, yet the radio waves it produced were traveling at speeds up to 4000 km/s. This suggests the radio waves were generated through the movement of magnetic waves along solar jets, rather than directly from the jet itself. The findings from this study may help scientists comprehend the underlying mechanisms of type II radio bursts, allowing for a deeper understanding of how particles are accelerated on the sun.

In a study of the 2HDM's latest developments, we've analyzed how it might affect B-meson decay observables, neutral particle decays, and collider measurements. Utilizing precise theoretical formulas for most calculations, we've found that even minor inputs from the doublets' parameters can result in significant influences on leptonic decays and future collider experiments. Specifically, our findings on lepton universality and the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron may soon restrict the 2HDM's parameter space to a point where a Higgs invertible truncation would fail, breaking various symmetry restoration theories. This phase transition model, however, still aligns with our predictions for gluon gluon fusion Higgs production and many other measurements.

We introduce an innovative numerical strategy to tackle three-dimensional fluid simulations by projecting random vortex dynamics onto a set of divergence-free control vortices. Within this framework, a Lagrangian method is employed, utilizing an adapted Kirby's pseudo-spectral scheme on an evolving grid. Our approach encompasses two key steps: periodically reconfiguring the flow by merging vortices with random natures and introducing new vortices influenced by the existing control vortices. By periodically introducing stochastic elements, the system breaks free from local minima, enabling simulation trajectories to span a broader phase space. Furthermore, the algorithm facilitates the emergence of complex geological patterns and diverse states, such as multiple columns and striped phases, without externally imposed spatial structures.

To analyze quantum states comprised of multiple photons, we utilize Gaussian random variables to approximate higher order photon distributions, then calculate their entanglement using the contiguity norm. It is evident that as the size of a subsystem approaches the total number of photons, the entanglement within the system also increases. Additionally, the width of the approximation's distribution in the subsystem simplifies to the quadratic form of the photon number, aligning with previous findings by SheikhAhmad et al.

One of the primary challenges in analyzing time-dependent gene expression data lies in efficiently identifying the relevant variables for machine learning models, specifically those requiring comprehensive information about gene profiles over various time points to train an accurate model. Researchers have developed a new method called Relevance-Learned Deep Network (ReLDN) that uses a deep learning approach to not only discover time points with the most expressive representations but also adjust weights according to importance. Consequently, a reduced version of the original data can be generated by replacing less significant time points with zeros, thereby reducing data complexity and enabling faster training. The proposed ReLDN method was evaluated using simulated and actual microarray time expression data courses. Results have shown that ReLDN outperforms current techniques in forecasting future gene expression values.

In temporally-deep, invisibly-observed control problems, determining an optimal policy necessitates an understanding of a system's hidden state, even if it can't be directly perceived.  A key finding here is that a recurrent neural network's hidden states closely mirror the beliefs of critical state variables in partially-observed environments.  Leveraging this connection, we've made several significant advancements: 1) Derivation of a theoretical framework for RNN hidden states, grounded in optimal control theory. 2) Proposal of an algorithm, based on reinforcement learning, to quantify RNN hidden state uncertainties. 3) Development of a method to fine-tune RNN models through optimal policy derivation. 4) Presentation of empirical results illustrating the accuracy of our theoretical framework and uncertainty quantification. 5) Display of RNN models optimized using zero-shot policy gradient methods and their alignment with theoretical frameworks. 6) Discussion of potential applications of statistical inference to neural networks.

The primary goal of action detection in video classification is to identify a specific action among various classes present within defined spatial locations on a video frame. This task has seen remarkable advancements thanks to recent improvements in video representation models and the increasing availability of annotated self-driving vehicle video data. State-of-the-art action detection methods currently rely on self-attention mechanisms for deriving content values from each spatial location and Graph Convolutional Networks for integrating action information from proximal locations. Building upon this foundation, we propose a novel approach that integrates content information from various locations while also considering the influence of action labels on each location. This novel technique is evaluated using the Steer3D and Wildtrack datasets, yielding performance enhancements of 2.3% and 18.6% respectively, when compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, detailed qualitative and quantitative analyses demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model in capturing contextual information among locations.

In various applications like search, retrieval, and protection, identifying identical images is a crucial task. A comprehensive evaluation of advanced image copy detection techniques will be presented, incorporating two key elements: (1) our newly optimized approach using Discrete Cosine Transformation and Hamming hashing, and (2) our revised interpretation of a cutting-edge method using multi-scale exact matching based on reference points. Unlike existing assessments focused on binary classification, our study prioritizes precision and recall through the utilization of the F-measure, and includes a thorough examination of the influence of parameter settings. Additionally, we introduce two new efficiency metrics: average recall and cost per recall. Notably, our Discrete Cosine Transformation method achieves nearly perfect accuracy, and our overall approach requires minimal computational resources, outperforming existing techniques.

The investigation of nonlinear parabolic equations with singular coefficients is ongoing, despite the absence of general results for initial-boundary value problems. This study focuses on interior and boundary regularity within a bounded domain, employing techniques like interpolation and extension principles to provide rigorous proofs and precise estimates for solutions to given problems. We demonstrate that the established results can be adapted to encompass key applications, including diffusion problems governed by reaction terms, governed by the fractional reaction-diffusion equation, and the fractional porous medium equation, all subject to various boundary conditions (Dirichlet and Neumann types). We note that these problems exhibit distinct characteristics due to their different boundary conditions and fractional diffusion processes.

At zero temperature, our analysis of nuclear matter in various Erice equations reveals 
that in the absence of a magnetic field, the energy and spin polarization decrease 
in proportion to the number of quarks. When a magnetic field is applied, the energy 
scales in a logarithmic manner and the spin polarization reaches its maximum at a 
specific value before decreasing. Notably, our results from different equations 
coalesce, providing a unified view of the effects of a magnetic field on nuclear 
matter. We have also identified and addressed a mathematical inconsistency in one 
of these models.

Federated learning methods often employ loss-protective techniques, such as differential privacy (DP), to prevent sensitive information exposure by limiting model updates to a predetermined federal compression size. Existing algorithms use varying amounts of federal compress sizes, making direct comparison and selection of the optimal size difficult without knowing their privacy levels. To address this, we re-evaluate DP in SLIM Regret Bound for Federated Learning minimax optimality under a strong convexity assumption, considering the impact of DP on compression size. We analyze DP's effect on loss and model updates, establishing a lower bound on DP-based loss protection. Given this protection, we derive a regret bound for DP-based FL under a strong convexity assumption. We compare our results to previous DP-FL models, showing improved DP-based FL minimax optimality under a strong convexity assumption, and providing practical guidance on DP-based FL federated compress size selection.

The primary source of the far ultraviolet (FUUV) spectrum in two distinct complexes - Taurus-Auriga-Perseus and Ophiuchus- Lupus is being investigated to determine its origin. Specifically, the far ultraviolet (FUV) intensity in these areas is shown to be comprised of a combination of two components, namely a radiation field produced by young stars and the fluorescent emission of molecular hydrogen. Our analysis indicates that the fluorescent emission accounts for a higher proportion in Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex while the fluorescent emission is relatively low in Ophiuchus-Lupus, contributing for a smaller proportion in this area. Additionally, the fluorescent emission has resulted in an observed discrepancy in the FUV spectrum in Ophiuchus- Lupus but a low signal has resulted in an uncharacteristic far ultraviolet spectrum in Ophiuchus- Lupus. Our analysis further suggests that the FUV spectrum obtained through several observational studies in Ophiuchus- Lupus should be modified by considering this fluorescent effect for enhanced accuracy. Our analysis, however, indicates that the FUV spectrum obtained through several observational studies in Ophiuchus- Lupus should be modified for enhanced accuracy but FUV spectrum obtained through several observational studies in Ophiuchus- Lupus should not be modified for enhanced accuracy. Our analysis further suggests that the FUV spectrum obtained through several observational studies in Taurus-Auriga-Perseus should not be modified for enhanced

Detecting and extracting data from documents has remained an ongoing challenge.
Recent advancements in document image analysis have leveraged Graph Neural Networks.
From a graph theoretical viewpoint, document images can be viewed as a connected
set of pixels, and by applying neural networks to these representations, we can
extract meaningful data from them. Current extraction methods rely solely on
pixel values, disregarding any underlying structural order in the document.
To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that combines both pixel-
based and graph-based methods. We treat table cells as nodes in a directed graph
and define edges based on cell arrangement in the page. Then, to capture cell
appearance, we employ a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network to produce
feature maps. Finally, we apply a Graph Neural Network to predict table cell
bounds. Experimental results on the widely recognized ICDAR 2013 dataset show
that our novel method achieves superior performance compared to prevailing
table extraction techniques.

In The Iterative Education Process game, a student (L) is taught by L levels of pre-existing teachers (H), each of which may or may not know how to facilitate the student's learning. The learning dynamics occur through a game where both the teacher and student evaluate each other's effectiveness, which dictates how much the student learns from the teacher. Subsequently, the teacher considers the consequences of his or her previous action and chooses a new strategy for the subsequent iteration. Theoretical analysis of this game reveals that while higher-level teachers excel at identifying the student's knowledge level and crafting optimal lessons, lower-level teachers struggle to do so, often leading to an equitable distribution of knowledge levels among students and teachers. Empirical studies utilizing The Iterative Education Process game demonstrate that students tend to internalize the teachers' strategies by replicating their actions, which in turn influences the number of levels that each teacher has mastered. Furthermore, experiments involving a variety of two-player games such as Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the sexes, and Rock-Paper-Scissors have shown that an equally divided distribution of knowledge levels among players yields the most efficient results, which aligns with our theoretical findings. Hence, in applications involving meta-learning and social learning, among others, developers should strive to achieve an equally divided distribution of knowledge levels among agents, which in turn facilitates the development of robust and efficient models. Additionally, our research offers fresh insights to scholars in the field of social game theory.

Predicting the coverage and user count of cellular networks is crucial for telecommunication providers, including rural broadband providers. To address this need, we developed and evaluated a method leveraging machine learning techniques to forecast the coverage and user count of rural broadband networks. Our proposed solution achieves enhancements of 0.3 to 1.1 percentage points and 3 to 8 percent in prediction accuracy, respectively, compared to a baseline approach. Notably, our approach surpasses a benchmark established by publicly available features, highlighting the importance of footprint area estimation in population predictions.

A better understanding of how to prevent cyber attacks through deep learning is crucial.
This work proposes an improved static filter that verifies the legitimacy of potentially malicious data without requiring a match, thereby preventing false positives and enhancing model efficiency.
By integrating a Berne filter with a deep learning model, a consistent filter is produced that shares the same distribution as the target distribution at each step.
In comparison to the original Berne filter, our approach displays superior performance on the large-scale Large Scale Malware Classification Challenge dataset from NIST.
Furthermore, suboptimal versions of our filter that require O(n) operations instead of O(n^2) are presented and validated for their efficiency in comparison to a weak strong classifier.
Ultimately, our approach is shown to prevent a significant number of attacks effectively while maintaining efficiency in terms of memory usage and computational speed.

We've developed an approximate classical model that retains the non-rigidity of a quantum system where Bose-Einstein condensates interact through Fano-Alexejev forces to create an unstable system leading to the conversion of atoms into molecules. By employing this model, whose stability is anchored in a conserved energy flow concept, we gain valuable insights into the system's behavior. Notably, our model helps explain why tight confinement often hinders atom-molecule transitions in experiments. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that an adjustable band structure can facilitate an increase in the rate of atom-molecule conversions, which could have significant implications for the creation of stable molecules using optical latties.

A new SPH framework is presented that seamlessly integrates different phase change techniques into a multi-phase model where solid and liquid states coexist below and above a critical temperature. This approach overcomes existing SPH methods' shortcomings in handling abrupt phase transitions, voids formation, and temperature discontinuities. Employing various artificial viscosity models, the method's ability to handle complex thermofluid dynamics and mix/enfold two-phase/one-phase flows is demonstrated through a range of test cases, including melting and solidifying solid objects, melting and solidifying metal spheres, and solidifying and melt ing solid objects near a heat source. This allows for an accurate simulation of solidifying metal solidifying on contact, as well as melt ing solidifying objects which may form voids due to anisotropic thermal diffusion, resulting in a more precise representation of melt ing solidifying objects which may form voids due to anisotropic thermal diffusion, with minimal artificial void formation. Furthermore, the model's performance in simulated a series of test cases which replicate various processes that were not covered in the previous test cases, the model's performance in simulated a series of test cases which repicate various processes that were not covered in the previous test cases, the model's performance in simulated a series of test cases which repicate various processes that were not covered in the previous test cases.

A potential application of quantum computing in clustering analysis is in the processing of large-scale data sets. Two types of quantum K-means algorithms have recently been introduced. One approach utilizes a single qubit to represent centroid estimates, whereas the alternative employs an encoded state to represent the estimated centroids. Both methods have complexities of O(K^r sqrt(n)), where K is the number of clusters, r is the number of features, and n is the dataset size. It has been found that the first algorithm's operation count is due to measurements required to update the estimate of the estimate, whereas the complexity of the second algorithm is due to the need to rotate the state against the statistical direction. A new quantum K-means algorithm has been developed that achieves a complexity reduction of a factor of sqrt(n) by utilizing measurements to update the estimate of the centroids directly.

Utilizing large speech datasets augmented with pitch variations can greatly improve the pitch control capabilities of speech synthesis models. In order to benefit from such datasets, which contain a wide range of pitches, our approach, called Progressive Text-to-Speech (P-TTS), empowers the model to generate speech at various pitches from a wide range of input texts. Our model, built on the Transformer, utilizes a discrete pitch embedding that is transformed into a continuous pitch embedding through a neural network, allowing it to work seamlessly with datasets featuring extensive pitch ranges. Our model has been rigorously tested with datasets containing very high or very low pitch variations (Degenerate Acute German and Metropolis, respectively) and has achieved superior performance in terms of pitch control. Notably, our model's results are comparable to those of state-of-the-art models that have been specifically fine-tuned for pitch control, as evidenced by the P-TSG 2021 challenge.

Objects in real-world scenarios often involve a sense of temporal progression, which current visual object recognition systems fail to address when performing task-specific reasoning. To tackle this challenge, our proposed framework learns to identify objects' spatiotemporal characteristics by leveraging a step-by-step sequence of images and focusing on key frames through high-low contrast training methods and attention detection. As our model can grasp both spatial and temporal features of objects, it outperforms existing approaches on public datasets designed for object-based reasoning and overall visual understanding. You can view and interact with the results on our dedicated website.

A simulation tool has been developed to study charged-current Drell-Yan events at the LHC and future hadronic colliders. Scheduled for presentation at the 2022 DIS conference, the code's main components are explained in this note. Its tunings with the public NNLO QCD parton distribution functions are detailed, along with its capabilities for predicting various Drell-Yan observables at different transverse momenta and rapidities. Additionally, the simulation is examined in contexts resembling ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC, along with predictions for future CKMT and FCC-Higgs colliders. Lastly, the simulation is used to assess the transverse-momentum distribution of lepton pairs in Drell-Yan events, which has been overlooked in the current standard parton distribution function fits.

To investigate the user experience of operating Telepresence Robots (TRs), we conducted two studies involving actual TR users, focusing on the visual, navigation, and control aspects of the system. Our research revealed that users easily adapted to the systems' visual, navigation, and control characteristics within a relatively short period of time. However, users demonstrated distinct preferences when it came to the design of the TRs. Our data prompted the development of a proposed design framework, known as the Telepresence Robot Evaluation Framework (TREF), which is set to guide the future development of TRs.

A method was developed to develop plant growth models, specifically using an individual-based approach, which was applied to two species. By creating three hierarchical models, researchers were able to analyze how global environmental factors, such as soil nitrogen levels, impact plant growth over time. Leveraging a novel model comparison procedure enabled the process of elimination to identify the most accurate model for each species' growth dynamics. According to the models, soil nitrogen levels have a significant impact on plant size, with high levels resulting in larger plants. It was found that a basic model providing a growth rate, maximum size, and mortality rate accurately describes the growth of both species. Despite initial reservations due to the model's simplicity, it effectively characterizes the growth patterns of red cattleye and yellow Jessamine. These findings highlight the importance of model efficiency in understanding plant growth dynamics.

Mafia is a complex real-life social game: its rules are unconstrained and shift over time and place. To overcome this, we developed a theoretical model that categorizes participants into two opposing groups, innocents and mafia members, to analyze the game's dynamics. Our research used random graphs to study how game dynamics are affected by network structures. Our key finding is that game outcomes rely heavily on network characteristics in terms of block independence and edge connectivity. These findings enabled us to create practical guidelines for playing Mafia, specifically by recommending the size of the mafia team based on network properties.

The similarities in mass among many closely spaced giant planets discovered by Kepler suggest they formed from the same protoplanetary disk. We simulated the formation of multiple giant planets in a closed system to see how planetary masses converge. Our results show that two planets orbiting each other can achieve similar masses through vertical diffusion of the disk's solid particles, which takes around one thousand years. Additionally, our simulations re-examine the phenomenon where multiple planets, formed from the same disk, accrete at varying rates. Our findings indicate that prior research overestimated the importance of vertical transport by nine to twenty times and underestimated the amplitude of vertical transport noise by a factor of ten to one hundred. Therefore, our data suggest that some parameters used in previous studies, such as the ratio of gas to solid particles, are reasonable and some parameters are likely to be adjusted. Moreover, our simulation indicates that convergence in planetary masses can occur within a range of stellar masses from 0.5 to one point five.

This paper examines the high-temperature transport properties in films made from achiral single-wall carbon nanotubes. The films, consisting of carbon nanotubes in their (5, 5) multiplex structure, are inherently non-superconducting due to their natural energy gap. The inherent nature of the energy gap, present even at room temperature, sets an upper limit on how much current can flow in the film. A study using electrical conductivity measurements discovers that this high temperature energy gap plays a critical role in the film's transport properties. The research also reveals that when measured under a magnetic field, the energy gap in the film closes at a field strength similar to that of the energy gap in a single carbon nanotube. The energy transfer mechanism responsible for transport in the film at high temperatures matches that of a single carbon nanotube. A single carbon nanotube is not the primary means through which energy is carried in the film, instead it acts as a means of energy transfer within the film. The energy transferred by the carbon nanotubes in the film is in a coherent state.

A novel fuzzy k-means approach is introduced that surpasses the capabilities of existing fuzzy k-means algorithms. By optimizing a modified objective function enhanced with entropy terms, this method displays superior cluster quality and membership accuracy. Comparative analyses with other fuzzy k-means methods reveal the superiority of our approach in achieving these metrics. Furthermore, this algorithm is complementary to current fuzzy k-means techniques, making it a viable alternative for various cluster analysis applications.

The episode-based learning algorithm for the mixture-of-experts model is designed to identify expert weights and location parameters within the patient dataset. Although the algorithm employed in our study is similar to the one proposed by Bojarska et al. (2017), it relies on an additional least squares optimization step to refine location parameters. In contrast, the alternative algorithm used in our comparison step refined both parameter sets simultaneously. We observed that the new algorithm significantly improves the estimation of expert parameters while maintaining accurate location parameter estimates. As a result, the prediction accuracy of the new algorithm surpasses that of the alternative algorithm. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the patient dataset can be effectively divided into distinct subgroups, where each subgroup corresponds to a specific expert component. We applied the new algorithm to a dataset containing data from rheumatoid arthritis patients and demonstrated that it successfully segments the patient cohort into two distinct subgroups. Furthermore, our prediction accuracy compares favorably to that of a machine learning method using random forests, especially for patients assigned to the subgroup with the lowest representation.

The subject of the relations between Jacobians and Prym varieties has been a central focus in algebraic geometry, particularly for nearly a century. Breakthrough discoveries made by Weil, Tate, and Matei have paved the way for further research. Building upon their findings, this study addresses a specific question regarding abelian varieties and their relevant properties. The main result is a classification of isogenous branches under the Jordan-Perelli isogeny $\mathcal{P}$, specifically focusing on the dimension and base points. The study also delves into the subvarieties associated with the relevant traits and demonstrates that the subvarieties exhibit exceptional characteristics, distinct from other types of varieties.

We put forth a novel concept of breaking global symmetries through gravity and derive a theoretical restriction for how much gravity can break desired global symmetries in various quantum gravity theories. Theories of quantum gravity, including certain string theories, that conform to this bound are shown to be compatible with a diverse range of global symmetries. As a result, gravity's influence on various composite particle phenomena can be precisely determined. Moreover, our bound has implications for theories of quantum gravity that aim to explain the origin of dark matter. Specifically, gravity's bound on symmetries could potentially resolve the dark matter problem, and we estimate the mass of dark matter that can be generated in this way. The bounds we've found are even strict enough to put constraints on gravity's impact on global symmetries in string theories involving D-branes. Additionally, our analysis sheds light on the behavior of matter in curved spaces, and we demonstrate that our bound has far-reaching effects, encompassing scenarios far beyond the context of particle physics based global symmetries.

Our investigation of NGC 6390's blue horizontal branch stars revealed the presence of two distinct sub-populations: a blue horizontal branch type I and a blue horizontal branch type II. BHHB I is characterized by a bluer mean B-V color, indicating a more blued distribution compared to BHHB II. A diagram of B-V vs. B magnitude showed BHHB I having a more uniform dispersion, while type II showed a clear trend of increasing dispersion with brighter magnitudes. Calculated mean B-V colors for BHHB I and II are -0.09 and -0.13 respectively. A comparison with asymptotic giant branch stars of a globular cluster revealed that some BHHB I stars may be part of a metal-rich population created through a globular cluster's interaction with the Milky Way. In addition, BHHB I's mean B-V color lies below a calculated transformation of the red giant branch, suggesting it may have undergone bluing due to helium emission. A two-component model was used to analyze the stellar population of NGC 6390, confirming its metallicity to be around 0.02 dex and a high star formation history ratio for the red supergiant population. A possible merger between NGC 6390 and M31 was suggested as a cause for the change in stellar populations of the globular cluster.

We explore the Madsen-Weiss theorem and establish a connection between its principles, the bordism principle, and the principles of homological localization and equivocation. A comparative analysis between Madsen-Weiss and van Kampen-Boone is also conducted, yielding implications for the development of a homotopy theoretical equivalent to the bo-Localization principle. Consequently, this leads to a reformulation of the bo-Localization principle in terms of the equivocation principle, resulting in the generation of new homotopy theoretical consequences. Furthermore, the study highlights the relationship between the Madsen-Weiss theorem, TQH duality, and the bo-Stability theorem, while suggesting the potential for a similar correspondence to exist between the bo-Localization principle and Td-Localization.

While deep neural networks' (DNNs) early layers are known to learn basic image characteristics that are transferable across different tasks, late-stage layers are thought to refine task-specific details. However, this widely held notion was put to the test when a DNN was asked to perform semantic segmentation on images taken with a blue filter. Without any special training, the DNN's green channel achieved remarkable performance, propelling it into the top 5 of a challenging dataset competition. A closer examination through ablation studies revealed the crucial role of the DNN's final layers, which were not only not the weakest links but also highly transferable. Furthermore, it became apparent that these final late-stage layers were designed to detect high-level image characteristics, particularly context-free details. As such, it is suggested that high-level context information is preserved throughout the DNN's learning process and output signals serve as a catalyst to unlock new insights from conventional 3D computer vision approaches. An open-source implementation of the project is also available on the GitHub platform.

Networks containing highly connected nodes (hub-like networks) promote information spreading. However, their optimal size for promoting information diffusion through the optimal modularity class of communities is closely linked to the amount of initial seed nodes or the size of the desired target cascade, influencing both network and system performance measures.

This work begins by introducing a global special Lagrangian branch for any given K\"ahler-Einstein metric on the K3 surface, regardless of its scalar curvature. We further observe that Lagrangians with lower Chern classes have smooth convergence patterns as they evolve over time according to the non-critical Lagrangian Lie transport equation. We derive various estimates to support these findings, including those influenced by Lagrangian angles and those influenced by curvature. In addition, our study confirms the existence of Lagrangians that remain unchanged under a period-integrated Hamiltonian deformation, which is an essential finding to validate the second variation formula for the non-critical Lagrangian Lie transport equation. We have also developed a novel method to express Lagrangian angles in terms of ADE-type orbifold factors of the K3 surface, along with explicit angle estimates that cover all possible variations. By combining these findings with the Lagrangian cone method, we have determined the optimal convergence rates for special Lagrangians in terms of Lagrangian angles. We have further discovered that Lagrangian cones on a K3 surface with negative self-intersection satisfy unique, minimal curvature properties, which are invariant under the wall-crossing operation related to their second Chern class.

We've developed a discrete-time channel model that starts from a critical analysis of
previous discrete-time models. Our model, founded on energy conservation and inspired
by a pioneering study, provides a detailed description of the input-output relationship of a
power amplifier, along with a comprehensive framework for testing its validity. Our findings
show that existing models are inaccurate, leading to a range of uncertainties, and our
theorems demonstrate that certain characteristics are difficult to determine. By utilizing real-world
measurements of a 4.5 GHz amplifier, we show that the proposed model significantly enhances
channel estimation and associated receiver performance.

Evasion attacks on machine learning (ML) classify input data in a manner opposite to a pre-determined target class, with current taxonomies focusing primarily on transferability and complexity. However, these sole metrics fall short in fully encapsulating such attacks, as they do not take into account other vital aspects like the training data set on which the classifier was trained, its robustness, and the level of sophistication involved. With this in mind, our proposal is for a comprehensive taxonomy that distinctively categorizes each type of evasion attack based on five key factors: the target class of data manipulation, the source of training data used to develop the classifier, the degree of manipulation required for data modification, the level of sophistication employed, and the extent to which method complexity is involved. This new taxonomy is viewed as an improvement as it covers a wider range of scenarios with lesser redundancy among categories in comparison to existing taxonomies, thus making it highly applicable and useful in this context.

A cloud-based system consists of containers, which are defined by a novel Ozy format that simplifies the setup process, reducing the time and effort required to establish cloud services. Ozy's cloud container can be integrated with existing virtualization technologies via a compatible adapter, allowing it to provide consistent service management on various platforms. Ozy's domain-specific description language facilitates efficient Ozy container creation, and its open-source design enables users to establish cloud services across multiple Ozy-compatible platforms.

This study demonstrates that the reentrant quantized phase that occurs when 2/3 fractional quantum Hall states are present lacks distinctive characteristics needed to identify it from closely related 1/3 fractional quantum Hall states such as the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases. In contrast, another reentrant phase distinct from these earlier states has been observed and is identified as a previously unknown 2/3 fractional quantum Hall state. A new fractional quantum Hall state, denoted as $
u_{2/3}^{+}$, has been observed and is characterized by its unlikeable behavior compared to the reentrant phase, as well as the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases, in magnetotransport measurements. Magnetotransport measurements of a two-component system with unequal densities also show that the $
u_{2/3}^{+}$ state exhibits contrasting characteristics. Moreover, $
u_{2/3}^{+}$ and a related reentrant phase possess distinct energy gaps as well as opposing responses to a finite-temperature heat bath. A crucial piece of evidence in differentiating the $
u_{2/3}^{+}$ state from previously observed reentrant phases comes from studying how the phases change in response to temperature. A newly developed theoretical framework suggests that $
u_{2/3}^{+}$ could be understood as a result of two particles interacting in a background of other particles. A related phase diagram has also been developed and is supported by our experimental

Researchers have previously assumed that primordial black holes obeyed the Schwarzschild metric, leading to restrictions on their formation rate based on their mass. However, a different model, the Thakurta metric, that represents a rotating, oscillating universe, includes an alternative representation of gravity with applications for both rotating black holes and gravitational waves. Reevaluating the formation process of primordial black holes using this Thakur metric reveals that the fluctuations in the potential energy and pressure allow more abundant black hole formation than previously thought, but surprisingly, constraints derived from the Schwarzschild model remain valid across various parameters. Ultimately, this revised understanding of primordial black holes does not rule out their potential role in dark matter.

The process of core formation within a protoplanetary disc is still not well understood, specifically when it comes to how dust accumulates and grows into a core. A new theory suggests that dust particles in the disc create ripples in the gas, creating rings of dust that can form around gaps in the gas. Research has shown that this ring formation can lead to the growth of a core, both by the accumulation of solid material within these rings and by the collapse of these rings under their own gravity. What's more, this ring formation can cause the surrounding gas within these rings to densify, facilitating the growth of a core. However, this process also relies on the pressure-related forces of a core forming in the rings. A new set of equations has been developed to study this problem further, giving us new insights into how a core forms in a protoplanetary disc. They suggest that a core forms quickly in the rings of gas, forming millions of kilograms in just a few years when certain conditions are met. This set of equations has been applied in a model of a developing disc, one that is low-mass and has a large distance between the star and the core forming area. They found that a core forms quickly in this scenario, and this is different from how a core forms in rings of gas that are not influenced by the pressure-related forces of a core forming in a pressure-related system. Deep learning models often require the collection and processing of substantial datasets, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain and process. Unfortunately, existing models often make unfounded assumptions about the characteristics of real-world data, assuming it is complete and accurately labeled. In contrast, robust learning approaches acknowledge that real-world data may be incomplete or imperfect, demanding fewer model parameters to compensate for these potential shortfalls. Although direct comparisons between robust and non-robust learning strategies have improved, differences in required model parameters remain a fundamental disparity between them. This study investigates the concept of minimal depth, which represents the fundamental complexity of a model capable of handling a specific task. This research demonstrates that a robust learner, focused on classification from incomplete data, can succeed with models having lower circuit complexity compared to a non-robust learner, which relies on complete data, for specific tasks involving natural images and comparisons between them. Furthermore, these findings are supported through experiments showing that robust learners require fewer parameters than non-robust learners on certain datasets and tasks.

Consider a countable abelian group $G$ and let $g_{1}, g_{2}, \ldots, g_{N}$ be elements of $G$ for some $N$. We can form upper Banach densities in this context by looking at sets of integers $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ for which the sum $A + Ng_{i}$ does not contain any Bohr sets. It is given that if $G$ contains elements other than the identity, at least one of these densities equals $1$. Conversely, it is also true that if $G$ is torsion-free and compact abelian, there exists a set of integers $A$ such that both $A + Ng_{i}$ and $A + Ng_{i} + g_{1}$ do not contain any Bohr sets, yet the direct sum $A \boxplus \mathbb{R}$ contains a Bohr set. This result answers an old question posed by Bergelson and Ziegler.

Optimization problems in transportation services often lack the necessary data to employ probabilistic models effectively, leading to time-consuming exact solutions methods. In this research, we focus on dynamic user equilibrium problems in transportation networks. We suggest a novel two-stage online algorithm that initially relies on fixed path information similar to the well-known Wardrop principle, later refining its efficiency by incorporating probabilistic models as more data becomes available. We demonstrate that by leveraging additional information about fixed paths, the computational requirements of an exact linear programming relaxation can be significantly reduced. We showcase the results of our proposed algorithm in simulation experiments and analyze its behavior in a real-world traffic context. We discover that when path probability data is readily available, the computational benefits can be substantial; however, the algorithm still performs well even with incomplete or evolving probability data.

In this research, we explore the potential of incorporating knowledge from various sources to enhance the resilience of multi-modal learning systems. To this end, we introduce Knowledge-Augmented Model Selection (KAMS), an innovative method that integrates knowledge across multiple sources to guide model selection and improve the robustness of multi-modal systems. KAMS is a unique approach that not only considers the inherent properties of each model but also how they compare to pre-trained models based on accumulated knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate that KAMS outperforms existing models, leveraging external knowledge to provide more reliable robustness levels in multi-modal systems, and our thorough ablation study highlights the significance of each component of KAMS and sheds light on its working mechanisms. Notably, our analysis shows that KAMS can adapt to diverse knowledge sources, encompassing scenarios with limited labels or multiple easy-to-obtain labels, and our model achieves great performance with minimal additional computational requirements.

Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive evaluations that compare unsupervised learning approaches against supervised methods for various tasks, including classification, regression, and link prediction, all in the context of AD prediction. Our objective is to rectify this by conducting a systematic evaluation of several existing unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised techniques using two distinct datasets. Initially, we will discuss the differences in performance when utilizing distinct datasets, highlighting that supervised methods excel in studies with larger sample sizes, but unsupervised learning often surpasses supervised approaches on smaller sample sizes. Additionally, we will compare the effectiveness of supervised techniques consisting of convolutional neural networks and support vector machines, while unsupervised learning will be represented by techniques such as convolutional neural networks, negative sampling, and deep unsupervised learning methods. It is found that the unsupervised approach featuring a convolutional neural network and negative sampling exhibits comparable performance to the supervised convolutional neural network method, and significantly outperforms the other unsupervised techniques and support vector machine method. This work not only fills the gap in knowledge by conducting a thorough investigation of supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning, but it also makes the code and datasets available for further research, aiming to promote replication and enhance knowledge in the field.

In practical scenarios, sequential data often exhibit long-term dependencies that depend on specific time intervals. However, current top-performing evaluation metrics like Backward Dropping Algorithm can't effectively capture these nuances beyond a certain time limit. This research introduces several new metrics that can account for infinite series and develops optimized versions of these metrics using techniques like grid optimization and calculus. Interestingly, findings reveal that certain proposed algorithms align with theoretical calculations from the 19th century. To address limitations of previous evaluation metrics, a novel method called Forward Dropping is also put forth. This method has been successfully applied to improve the performance of Long Short-Term Memory networks.

To analyze the impact of spin-orbit interaction on the Mott transition, we use a multiband Hubbard model with strong electron-correlation to solve a tight-binding model for half-doped pseudosuperfluidity, where we project it onto a multiband Anderson Hubbard model for comparison. By adjusting the number of bands and electrons, we recreate various situations of electron-doped and hole-doped materials. Assuming a constant electron lifetime near the Fermi surface, we calculated the Drude weight as a function of interaction strength, showing that spin-orbit interaction enhances electron mobility before the Mott transition point. This enhancement occurs because SOC weakens the electron tunneling between materials with different band orientations, reducing competition with electron hopping and electron number fluctuations. As a result, the mobility increases with growing tunneling between materials. However, the mobility decreases at higher tunneling rates, a phenomenon that can be compared with experimental findings on cuprates. Our research provides a fundamental understanding of electron physics in materials and sheds new light on the impact of spin-orbit interaction on the transition to electron localization. Future studies should focus on the impact of spin-orbit interaction on the transition to electron localization. Future studies should focus on the impact of spin-orbit interaction on electron localization.

In a theoretical model where dark matter interacts with Standard Model particles through the Higgs field, a time-varying relationship between dark matter and the Higgs sector occurs, especially during the early Universe when the Higgs field's value changed rapidly. Consequently, this affects the production of dark matter and influences constraints based on direct and indirect observational results. Additionally, dark matter's equilibrium temperature can be constrained in a specific Higgs mass range. When considering a fixed Higgs mass of 125 GeV, our findings reveal that a time-varying interaction can relax constraints derived from direct experimental results, especially for small dark matter masses, thereby making more scenarios feasible within the framework of the singlet extension of the Standard Model.

The success of black-box algorithms in medical imaging is largely due to their ability to identify the most likely outcome, even in complex situations. Nevertheless, the process of training these algorithms can be challenging, as it relies heavily on large datasets and time-consuming, high-cost computations with cutting-edge technology. In our study, we employed techniques for estimating prediction uncertainty, specifically conformal prediction, to assess the reliability of various black-box models. The results not only facilitated the comparison of different algorithms in a more informed manner, but also provided insight into their overall performance. By presenting their strengths and limitations, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective image classification and regression models, ultimately leading to new developments in the field.

The RBB-NA algorithm employs a restricted Boltzmann machine to analyze distorted DNA and RNA base pairing preferences. This machine learning tool complements existing methods like NN-Seq, allowing for the examination of non-standard base pairing patterns in nucleic acids. In a comparative study with NN-Seq, RBB-NA demonstrated its suitability for investigating artificial samples and real-life data, such as protein-nucleic acid complex structures. Notably, RBB-NA was able to identify a previously unknown A-G base pairing phenomenon in a complex with a specific protein and RNA molecule, which could not be discovered using NN-Seq. Furthermore, RBB-NA helped validate the experimental findings of Kim et al., related to G-quadruplex structures within human telomere sequences. By generating comprehensive pairing probability maps, restricted Boltzmann machine-based analysis offers valuable resources for researchers working with complex, nucleic acid-protein systems.

This study proposes an improved variant of fixed accuracy rANS (variable length code) that enhances efficiency by optimizing integer division within the process. Known rANS techniques, such as rANS with fixed accuracy, use a parameter 'd' to ensure a maximum integer result from division by 'd'. However, this technique is time-consuming due to repeated integer divisions. Our variant overcomes this by converting integer results into fractions and using a look-up table to replace divisions with table-based operations, significantly decreasing computation time. In comparison to rANS with fixed accuracy, our variant displays a substantial time-saving effect, particularly noticeable in scenarios with smaller 'd' values. This results in our variant being a viable option for applications like $k$-means compression, especially when 'd' is small and table-based operations can be performed in parallel.

The observation of dielectric properties can serve as an effective early warning system for monitoring the state of concrete foundations, and thus the reliability of its structure. Given the complexity of concrete's dielectric properties, they vary according to age, temperature, and moisture levels. Consequently, an accurate determination of dielectric properties in situ becomes a challenging task. In our investigation, we focused on determining the dielectric properties of in-situ concrete at various stages of its development, and we used the results to create a non-destructive method for monitoring its condition. First, we established a new approach for representing concrete's dielectric properties, based on frequency- and temperature-dependent models. Additionally, we developed a conversion formula to apply the laboratory-measured dielectric properties under standard conditions to their actual state. We validated our methodology using data collected from a concrete bridge slab equipped with temperature and humidity sensors. We demonstrated that our methodology can successfully correct dielectric property measurements under arbitrary temperatures and frequencies, thereby enabling non-destructive monitoring of in-situ concrete temperature and moisture levels. Furthermore, we developed a statistical model to create a database of dielectric properties for diverse concrete ages. We utilized this methodology to establish a diagnostic system for monitoring concrete's in-situ condition. We tested our methodology on data collected from six analogous concrete bridges equipped with sensing modules that measured dielectric properties. Using the diagnostic system, we identified early signs of freeze-thaw damage on two bridges and detected frozen water regions in another bridge. Moreover, we identified

The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, composed of a heavy quark and a heavy
hadron (e.g. $\Xi_{bb}$), is considered plausible due to their straightforward formation
mechanism. This study calculates the binding energies of these molecules in the context
of the Q$\bar{Q}$ potential model. The predicted binding energies for $BBQ$, $BCQ$, and
$CCQ$ systems are derived using numerical values for the spectroscopic coefficients.
Additionally, lower limits on the depth of the potential's attractive tail are established
based on observations in experiments.

The increased emphasis on unmanned military operations has prompted many nations to invest heavily in unmanned systems, with a particular focus on drone technology.  Driven by the strategic potential of these systems, many nations are diverting significant resources towards military drone research, with a goal of utilizing them in large-scale operations.  Our drone research dataset, which covers the period from 2013 to 2020, tracks the progress of 65 top nations in this field.  The data collection process involved analyzing the capabilities, procurement plans, as well as the research strategies of these countries.  Our analysis reveals China and Russia to be the leading adopters of military drones, while the United States leads the world in drone research.  Our dataset may be accessed online at: https://github.com/cyberjunkie/military-drone-research

A nonlinear relation between density fluctuations, $\sigma_8$, and the rate of particle growth, $f\sigma_8$, exists in theories beyond the standard cosmological model. These theories predict a fundamental relation where its deviation is indicated by the differential growth parameter, $f d\ln \sigma_8$. By analyzing the latest Planck data in combination with redshift space clustering information at $z_{ef}=2.3$, we have evaluated the significance of this deviation to be approximately $2.2\sigma$. Furthermore, our findings suggest that if the standard cosmological model holds true, this particular redshift range can distinguish between different cosmological models with a confidence level of at least $2\sigma$. When constraining the matter density parameter, $\Omega_m$, using this cosmological model, our analysis reveals a confidence level of at least $2.5\sigma$ if the standard $\sigma_8$ parameter constraint is relaxed. In a different scenario where the standard $\sigma_8$ parameter constraint is relaxed, our analysis shows that if the standard cosmological model holds true, this particular redshift range can place a more stringent lower limit on $h$, the dimensionless Hubble parameter, at $z_{ef}=2.3$ with a confidence level of at least $2\sigma$.
