MHD isentropic two-dimensional systems undergo a change in their energy function when they form intermediate shocks. For a specific subset of these systems, like the magnetohydrodynamic $\beta$-wave, there's an established inversion theorem which links the flow's contraction properties across an shock wave to its variation in a specific gradient. This paper further expands on this connection by making a proven comparison between an expansion gradient and a specific gradient that's known to change in shocks. As a result, it provides insight into the flow's contraction properties across strong shocks. If the initial state lies within a specified convex region, then for any shock wave, the variation in a specific gradient does not change; this result, in turn, proves an inversion theorem for two-dimensional isentropic MHD magnetostatic shock waves. Furthermore, it shows that for a specific system that adheres to a particular convexity property, the variation in a specific gradient, albeit dependent on the type of magnetization, does not change either.

This research targets the challenging task of generating an endless view perspective from a single scene picture, akin to a 360-degree panorama, but with varying angles and depths of view. Different from traditional approaches that also consider depth, our experiment focuses on depth-free images and involves less involved inputs, yet produces a broader range of views. We've established a new method called RotoView and evaluated it against current best practices using a widely available dataset. Notably, our results show an improvement in view quality as the image resolution increases, and RotoView outperforms baseline methods even when resolution is low. We've publicly shared our code and demonstrate its capabilities through an animated video demonstrating an almost 360-degree view perspective with little input distortion. You can access the code at https://github.com/alexandryounger/RotoView.

In large-scale complex networks, frequent measurements lead to considerable computational costs when applying methods such as model predictive control. To mitigate this, a more efficient approach is proposed that takes advantage of the Koopman operator's properties. This new method emerges as a special case of certified policy iteration, a technique primarily developed for Markov decision processes. By analyzing inner iterations, we demonstrate that certified policy iteration can produce better controllers at a lower computational cost, yet may not always yield the most efficient results compared to other methods in terms of performance or computation. To overcome this limitation, we incorporate policy iteration and certificate checks in parallel, offering a promising alternative for large-scale complex network control.

A thin layer of a viscous liquid surrounds a thin fibre with an irregular surface. The irregularities in the fibre create areas where the liquid can stick or slip. Due to the effect of irregularities, parts of the liquid film pull apart, forming small droplets. The process of forming these droplets is studied, focusing on the location, size, and number of droplets. Theoretical calculations show how the location, size, and number of droplets change in response to changes in the speed at which the fibre moves through the liquid, the strength of the force acting along the fibre, and the characteristics of the irregular surface features. The findings are verified by comparing them to the results of numerical simulations.

The Lagrangian description of fluid dynamics uses a single global coordinate framework identical to the Eulerian approach, but differs in the calculation of local velocity and pressure. In Lagrangian formulation, these metrics are derived from a potential function, resulting in perfect continuity. We compare the Eulerian and Lagrangian methods by applying these formulations to four fundamental fluid scenarios: uniform flow, rotating flow, inviscid flow, and flow with uniform acceleration. We demonstrate that Lagrangian continuity leads to simplified first-order differential equations, enabling uniform and rotating flow solutions identical to Eulerian methods, and a combined solution to a mixture of Eulerian and Lagrangian differential equations for flow with uniform acceleration. Furthermore, Lagrangian formulation allows for a direct and simple expression of vorticity in the Eulerian framework.

To assess the accuracy of robotic ultrasound for measuring spine angle in scoliosis patients. 
20 patients with scoliosis were positioned on their backs on a treatment table with their arms elevated. 
Two human ultrasound experts simultaneously took measurements of the C7 to L1 spine angles using a robotic ultrasound device. 
One of the experts obtained 10 manual readings of each spine angle, which were then averaged and serving as the standard reference, 
the other expert obtained 10 readings as well,

To capture the varying lengths of critical events like press releases and earnings announcements, a time-to-event model specifies a probability distribution that outlines the possible durations. However, this approach has a limitation where the probability of extreme events must add up to a finite value, which is not the case in real-life situations. A way to overcome this issue is by using a Pareto distribution, but this would require a hybrid model that combines discrete and continuous periods, which adds complexity to the estimation process. Alternatively, the exponential distribution offers an easier alternative, but is also prone to the same issue. A more recent development is to use the gamma distribution, which can flexibly represent different distribution shapes, and is capable of handling infinite maximum values, a characteristic that is not found in common models like the Weibull or log-normal distributions. The duration model in question makes the common assumption that the length of events follows a gamma distribution, which is non-negative and has infinite maximum values, which can be a feasible scenario for events like press releases. The model also makes another assumption that the likelihood of events that last longer is determined by the past events, which can be substantial amounts, a hypothesis that can be validated through tests or real-world data analysis. The researchers also outline a critical testing method that can be used to verify or reject the model in practice.

This study presents an integrated framework that detects hate speech within social media posts by combining Natural Language Processing techniques, including transformer models and lexical analysis. An experiment was conducted using a Twitter-based dataset consisting of 1,555 labeled messages, each categorized as hate speech or not, to assess the effectiveness of NLP features in prediction tasks. Focusing on binary classification, the present research investigates and compares the performance of five different NLP features, namely, word embeddings, lexical semantics, syntactic analysis, affective computing, and transformers' universal syntax representation. Among these features, the application of BERT-based universal syntax representation was found to be the most successful in achieving high accuracy rates. Furthermore, the present study abides by ethical principles when processing social media data, including obtaining users' consent, maintaining anonymity, and employing deidentification techniques to analyze data in a responsible manner.

A recent advancement in MIMO technology, the MIMO framework has efficiently extracted intricate features from multidimensional signal arrays. Nevertheless, the initial design of MIMO is susceptible to failure in cases of incomplete data such as when central pixels are missing from 2D matrices. To address these limitations, a novel method called MIMO-CP is presented and incorporates a refined unmixing step to successfully apply the generalized random walk to multidimensional signal arrays, even in situations of incomplete data. Moreover, a fast and highly efficient algorithm called MIMO-CP GLS has been developed to accelerate the model's performance. Both theoretical and experimental evaluations have demonstrated that MIMO-CP is capable of achieving optimal solutions and outperforms existing versions of MIMO in terms of speed and effectiveness.

One significant obstacle in historical document analysis is the lack of a single, comprehensive dataset that caters to diverse research tasks across various languages. Our proposed solution involves creating personalized dataset recommendations based on researchers' specific requirements, taking into account their preferred language, research objectives, and area of expertise. By applying a collaborative filtering technique, our system can suggest relevant datasets according to their professed interests. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated through its ability to recommend datasets for a diverse range of researchers, including those working on French documents from the 16th to 18th centuries, and English, Dutch, German, Italian, and Spanish documents from the 16th to 20th centuries.

This research proposes an innovative compliance method that enhances the accuracy of industrial robots tracking precise trajectories. Unlike existing techniques, our approach adjusts the robot's joint speeds rather than its task space velocities, making it better suited for tracking trajectories. We present two strategies, referred to as the First-Order and Second-Order Adjustments, that allow the robot to correct its velocities based on its positioning errors and task space Jacobians. By incorporating these adjustments into the robot's control law, its joint velocity trajectories exhibit significant improvement, resulting in more precise tracking performance.

Myocardial infarction survivors face significant challenges in managing their health, particularly when trying to avoid future heart disease. There's a need to better understand people's lives following a heart attack, the everyday problems they face, and how these vary among different populations and health conditions. This research involved analyzing a large dataset from England containing the healthcare records of over 300,000 patients who had myocardial infarctions between 1992 and 2014. By employing advanced statistical analysis, we were able to track changes in patients' health over a long period following their heart attack, identify patterns among different groups, and pinpoint variations in care received by patients with similar heart conditions. This work lays the groundwork for research focusing on individualized predictions of patients' future health outcomes based on their specific circumstances, the complexities of their health situations, and their varied responses to treatment.

To address convergence issues in the electronic continuum, a modified version of Becke's scheme has been developed and implemented to compute integrals such as $\langle \mathbf{p}^k \mathbf{s}^m | e^{-(\alpha + \beta r)^n} | \mathbf{p}^k \mathbf{s}^m \rangle$. This implementation is based on grid-based methods for computing integrals and utilizes a modified version of Becke's scheme to evaluate the integrals over the electronic distribution, which is compared to the direct integration method in auxiliary basis sets. The developed routine is named EES and is part of the Py SCM library, which is used in real-space computations. We present results from numerical tests to assess the accuracy and efficiency of EES and demonstrate its potential in various electronic properties computed in real-space computations.

Within the realm of Graph Theory, our research focuses on the Metric Dimension problem, a challenge that involves selecting the smallest possible set of vertices from a given graph, where these vertices can pinpoint any point within the graph by utilizing the shortest distance to each chosen vertex. By using Trinity graphs, our analysis demonstrates that the Metric Dimension problem, parameterized by the number of vertices, has a complexity of W[1] and, parameterized by the number of edges, the problem has a complexity of XP with an exponential time complexity of at most O(3^k |V(G)|^3), where k represents the size of the metric set and G is the input graph. Furthermore, our research establishes that the Metric Dimension problem, when parameterized by various graph parameters such as the color number, cluster number, and domination number, does not possess a polynomial-time complexity that scales linearly with the parameter value, which indicates that these parameters are also insufficient for fixed-parameter tractability. Finally, our research, parameterized by the size of independent sets, demonstrates that the Metric Dimension problem does not possess fixed-parameter tractability and, consequently, is W[1]-hard.

In a directed space, the topological versions of upper, lower, and convex powerspaces have distinct definitions from their ordered counterparts for dcpos. We demonstrate that in a directed space, these powerspaces can exhibit topological properties not found in their discrete counterparts for Scott topologies on dcpos. Specifically, we show that a directed space may have a compact convex powerspace without being compact or having a compact lower powerspace without being compact or having a compact upper powerspace. We also establish that a lower powerspace for a directed space is always convex, but a directed space may have a convex lower powerspace without this property holding for the lower powerspace itself. We explore the relationship between the interrelations of these powerspaces, especially a directed space's lower and convex powerspaces, and a specific topology on dcpo's convex powerspaces, the $l$-topology. We research a directed space's properties based on the relation between its $l$-interpolation property and the $l$-topology, and a particular condition involving a space's convex lower powerspaces, the double lower vector space interpolation property, in relation to the interrelations of these powerspaces.

In harsh environments far from the equator, the atmosphere regulates the water content in the air, leading to unique climate patterns characterized by more water in the lower atmosphere than in the upper atmosphere. This results in a system where heat emitted by water particles amplifies existing warmness, reducing the frequency of clear skies and stimulating the formation of clouds. This process, characterized by low-level cloud cover, is distinct from the cloud-lucid sky relationship observed in temperate climates. Using a advanced computer model, researchers analyzed the responses of this system to variations in cloud amount, discovering that in more water-rich climates, evaporative cooling has a lesser impact than radiative cooling in shaping precipitation patterns. Unlike in normal climates, in harsh environments, precipitation is lowest when clear skies prevail, and significantly increases as water content in the air rises. These findings in turn affect how heat is distributed and processed within these water-dense systems, contributing to their stability and ability to regulate themselves. These results in turn hold significant implications for understanding Earth's climate system and discovering potential analogs on other planets.

We examine the higher-spin generalization of Yang-Mills theory, which follows from a novel principle that leads to a specific BRST operator configuration. This, in turn, results in type I and II string theories with various properties. Two scenarios are possible: the higher-spin tensor action coincides with the higher-dimensional cohomology non-linear $\sigma$-model action, or it remains distinct from the latter. Additionally, we find that the TRS operator in type I strings with higher-spin interactions satisfies a specific algebra, which contrasts with the situation in type II strings.

Deep learning models are susceptible to noisy labels, which can severely impact their performance. Existing methods often rely on robust label corrections, but such corrections are not consistently available. This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach to label correction by reframing the process as Bayesian statistics guided label refurbishment mechanism (BLRM). BLMr can dynamically identify and correct noisy labels without access to a reliable label correction source. By integrating BLMr with popular training techniques, we achieve significant improvements in noise-resistant training. When applied to popular deep neural networks on various datasets and types of noisy labels, the proposed system consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving BNM-99% accuracy on datasets with low noise levels and BNM-95% accuracy on datasets with high noise levels.

A fundamental issue in finite element methods concerns the construction of an approximate solution to a continuous function by interpolating within a regular simplex formed by combining elements of a partition in the n-dimensional unit cube [0,1]^n. The feasibility of interpolation depends on the arrangement of a set of points (t_1,...,t_I) within each simplex. This paper addresses the problem of determining the minimal requirements that must be met by the number of these points I and the coordinates t_i to ensure the existence of a non-degenerate regular simplex R_n with an interior that is completely enclosed by the cube Q_n. In the case of an n-cube with side-length 1, the feasibility of the interpolation can be guaranteed by choosing I equal to the number of nodes (n+1)(n+2) and appropriately labeling the coordinates t_i with values from the set {0,1}, with the constraint that the resulting simplex R_n has a significant overlap with the cube Q_n, meeting specific distance and ratio criteria. These results will be proven through the application of an existing set-theoretic operator T that plays a key role in the construction of an extreme set X(I) consisting of properly arranged simplexes T_i with interior points t_i.

We analyze a continuous time correlated random walk (CTCRW) with specific properties where at any given time t, the probability distribution over all possible states follows a detailed balance equation, which implies the probability matrix is stochastic and describes a global flow along with its characteristic polynomial, used to derive this characteristic polynomial from the CTCRW's transition rate matrix. This polynomial is shown to be positive for all non-zero eigenvalues of the transition rate matrix. Additionally, a fundamental theorem connects the CTCRW's lifetime to its largest transition rate element and a key singular value, which is further utilized to establish bounds and general limits on the CTCRW's lifetime, state transition frequency, and related measures. Lastly, we explore a broader class of discrete-time correlated random walks (DTCRWs) with absorbing states and develop analogous techniques and formulas, including criteria for the CTCRW's lifetime limits in terms of a key singular value and measure of 'buried states'.

The focus of this study is on simplifying termination proof development in 
Terminator, a tool used to automatically establish termination proof based on 
a complexity-driven approach. We present a new method to express a clock minimization 
process within the function definition component of the complexity-driven approach. 
By integrating this clock minimization process, we are able to reduce the complexity of 
termination proof development in several key areas: first, by limiting the clock 
range in final statement conditions to a single value, and second, by ensuring clock 
values in recursive steps match the value in final statement conditions. However, 
this method is subject to limitations, where the clock value in final statement conditions 
must be zero. Despite this restriction, clock values can still be undefined. We 
extend the method using a clock analysis algorithm that identifies these undefined 
values, thereby allowing us to specify a lower bound on the final clock value.
Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity of this algorithm and demonstrate 
that it operates within a logarithmic time frame with respect to the represented value. Through various case studies, we validate the effectiveness of this method.

In simulations and experiments of wall-attached flow turbulence, the hairpin packet has emerged as a promising model for representing turbulent phenomena down to the scale of the distance from the wall. It is proposed that specific features of wall-attached flow turbulence can be understood by considering a subset of hairpin packets, in which the main vortex resides entirely above the layer where the distance from the wall measures half of the total distance between the opposite wall and the innermost point of the turbulent zone. Specifically, it is suggested that the packet's base spreads out across the total distance between the opposite wall and the innermost point of the turbulent zone. Based on this idea, two statistical properties are defined: the first reflects the extent to which a given vortex's base is situated near the wall, and the second describes how the turbulent vortex structures spread out horizontally. By examining the behavior of these characteristics in vortices both within and outside of simulations and experiments, it is found that they exhibit comparable trends. Furthermore, it is observed that when the turbulent vortex structures reside closer to the wall, they tend to possess smaller sizes and curvature frequencies, and that as they move further away from the wall these characteristics increase. It is suggested that the increased characteristics near the wall represent a specific mechanism through which the adherence of turbulent flows to the wall can be influenced by the turbulent patterns that they contain.

A modified version of the baby Skyrme model, incorporating a $U(1)$ gauge field, recent studies have demonstrated the existence of stable vortex structures. In our research, we have examined the gauged baby Skyrme model's two-dimensional reductions, yielding three distinct soliton profiles: translationally invariant, rotational solitons, and those possessing $Z_n$ discrete symmetry. We have also derived the mass spectra for each type of soliton through a straightforward approach. Furthermore, in the presence of a non-zero temperature, we have investigated the gauged baby Skyrme model's thermodynamic properties, focusing on the vortex structures exhibiting $Z_n$ discrete symmetry. Specifically, our analysis revealed the thermodynamic quantities' n dependence, which aligns with the expected behavior at a specific point, namely $T=T_c$, via a logarithmic relationship.

We study a lattice version of a Weyl semimetal model that exhibits both
symmetry and antisymmetry. Due to its non-trivial crystal structure, the
model's form of the Haldane term is determined by both the shape of the unit
cell and the specific symmetry properties. As a result, we see that the type of
phases created depend on the cell shape, leading to either a uniform
topological insulator or separate topological and non-topological parts. We
also find that the presence of crystal structure changes how we interpret the
model's band structure in relation to the Haldane term. Additionally, we explore
the effect of symmetry-breaking terms on the model. When these terms become
large, they transform the model into a type of quantum anomalous Hall effect, 
and for very large cell shapes, they turn it into a uniform topological 
insulator, regardless of the Haldane term.

Our design concept, developed using coupled mode theory and optimized via machine learning, enables the independent tuning of optical nanoantenna resonances to match those required for enhanced four-wave mixing and CHAOS applications. Specifically, we present a design for a titanium dioxide nanoantenna that can achieve the desired spectral characteristics for applications involving classical harmonic generation operating within the telecom and near-infrared spectrum. Our results validate the potential of machine learning in guiding the design of nanophotonic devices.

Amorphous materials have long been overlooked due to their lack of translational symmetry, but their unique disorder brings forth plastic events that significantly impact their mechanical properties and set boundaries on their deformability limits. The intricate interplay of local strain bursts in amorphous materials results in their ultimate failure, with prior approaches mostly concentrating on individual factors such as energy partitioning or entangled network rigidity. We have developed a framework that sheds light on how geometric disorder within the material's microscopic structure influences its deformation resilience. We observed via molecular dynamics simulations of three different amorphous metals that disorder fluctuations in a specific manner govern how the material resists deformation under various stresses, unlike crystalline materials that follow traditional failure principles. Specifically, geometric disorder directly affects how the material sets bounds on its deformability. We have also developed a comprehensive model that explains geometric disorder's effects on material properties based on its chemical composition and the rigidity of its intermolecular bonds, broadening understanding of disorder's complex role in material deformability.

The effect of charge transfer and Hund's coupling within Mn-decorated silicene has been investigated using a computational model based on density functional theory. Analysis was conducted on silicene bonded to a single Mn atom at two different settings: one where Mn sits atop a silicon atom with adjacent Mn configurations, and another where Mn sits amidst three silicon atoms with Mn atoms placed adjacent to it. Compared to a flat, hydrid-like arrangement where water is substituted with Mn and silicon atoms, the onsite interaction between electrons was found to be substantially greater for Mn-decorated silicene. The decision to situate Mn central to the hexagonal structure, as opposed to on top of it, was seen to be crucial in determining the onsite interaction parameter, which was found to be significantly influenced by the way in which Mn and water atoms bonded. It has also been established that Mn-decorated silicene possesses properties comprising multiple half-fillings, thereby showcasing an inherently complex nature comprising both one-dimensional and pseudo-dapticel electron configurations. This is exemplified by the existence of various possible electronic arrangements, some of which are characteristic of one-dimensional systems (featuring electron waves moving in opposite directions) and others that are indicative of electronic interactions within a system (featuring push-pull dynamics of electron waves).

The origin of the spectacular jet-like features on either side of the Sgr A East nebula remains unclear, despite ongoing research. We investigated the likelihood that these features are the result of a nearby supernova explosion triggered by a massive star that was once orbiting the Sgr A* black hole. Our analysis indicates that the explosion occurred approximately 0.1 parsecs from Sgr A*, which is significantly closer than the Sgr A* cluster's typical formation distance. Furthermore, we found that a massive star that fed a low accretion rate to Sgr A* over a prolonged period is a feasible explanation for the observed energy dynamics. Our findings also suggest that radiation feedback from this star could have impacted the surrounding gas in the Sgr A* cluster during its evolution, which may have influenced the formation of Sgr A*. However, our proposed scenario does not account for any observed star formation in the Sgr A* cluster.

Recent breakthroughs in the field of a/a recognition largely attribute to deep neural networks (DNNs) from a computational learning theory perspective. Our investigation examines whether DNNs benefit more from advances in computation than do traditional algorithms like KNN and SVM. We analyzed the performance impacts of various computational methods, data preprocessing, and other factors on both KNN and DNNs. We discovered that DNNs are more resilient to reductions in computational resources, data quantization, and training set reductions, also exhibiting fewer discrepancies across multiple algorithmic implementations. Furthermore, we found that the benefit of DNNs on out-of-distribution samples is illusory. Ultimately, we found that DNNs' superior handling of imbalanced data rather than inherent advantages explains their superior A/a performance.

This paper conducts an in-depth analysis of the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local news by collecting and studying a large dataset of 1.3 million articles from 1,636 newspapers across the United States over a period of 289 days. Our research encompasses two primary areas of examination. Firstly, we focus on the overall output of local news outlets, identifying any alterations in volume caused by COVID-19-related funding issues, labor restrictions, and shifts to remote work. Secondly, we concentrate on the substance of local news stories, using both human and automated evaluation methods to determine how the pandemic affected the topics, tone, and format of news content. Our comprehensive findings reveal changes in both the quantity and quality of local news across various sectors and population groups, with key variations observed among communities of lower income and minority groups.

A new N-body implementation is introduced within the PMBOX code, utilizing a Fast Multipole Method to boost efficiency and allow for simulation scenarios that would otherwise require extremely large time budgets to achieve spatial accuracy. By leveraging a framework designed for dynamic grids, the code adapts a standard matrix completion-based FMM implementation to fit within a particle-based framework. A novel approach is developed to split matrix completion from the standard pair-wise calculation in a quasi-newton optimization loop, enabling the data transfer to occur outside critical timing loops. A novel tree restructuring strategy is also proposed which greatly reduces execution time by splitting complex matrix operations from optimization loop and offloading to CPU idle times. This new design is evaluated across a range of astrophysical conditions, yielding results. For instance, simulations requiring a time step of 5 years with 10^6 particles demonstrate a 7.18x improvement in time resolution with 10% error at the current code state, expectation is a 20% hit to error from refinements, observations suggest matrix completion occurs at 90% efficiency. Furthermore, simulations requiring a 10% error level demonstrate a 3.3x improvement in time resolution with 10^7 particles and a 6.25x improvement in time resolution with 10^8 particles, all at a 90% efficiency of matrix completion.

A specific type of double spin asymmetry associated with the process where an electron collides with a proton and produces an omega particle, which involves one of the proton's spins, has been studied. This particular asymmetry is known to be highly sensitive to the distribution of polarized gluons within the proton and is particularly difficult to model accurately. Furthermore, analyzing this process under the conditions where the omega particle is produced at a specific rapidity and is scattered at a given angle can provide valuable insights into the polarized gluon distribution functions, specifically in certain kinematic regions. Ultimately, our analysis has shown that this process could potentially rival other methods of measuring polarized gluons and might even serve as an effective method for making more precise adjustments to the existing models of gluon distribution, particularly in experiments conducted at an electron-ion collider.

Deep reinforcement learning has made significant strides in addressing various
control issues, but the process of transferring knowledge from experienced to less
experienced agents remains challenging, particularly in situations with numerous
dimensions of control. To facilitate knowledge transfer between policies of
varying complexities, we propose an approach where the student policy mimics
the teacher policy through behavioral cloning. However, conventional behavioral
cloning methods are inefficient and prone to failures for high-dimensional control
problems with large observation spaces. Therefore, we introduce an augmented
behavioral cloning technique where the teacher policy embeds its knowledge into a
reduced-dimensional observation space, enabling the student policy to learn its
original structure. Our results demonstrate that our approach enables policies with
reduced dimensions to acquire the capabilities of their corresponding original,
untransformed policies through supervised learning. Moreover, we found that the
student policy can seamlessly transfer its knowledge to new environments, a trait
not exhibited by the untransformed teacher policy. Our augmentation technique is
successful on complex robotic control problems with numerous dimensions of
control and observation.

In a study, the production of a Higgs boson with associated single top quark production in the electroweak process was analyzed using data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider from 2015-2016. The data collection involved 36.1 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The analysis focused on determining the polarization of the top quark and identified final states with one or two electrons, one muon, and four or five jets, representing the contribution of t-channel and other background processes. In the analysis, the team searched for signs of new physics that may affect this process by looking at the angle between the thickest jet and the missing transverse momentum. The results revealed that there was no significant deviation from the Standard Model prediction in the Higgs boson and top quark production cross sections for various mass assumptions about the new spin-0 resonance. The resonance masses analyzed included 70, 110, 150, and 190 GeV for a neutral heavy scalar and 110, 150, and 190 GeV for a neutral pseudoscalar in scenarios with two Higgs doublet extension and a universal extra dimension with additional dimensions.

Digital signal processing has revolutionized our understanding of resonant spin masers by incorporating advanced analysis and real-time measurement techniques. These processing methods can significantly enhance the capabilities of traditional spin maser experiments, yielding insights that may have been overlooked using conventional methods. In this research, we detail certain investigations that benefited greatly from the integration of digital signal processing, focusing on aspects such as long-term stability, quantum coherence, laser-related interactions, and real-time detection parameters.

We've found an approach to classify the hypergeometric groups generated by the period vectors of K3 surface extremal reflections, which helps us understand certain automorphisms of K3 surfaces. This work on reflection-generated K3 surfaces overlaps with Furusho's research in a predictable manner. Nevertheless, our investigation doesn't address the challenging case of non-extremal period vectors, a topic previously explored by other mathematicians.

We propose a novel method for observing neutralino decay in the context of 
a facetized Wilson-Chevalier framework, where we concentrate on the visible
sector neutralino's energetic gamma ray production and subsequent absorption by
its counterpart in the hidden sector, where it causes an observable signature in
the XENON1T dark matter search experiment's data. The situation arises in a
specific Wilson-Chevalier configuration characterized by a low energy threshold
separating the two neutralinos and a heavy-hiding mass for the visible sector 
neutralino. Given these conditions, we demonstrate that the visible sector 
neutralino's decay can be detected via its influence on the XENON1T dark matter
search experiment's dark matter narrative, where we observe a considerable 4 
sigma increase in the credibility of a null result in the event of a decay, 
whereas a pure dark matter scenario yields a 2.7 sigma credibility. Additionally,
we detail a feasible detector design for detecting gamma rays originating from 
the high-latitude sky, capable of detecting similar signals in the IceCube experiment.

A comprehensive study of Fukaya categories and their relation to branched covers is presented, with a particular focus on how the genus of a graph influences this connection. Through the application of harmonic analytic techniques and the use of closed roots, we demonstrate that for any d-fold branched cover of a surface corresponding to a graph with g edges, the resulting Fukaya category exhibits a structural analogy equivalent to a (2d-1)(g-1)-dimensional Heisenberg product of copies of the Fukaya category of a d-fold branched cover of a genus g surface.

In stochastic optimization, progress can be made in either sample or parameter space, and these two modes are typically studied individually. However, our paper reveals that many methods are versatile and can accommodate both scenarios. We take a novel approach by categorizing and analyzing these methods based on their communication rounds, leading to a unified understanding of various methods like SDP and Catalyst. This new perspective enables us to improve existing algorithms by reducing the number of communication rounds. Specifically, we modify the first-order catalyst to minimize communication in the parameter space and still maintain convergence at the rate of second-order methods. Furthermore, we develop a dual-free catalyst for stochastic convex optimization that requires only a single interaction with the oracle, along with strong convergence results and theoretical proofs for these improved algorithms.

Our goal is to improve the State of the Art of Portuguese models by cross-training, where we found that multi-task training significantly boosts model performance in high-resource languages. By leveraging this knowledge through transfer learning, we can enhance the training of models for languages that share a common ancestor. To accomplish this, we selected three diverse Portuguese languages: Brazilian, European, and Amazonian, which are respectively based on European, the superdiverse dialects of Rio de Janeiro, and Tiriyó and Karipúna. These languages were annotated with POS tags, and we trained BERT-like models for each language. Next, we performed multi-task cross-training, involving the three languages, to adapt a model trained on Amazonian Portuguese. Interestingly, the results indicate that multi-task cross-training yields better results in Amazonian, while matching the performance of Brazilian and European Portuguese. Furthermore, we found that zero-shot POS tagging using T5 results in similar accuracy to the multi-task cross-training approach. By combining these methodologies, we are one step closer to developing a unified model that encompasses the diverse traits of all three Portuguese languages. Additionally, we are contributing towards more efficient training processes in NLP for languages that share a common origin.

In general, particle recoil sensitivity is optimized using observables such as total kinetic energy, momentum, or angle of incidence. However, in gaseous TPC detectors, which measure particle trajectories and recoil properties, their effectiveness in differentiating between electron and nuclear recoils is limited due to the spread in their distributions. New observables have been introduced that enhance the sensitivity of these detectors to low-energy events, particularly by analyzing the recoil's transverse movement at the point of interaction. Using simulations of WIMP interactions in various target materials, a comparison is made between the efficiency of the original recoil observables and the new transverse movement observables. It has been found that these novel variables substantially improve the efficiency of detecting WIMPs, reducing the required exposure to achieve a discovery in certain scenarios by as much as two orders of magnitude.

The evaluation of driver behavior is crucial for improving road safety and optimizing traffic flow. With the integration of transportation data, research has effectively quantified driver behavior. Yet, there is still a gap in understanding how driver behavior is influenced by external factors like weather and time of day. To bridge this gap, expert input is necessary to interpret driver behavior in various contexts. However, incorporating expert opinions is often constrained by time, expenses, and the need for significant technical infrastructure. Furthermore, conducting multiple inversions to refine predictions is impractical. To address these limitations, we propose a novel solution. Firstly, we model the behavior of drivers as responding to a set of environmental factors, including weather and time characteristics. Using data on driver behavior and its causes in Western Australia, we trained a machine learning model that accurately predicts driver behavior based on expert definitions. Using this model, we were able to incorporate expert input into our models, which significantly improved their accuracy in understanding driver behavior in multiple scenarios. Secondly, we developed a method to combine expert and quantitative knowledge into an model that effectively combines all available information. Through testing using various invasion scenarios, we found that our model, which combines expert and quantitative data, performs well in forecasting driver behavior and can substitute for human expertise in complex situations.

Despite notable progress in automatic scene text recognition, matching human performance remains a lingering challenge. This research introduces an updated Out-Of-Vocabulary dataset with diverse and challenging reading materials, surpassing previous offerings in terms of variability and visual abnormalities. The proposed dataset is anchored by AI-Benchmark, a newly established benchmark that assesses a model's ability to extract text information from images. Incorporating AI-Benchmark into the widely-used VRD dataset reveals a surprising disparity between existing evaluation methods and real-world capabilities. Furthermore, AI-Benchmark yields superior outcomes compared to other existing benchmarks. To bridge the gap between human and AI capabilities, this research investigates and showcases an advanced training pipeline. The study also explores several reading techniques and demonstrates their impact on reading performance. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Dataholt/AI-Benchmark.

Two fields of random variables, each defined within separate domains of general significance, can share similarities that appear statistically insignificant when measured individually. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach has been developed to gauge the similarity between such disparate fields by leveraging their respective contributions to a joint statistical outcome underpinning their shared physical principles. This methodology is exemplified through the analysis of two influential models from materials science and quantum physics.

We conducted an experiment using a tank with a circular shape, similar to
research by Avila et al. in 2006, at the Technological University of
M\"{o}ssen, utilizing a magnetic levitation system to reduce the impact of
disturbances on the fluid surface. This setup significantly minimized the
initial perturbations, as measured by the camera, allowing for undisturbed
experiments. Notably, we were able to maintain a stable, flat surface on the
fluid despite the rotating magnetic coil, which facilitates precise
measurements of the Taylor-Prandtl system. Furthermore, our study investigates
the dynamic processes occurring near the critical point where the system
transitions from a stable spiral pattern to a chaotic, chaotic spiral state.

Our findings reveal that SL2(Z) cusp forms possess L-functions (Hecke) characterized by a sharp "kettles" distribution within the critical strip, mirroring the pattern previously observed by Hughes for Spn(Z) cusp forms, while Hollaust has shown similarly concentrated behavior for GLn(Z) L-functions (Hecke). Notably, this pattern is also observed in higher rank forms for the symplectic group SL2n+1(Z), as shown by a combination of the tensor product and rank one scaling property, initially developed in relation to GLn(Z) scaling laws. These newly obtained laws also allow for derivation of rank one scaling property endpoints, initially observed by Hughes for SL2n+1(Z), as well as the prediction of further scaling property occurrences across various reductive groups. We computationally investigate a graphene ring connected to conventional metals and
nanowires via tight-binding model, exploring the impact of electronic structure on
electrical properties. The analysis of transmission and I-V curves reveals distinct
characteristics for graphene-conductor and conductor-graphene contacts. A finite bias
voltage generates a significant non-equilibrium charge distribution, leading to a flow
of current through the structure, and a notable influence of non-equilibrium dynamics on
Coulomb blockade in graphene nanowires coupled to conventional metals.

This study investigates the conditions under which the Krasnoselskii-type theorems can be applied to fixed point analysis in Banach lattices. Specifically, we demonstrate that weakly nonlinear and monotone operators meet the required compactness criteria in $l^p$-spaces for all p values between 1 and infinity. Additionally, we establish comparable conditions for operators with sublinear properties. As a result, we obtain multiple existence theorems for certain functional equations within Banach lattices.

Our primary objective is to investigate certain distinct graph characteristics including pancyclicness, Hamiltonian cycles, and optimal packings of pancyclic subgraphs. Furthermore, we aim to establish relationships between the independence number and the parameters mentioned earlier for specific graph types. In particular, we seek to determine the optimal value of the independence number for pancyclic graphs without odd-gons of a particular size. To achieve our goals, we will utilize the standard approach of constructing a pancyclic graph by adding vertices to a base partially pancyclic graph. Our findings will often reveal relationships between the independence number and the parameters of the resulting pancyclic graph. In the process of our investigation, we will also delve into unrelated characteristics such as the presence of odd-gons in graphs and the possibility of obtaining a cycle by combining two independent vertices with a vertex from a particular subset.

The course of partonic expansion and subsequent hadron evolution, governed by the equation of state (EoS), depends heavily on the initial conditions provided by the EoS. To analyze this phenomenon, we implement the EoS into PYTHIA, yielding two distinct versions: one that incorporates the EoS into PYTHIA's initial state and another that incorporates the EOS into PYTHIA's final state. By comparing the flow patterns of various versions, we are able to identify the initial effects on the development of pressure gradients, transverse flow velocities, and velocity profiles, which in turn affect the distribution of baryon abundance. Furthermore, we use versions of PYTHIA that incorporate the initial conditions to predict how this affects the abundance of various particles, including their spatial and momentum distributions, and the ratios of net protons to pions, which are relevant when analyzing net proton ratios in collision experiments.

In this research, SASK, an accelerated model reduction technique for partial differential equations, is introduced and applied to solve the 1D linear heat equation. By combining Physical Space Domain Decomposition with Approximate Bounded Error Mapping, SASK offers improved efficiency over conventional methods. To achieve further efficiency, SASK integrates the Strongly Orthogonal Sparse Basis technique for Fast Multipoint Condition approximation. A thorough theoretical framework, including convergence, error estimation, and linear complexity for solving time-dependent problems is established. Moreover, SASK's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparisons with traditional model reduction methods in several numerical experiments.

We employ the Fourier grid Hamiltonian method to calculate the vibration and translation of a water molecule in a homogeneous DC electric field up to approximately 1.0 GV/cm. The accuracy of our resonance parameters is verified through comparison with established literature values, with results showing significant improvement, with differences in energy levels reduced by multiple orders of magnitude. Additionally, we calculate the matrix elements involving vibration and translation and compare them to available experimental data, showing satisfactory agreement. Furthermore, using these results, we calculate the diffusion coefficient of water in air under electrically charged conditions and compare it to existing experimental data, showing sufficient correspondence at lower electric field intensities up to 700 V/cm. However, our calculations exceed experimental limits at higher electric fields. Finally, we extend the range of our calculations to 2.0 GV/cm by using the optimized Fourier grid steps from lower electric fields, demonstrating the effectiveness of the method.

This research expands upon the Sinkhorn algorithm in relation to the Schrödinger problem, primarily using real vectors as its cotangent map. We investigate the Sinkhorn algorithm at the cotangent level and discover under mild conditions, it yields a approximate solution to the original problem. We find this approximate solution possesses a regularization effect, which addresses singularities that render the original problem unsolvable. We provide a practical example to demonstrate how this algorithm can be applied to the Sinkhorn workflow and show that it can also provide a family of solutions to the original problem. We discover that OT and quantum entanglement have common mathematical structures which implies the Sinkhorn algorithm can be used to quantify entanglement. We use this algorithm to estimate the von Neumann entropy of a bipartite state.

A precise measurement of the cross-section for producing top-quark pairs in proton-proton collisions at a high energy ($\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV) is reported by the CMS experiment. The measurement is based on data collected in 2016, and it spans the production of top quarks with rapidity up to 2.4 and transverse momentum levels above 250 GeV, and it utilizes a peculiar signature with exactly one charged particle and four jets. It is found that the measured cross-section of 445 ± 70 (statistical) ± 44 (systematic) ± 12 (theoretical) +5-10 (luminosity) pb aligns with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics, demonstrating a notable agreement after accounting for statistical, systematic, and luminosity uncertainties. Additionally, the measured cross-section of 445 ± 70 (statistical) ± 44 (systematic) ± 12 (theoretical) +5-10 (luminosity) pb aligns with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics, and these results provide a valuable validation of the accuracy of non-perturbative probability distributions in the initiation of strong forces at high energies.

Our research examines how the entanglement in a disordered spin system develops over time when a central qubit or cavity is present.  Through both numerical and theoretical analyses, we discover that having a central qubit connected to the other spins causes the entanglement to grow asymptotically as the system size increases, whereas the entanglement remains constant if the central qubit is not magnetically susceptible.  Furthermore, our research verifies that the asymptotic values can be attained relatively quickly and determines how long it takes based on the level of disorder present.  These discoveries are relevant to a specific experimental technique known as cavity magnon spin squeezing, as well as other methods that rely on entanglement.

This study seeks to identify specific conditions under which the generalized Bessel function, given by $G_{r}(z)$ for $|z| < 1$, exhibits Janowski convexity and starlikeness properties in the unit disk. The work relies on certain restrictions applied to the real parameter $\alpha$ and the complex parameter $r$. The findings are then compared with previously established criteria for Bessel functions of the first kind, as provided by R. Ghoshal and A. Deep.

The COVID-19 pandemic underwent distinct phases and responses across the globe, resulting in varying forms of mobility restriction. A closer look at mobile phone data from ten countries and four continents reveals how these restrictions influenced people's movement, highlighting differences in urban encounter diversity and community resilience during the pandemic's distinct phases. While initial responses often minimized individual mobility, subsequent phases exhibited increased mobility and frequency, differing significantly between countries. Furthermore, our analysis explores long-term effects of the pandemic on urban encounters and community resilience, suggesting a complex pattern of adaptation marked by prolonged periods of minimal change followed by sudden increases in urban activity.

Serial and parallel mass storage implementations of an explicit FSMSN method, developed for solving the steady-state form of the NEA benchmark case, demonstrate high performance and efficiency. By dividing time and spatial domains into equal parts, this approach avoids complex sub-step calculations, unlike the traditional Sequential Fully Implicit solution strategy. Measured in terms of wall clock time, FSMSN's performance improves twice as much as Sequential Fully Implicit, and it achieves nearly equivalent speed-up rates in parallel processing.

A chiral optical cavity made from anisotropic material is proposed to enhance a light-matter interaction between identical single chiral particles and the cavity mode. Unlike previous chiral cavities made from bipartite objects, this design achieves enhanced coupling between a chiral emitter and the cavity without requiring interaction between the two parts of the cavity. As a result, the cavity's ability to select and enhance specific optical transitions in a chiral molecule is improved. Furthermore, the presence of the cavity's handedness symmetric mode strongly enhances a process called superradiance, without the need for external manipulation. This research introduces a chiral optical cavity designed to enhance light-matter interaction, offering opportunities to study processes faster than previously possible, and observe interactions that would otherwise be too weak to measure.

Two-dimensional anti de-Sitter spaces within the context of two-dimensional string theory hold significance due to their connection to quantum cosmology and the semiclassical limit. A novel construction method is introduced that facilitates the creation of solutions describing $SO(d, 2)$-invariant anti de-Sitter spaces encompassing $S^{d-1}$ and carrying a central charge. These newly found solutions can easily be modified to include a non-zero cosmological constant and describe a universe with bounded spatial dimensions, akin to de Sitter space in a mirror image sense. Furthermore, observing scattering processes in the CFT (conformal field theory) on this constructed anti de-Sitter background reveals a mirror-like reflection of particles across the anti de-Sitter boundary, consistent with expectations of an expanding de Sitter universe's replica symmetry.

Researchers have attempted to obtain an analytical solution for the stable Alcubierre warp drive, using a vacuum interior and massive energy wrapped around it, within a flat spacetime framework. Although previous studies found no stable solution in this setup, we have rediscovered the need for matter or energy configured in specific ways to achieve stability, rather than the previous assumption that only gravitational waves matter. Our study suggests that a massive shell or string placed outside the warp bubble could provide the required configuration. However, further analysis reveals that in a warp drive setup, energy transfer due to perturbations of massive sources does not conform to d'Alembert's equation as assumed in previous studies, leading to incorrect assessment of stability. Our findings correct these errors and their impact on previous conclusions.

This research introduces the GUIDES framework, designed to assist urban planners in making more informed, data-driven decisions about the complex network of underground infrastructure systems (UIS). The proposed framework leverages a comprehensiveUIS model, incorporating physical projections and future scenarios, as well as advanced computer simulations and predictive modeling. This enables UIS components to be assessed under various future conditions. The GUIDES framework facilitates multiscale and multitype UIS component planning, while also allowing for cisGIS and caBIG data management capabilities. The system includes a range of tools, including GIS, UIS data, UIS models, and analytical models. Additionally, it incorporates external databases and decision support models. By integrating UIS modeling and planning, the GUIDES framework aims to enhance the overall efficiency and effectiveness of UIS systems. The planning capabilities offered by the GUIDES framework are demonstrated using a small UIS system in the city of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

To find the ambient heating rate of a two-dimensional Coulomb crystal in a Penning trap, we employed a precise statistical method. A uniform gas of electrons was created in the trap and the crystal's electron distribution was measured and analyzed over time. By utilizing the characteristics of Coulomb clusters and their evolution, we were able to determine the rate of ambient heating. Our experiments indicated that the heating rate exceeded the theoretical limit of spontaneous three-body recombination, leading to the conclusion that the dominant source of ambient heating is the collision of electrons with residual gas particles in the trap. Moreover, we calculated the ambient temperature based on the measured heating rate and compared it with the expected value from previous research. Finally, we discussed the potential implications of our findings on future electron qubit scalability.

Tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, particularly when combined with scanning tunneling microscopy, allows for the examination of EM-enhanced electromagnetic properties at the atomic level as well as the study of chemical reactions on a molecular scale. The EM properties manifested in TEERS arise primarily due to plasmonic enhancements triggered by the TM polarized electromagnetic field near the tip. In contrast, the chemical effect inherent in LEIRS is driven by the E polarized field. To fully utilize the capabilities of TEERS, it's crucial to understand the distinct effects contributed by the TM and CM polarizations. This knowledge is essential for optimizing responses from electrons and photons in various photoemission experiments and Raman spectroscopy. Through numerical simulations involving a highly curved metal tip under bias, our research reveals the intricate interplay between EM and chemical effects in TEERS. Moreover, our findings suggest that the EM effect can be selectively amplified through adjustments to the bias voltage. This discovery provides a framework for maximizing the potential of TEERS and enables the precise labeling of molecules using optical Raman spectroscopy, thus simulating the behavior of LEIRS in the process.

Our past research into Aluminum-Manganese Events in the Pinwheel galaxy (M51) has led to new insights and search strategies for these events in the Spiral galaxies (Sbc-Sd). The key factors for a successful search are the galaxy's age, metal abundance, presence of young star formations, dust, and a reasonable distance. We recommend the use of optical-NIR distance measurements to filter candidates. We have identified five candidate events in the UGC1213 and NGC4538 galaxies, all of which are relatively close and young (age=10-500 Myr). The events' metal abundances are either low or unknown. We suggest that the events in the NGC4538 galaxy are likely to be the result of a single supernova event. We also found no clear evidence of the events in the UGC1213 galaxies. Our findings provide a range for the time interval between two major AME events in the Pinwheel galaxy (12-690 Myr) as well as the proportion of spiral galaxies that experience AME events (0.8-1).

We employed mantle X-ray photoluminescence spectroscopy to investigate the displacement of nitrogen K-edge in ammonium sulfate as it undergoes the ferroelectric phase transition, and observed an entropy increase per formula unit of 0.37 R upon this transition. Since the ammonium ion's vibrational modes are integral to the crystal's symmetry, we attribute the observed entropy change primarily to the disorder introduced in this ion. Additionally, we found that this entropy change is largely offset by an accompanying entropy loss associated with the disordering of sulfate ions, allowing the total crystal entropy to remain stable throughout the phase transition.

Individual variation in the frequency of probability-matching strategies has often been linked to expected payoffs in previous research, however we argue that this is due, in part, to a larger issue. We propose that people who frequently engage in probability-matching tend to put more emphasis on past losses while learning new tasks because they give these losses more weight in their calculations than they do for gains. We support our hypothesis using a cognitive model of how people process feedback, and further verify our assumptions through a series of additional studies that also reveal more about the underlying principles. We found that people seeking probability-matching strategies tend to have slower learning rates when confronted with new tasks because they overemphasize past losses which leads to more extreme reactions to both gains and losses. In contrast, those who rarely engage in probability-matching behaviors, instead focusing on the effects of their most recent actions which we found to be less extreme in their reactions to either.

We propose a concept of interrelated quantum states, referred to as a cohesive set, where distinct configurations exhibit shared nonlocal or contextuality characteristics. We identify two types of coherent groups: one comprised of local state collections and another consisting of robust contextuality collections. Our research reveals that the dimensions of global contextuality spaces can be determined through the evaluation of specific invariants, namely, the chromatic and orthochromatic numbers. In particular, we demonstrate that an integer division of $n$ by $d$ is a prerequisite and upper limit for achieving certain values for global contextuality numbers from individual sets of size $d$. Additionally, we establish a standardized protocol for experimenting with quantum systems consisting of identical, repeating components, like atoms in rings or loops. This protocol, referred to as the Gapped Ring Experiment, is capable of reaching an arbitrarily high global contextuality score, yet constrained by the impossibility of reaching a perfect score. Our findings also encompass the fundamental principles governing strong contextuality spaces associated with quantum systems comprising repeated copies of arbitrary quantum systems, referred to as the Multiple Gapped Copies Framework.

For the widespread adoption of quantum computers, error mitigation strategies are required that are both efficient and applicable to large-scale devices.  We propose a novel unfolding method to tackle measurement errors that can process multiple influences without the need for prior knowledge.  Combining this method with Bayesian unfolding allows us to unfold experimental data obtained from inferences influenced by various noise sources.  Our proposal utilizes a pyQBD algorithm to facilitate the learning of quantum density operators, making it possible to unfold measurements based on arbitrary priors.  Moreover, incorporating an iterative Bayesian learning process enables the unfolding to adapt to changing noise sources, even in real-time.  Our experiments on IBMQ devices demonstrate the capacity of our unfolding method to accurately reproduce input states, and the advantages of combining it with Bayesian unfolding for error mitigation.  We demonstrate that folding and unfolding is a covariant operation, allowing us to achieve this goal even when dealing with circuits that have no unitary invariant structure.

In social learning settings, humans demonstrate a capacity for reverse-engineering a robot's decision-making processes. However, the impact of efficiency when a robot's task mappings are unintentionally revealed remains unclear. This study investigates how other tasks are affected when a robot's task mappings are unintentionally shared. We designed a syntax-based assembly task mimicking a real-world manufacturing setting, involving humans, a robot, and shared workspace. Two participants were involved - one human instructed the robot and the other human monitored. We varied the degree to which the monitoring human understood how the robot was selecting tasks, and measured how this affected performance on a different task with similar characteristics. We found that when a robot's task mappings were easily inferred, this negatively impacted our subject's efficiency in a similar tasks setting, although we also found that most learning occurred initially and subsequent training was minimal. This implies that although a robot's process transparency might decrease efficiency, this efficiency loss could be minimized by delaying the revelation of the robot's process to the monitoring human. This is an abstract of a paper that will be presented at the 15th annual ACM/IGAC conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems.

Global metric maps are efficient for navigating complex environments but have limitations when accounting for the impact of obstacles on navigation. A new topological representation, HiTMap, is proposed, incorporating environmental constraints to facilitate safer navigation. By integrating Euclidean rewards and fractional harmonic rewards, HiTMap captures the importance of both distance and obstacle avoidance, and demonstrates better convergence to a more relevant representation for navigation. A new algorithm, HiTMap Update, is also developed to facilitate the parameter tuning of HiTMap, and is evaluated using a simulated robotic scenario, with results indicating that HiTMap yields more robust performance than traditional global metric maps.

A novel two-dimensional Z-complementary array code set (ZCACS) is designed 
using a novel construction approach for generating code sequences that are not 
inversely related to each other, expanding the traditional Boolean generalized 
functions method. Based on this, a few instances of two-dimensional ZCACS are 
presently illustrated with different Boolean functions.

A comprehensive approach to low-dose computed tomography (LD-CT) image enhancement is proposed, addressing the two primary challenges of image acquisition, namely, the type-dependent noise pattern and limited protraction data. While traditional methods effectively manage one type of noise, they fall short with its opposite. Furthermore, existing techniques often rely on extensive a posteriori parameter fine-tuning for optimal image quality. Our novel, versatile image reconstruction model successfully handles diverse noise patterns and limited protraction data with minimal required adjustments. Its adaptability is attributed to the wavelet transform, which separates signal components from noise, enabling their independent processing. Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on real CT scans and simulated datasets, yielding superior image quality in comparison to state-of-the-art methods.

For galactic magnetic fields, the local Taylor's model is often used to simulate the magnetic field's direction based on the positions of pulsars. Nevertheless, this simple analysis is insufficient, as variations in the magnetic field's strength still need to be determined. Therefore, an enhanced model has been developed by integrating the local Taylor's model within the context of an isotropic Gaussian gap, resulting in the "effective gap width" approach. By analyzing the magnetic field's role in the termination shock, this methodology is applied to 15 pulsars, yielding more accurate predictions regarding the geodesic drift and pulsar speed through the "effective galactic frame drift velocity." Consequently, this new model is shown to be more precise than the traditional local model based on Taylor's approach.

Contextual named entity retrieval systems use contextual, or context-free,
named entity discovery and disambiguation to retrieve entities from free
text, with context provided through a query or from a relevant entity previously
identified. A key aspect of these systems is the ability to gather user feedback,
processing it into training data for training contextual search models. However,
existing research has focused solely on the initial search process, neglecting
subsequent retrieval tasks. This study addresses this gap by introducing a
multi-stage contextual search process starting with initial search, followed by
recall and re-ranking based on user feedback and relevant entity attributes.
Our findings indicate that our proposed method outperforms the current
state-of-the-art in recall and re-ranking, according to metrics like mean
average precision and expected recall. Moreover, user studies demonstrate
substantial user satisfaction improvements in over 30%. Our code and data
are publicly available via GitHub at the address: https://github.com/mdillon/Contextual_NER

This document offers recommendations for creating temporal data visualizations and suggests ways to enhance them by adding interactive features. A comprehensive overview of temporal data and visualization elements is provided, along with specific suggestions for displaying temporal data. Additionally, we discuss the potential for incorporating advanced interactive elements, such as linking temporal plots to other views or allowing users to manipulate temporal scales. A proposed research area is presented, focusing on democratizing interactive temporal data visualization expertise.

Recent breakthroughs in heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) have led them to become promising solutions for modeling associations within Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which contain valuable information on patient relationships and various clinical data. However, current HGNNs have limitations when dealing with patient identity and clinical knowledge graph structures, which restrict their ability to generalize patient similarities beyond similar cases, leading to subpar performance on new unseen patients. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative HGNN called Meta-EHR-GCN, which combines graph convolutional networks with meta-learning on node embeddings, along with a patient-relation-aware strategy that boosts the model's capacity for generalizing knowledge to new unseen patients. Our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art HGNNs, achieving improved results on both synthetic and real-world EHRs in terms of both accuracy and clinical generalizability.

Classical simulations of electrolytes reveal unique behaviors. The system's dynamics are dominated by two length scales - the cutoff radius c and the ionic size. For distances greater than the size of the ions, the system's properties resemble those of a continuous system, where its characteristics are defined by a relatively straightforward equation. As ionic size increases, the characteristics of the continuous system are found to undergo a significant change. The equation that defines the characteristics of the continuous system needs to be adjusted by adding an additional parameter to accurately describe the system, where the added parameter is directly influenced by the variance of the electrostatic potential between two ions, the distance between which is much larger than their size. The added parameter is further influenced by the faster it reacts to changes in the system. The equation that needs to be added also contains another parameter - the transverse speed of the ion, the influence of which can be reduced in the equation if the reaction speed of the ion is much faster than the frequency of the oscillation, the magnitude of which can be determined through another relationship. The relationship that needs to be established to determine the magnitude of the oscillation frequency involves considering an ion in an infinite bath of the same electrolyte, where the frequency can be determined through a much simpler relationship. Understanding end user stated and implied requirements is a challenge in software requirement engineering. Various studies have been conducted to address this problem, involving the analysis of text data from sources such as PR2 and TRECQSR, to develop models for requirement extraction. In our study, PR2 data was utilized to evaluate BERT, compared to fastText and ELMo, to assess its efficacy in requirement extraction tasks. We also established a baseline for measuring performance of requirement extraction tasks on the PR2 dataset. Our work also analyzed the effectiveness of pre-trained models based on different tokenization techniques, such as WordPiece and fastText, on the requirement extraction task. In our study, BERT was found to outperform ELMo and fastText models in requirement extraction, achieving better results based on various evaluation metrics, including micro average accuracy, F1 score, AUC, and ROCAUC. Our study further observed that pre-trained models can learn to compensate for limitations of existing studies, such as data splitting and feature engineering. In our study, our own dataset-based feature engineering process was developed to take advantage of the BERT model's ability to learn features in-depth, a capability lacking in earlier studies. Our analysis also showed that the BERT model can perform well even with minimal features, significantly surpassing existing studies.
